Key findings relevant to biosecurity: - AI models have "far surpassed PhD-level expertise in chemistry and biology" (per AISI blog and factsheet summaries, December 2025). - Self-replication evaluation success rates went from 5% to 60% between 2023 and 2025. - Models are improving at cyber tasks across all difficulty levels. - The report synthesizes evaluations across cyber, chemistry & biology, autonomy, and software engineering domains. The AISI's role as a government-backed independent evaluator gives its findings significant weight. If AISI publicly identifies capabilities in a future evaluation that meet a lab's own highest-tier threshold, the lab faces strong pressure to acknowledge this. The AISI has tested more than 30 frontier models and continues to expand its evaluation program. International AI Safety Report 2026 (published February 2026): This report, produced by a multi-stakeholder group with UK AISI secretariat support, provides critical evidence [349e31]: - Frontier models now match or exceed expert performance on benchmarks measuring biological weapons-relevant knowledge. - A recent model outperformed 94% of domain experts at troubleshooting virology lab protocols. - Leading AI systems have approached or exceeded expert baselines on benchmarks for "Biological weapons of mass destruction knowledge" and "Multimodal virology troubleshooting." - The report documents that OpenAI designated GPT-5-Thinking and ChatGPT-Agent as "High capability" under their Preparedness Framework, applying heightened safeguards. - Anthropic released Claude Opus 4 at AI Safety Level 3 (ASL-3) under their Responsible Scaling Policy, noting they could not rule out that the model had reached relevant capability thresholds. - Google DeepMind's Gemini 2.5 Deep Think triggered a "Critical Capability Levels" early warning alert for chemical and biological risk. These findings demonstrate that independent evaluators are already documenting capabilities approaching the highest risk tiers. METR METR (formerly ARC Evals) maintains an ongoing index of frontier safety policies. As of December 2025, METR tracked 12 companies' safety frameworks [e51f3e]. METR: - Conducts independent evaluations of autonomous capabilities of frontier models, including partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. - Published a comprehensive reference for frontier AI safety regulations (January 29, 2026) mapping regulatory requirements. - Documents common elements across safety policies, including capability thresholds for biological weapons development. - Measures task-completion time horizons for public frontier models. METR's independent evaluations create a check on lab self-assessments. If METR's evaluations reveal capabilities beyond what a lab has publicly acknowledged, this creates an accountability gap. --- ### 2. Regulatory Bodies California SB 53 (Effective January 1, 2026) Governor Newsom signed SB 53 on September 29, 2025. Key requirements active during the March–December 2026 window: - Safety Protocols: Frontier developers must implement and publish safety protocols to manage and mitigate catastrophic risk before training new frontier models. - Transparency Reports: Developers must publish a transparency report on their public website before or concurrently with deploying new frontier models. - Risk Assessment: Developers must conduct ongoing risk assessments, including for capabilities that could facilitate mass harm. - Incident Reporting: Developers must report "critical safety incidents" to the California Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES) within 15 days of discovery, or within 24 hours if the incident is ongoing. - Whistleblower Protections: Strong protections for employees involved in risk assessment or management, prohibiting retaliation against covered employees who report safety concerns. - Enforcement: Civil penalty for noncompliance enforced by the Attorney General. - Applicability: Applies to "large frontier developers" creating frontier models above certain capability thresholds. SB 53 is sometimes called "transparency without substantive safety mandates" (per Stanford Law gap analysis, January 11, 2026), but its transparency and incident reporting requirements could compel disclosure even if the law doesn't mandate specific risk-level classifications. EU AI Act – General-Purpose AI Obligations (Enforcement from August 2, 2026) Key dates within the forecast window: - August 2, 2025: GPAI model obligations became applicable. Code of Practice signatories expected to comply. - August 2, 2026: European AI Office begins enforcement of all GPAI obligations. Fines can be imposed for non-compliance. This is also the date when the bulk of remaining high-risk AI system obligations take effect. For GPAI models with systemic risk (which includes frontier models above certain capability thresholds): - Providers must conduct model evaluations, including adversarial testing. - Providers must assess and mitigate systemic risks, including through red-teaming. - Providers must report serious incidents and ensure cybersecurity protections. - The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice (finalized mid-2025) covers transparency, copyright compliance, and systemic risk management. The shift from voluntary compliance to enforced obligations in August 2026 creates a significant new pressure point. New York RAISE Act (Signed into law; effective July 1, 2027) While the RAISE Act's effective date falls outside the March–December 2026 window, its signing creates anticipatory pressure. Key provisions: - Requires 72-hour incident reporting (faster than SB 53's 15 days). - Imposes transparency, compliance, safety, and reporting requirements on frontier model developers. - Signals growing state-level regulatory momentum. --- ### 3. Whistleblowers and Leaks Historical Context: - In July 2024, OpenAI whistleblowers filed a disclosure with the SEC alleging the company issued "overly restrictive employment, severance and nondisclosure agreements" that barred staff from airing safety risks (Washington Post, July 13, 2024). - Former OpenAI employees led a public push to protect AI whistleblowers. - OpenAI subsequently published its full whistleblowing policy—the only major lab to do so—but reportedly only after media exposure of restrictive clauses [97f06f]. Current Landscape (2025–2026): - The AI Whistleblower Initiative (AIWI) published an assessment of OpenAI's 2024 Raising Concerns Policy in January 2026. - A digital safe platform (PSST) has launched to allow international AI workers to anonymously report safety concerns (Rest of World, 2026). - California SB 53's whistleblower protections (effective January 1, 2026) provide legal backing for employees who report safety concerns at frontier AI labs. - The Future of Life Institute's AI Safety Index found that only OpenAI has published its full whistleblowing policy, indicating a major gap at other labs [97f06f]. The strengthening of legal protections and institutional infrastructure makes it increasingly feasible for insiders with knowledge of highest-tier evaluations to disclose them, either through official channels or leaks. --- ### 4. Biosecurity Incidents Current State (as of March 2026): No publicly known AI-enabled biosecurity incident has occurred. However, the threat landscape is escalating: - The International AI Safety Report 2026 documents that AI models can provide "tacit knowledge" relevant to biological weapons—practical expertise usually gained through hands-on laboratory experience—to novices [349e31]. - Labs have already triggered elevated internal risk alerts related to biosecurity (documented in Box 2.2 of the International AI Safety Report 2026) [349e31]. - A RAND-NTI workshop at the 2025 AI Action Summit specifically addressed biosecurity governance challenges from AI advances. - The Council on Strategic Risks published its "2025 AIxBio Wrapped" (December 22, 2025) reviewing AI-biosecurity milestones. - CSIS published analysis on opportunities to strengthen US biosecurity from AI-enabled bioterrorism (2025), including noting that one lab stated it would treat its agent model as "highly capable" in biological assessments (July 2025). - Academic research continues to demonstrate increasing model capabilities: mid-2025 studies measured LLM assistance on novice performance in biology-relevant tasks (arXiv, February 2026). A biosecurity incident—even a near-miss, a demonstration by red-teamers, or a published paper showing successful AI-assisted bioweapons synthesis steps—could create overwhelming public and political pressure for formal highest-tier classification. --- ### 5. Civil Society Organizations Future of Life Institute (FLI): - Published the AI Safety Index (Summer 2025, July 17, 2025), grading seven frontier AI companies across 35 indicators [97f06f]. - Found the industry "fundamentally unprepared" for its stated AGI ambitions. - Grades: Anthropic (C+), OpenAI (C), Google DeepMind (C-), Meta (D). - Only Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind conduct substantive dangerous-capability testing (including bio- and cyber-terrorism). - Anthropic is the only lab conducting human-participant bio-risk trials. - Explicitly called for legally binding safety standards, arguing "self-regulation simply isn't working." - The Index serves as a public accountability mechanism, identifying specific areas where each lab falls short. Other Civil Society Actors: - Stanford Law School published a gap analysis of California's SB 53 (January 11, 2026), identifying it as "transparency without substantive safety mandates." - Council on Strategic Risks maintains ongoing AIxBio monitoring and published year-end reviews and projections. - Concordia AI published a Frontier AI Risk Management Framework (v1.0, July 2025). - Oxford AI Governance Initiative published "Open Problems in Frontier AI Risk Management" (February 2026). - Frontier Model Forum published issue briefs on Frontier AI Biosafety Thresholds, helping define what constitutes various risk tiers. These organizations create sustained reputational pressure through public reports, media engagement, and policy advocacy. Their monitoring makes it difficult for labs to maintain internally recognized highest-tier classifications without eventual public disclosure. --- ### Regulatory Deadlines Within the March 19 – December 31, 2026 Window | Date | Requirement | Source | |------|-------------|--------| | Already in effect (Jan 1, 2026) | California SB 53: Safety protocols, transparency reports, incident reporting, whistleblower protections | California Legislature | | August 2, 2026 | EU AI Act: European AI Office begins enforcement of all GPAI model obligations, including systemic risk evaluations and incident reporting; high-risk AI system obligations take effect | EU AI Act | | Ongoing | UK AISI continues evaluations and may publish additional reports during this period | UK Government | | Ongoing | METR continues independent evaluations and regulatory monitoring | METR | --- ### Summary of Pressure Dynamics The external pressure environment in the March–December 2026 window is substantially stronger than any prior period due to: 1. Legal teeth: SB 53 is in force; EU AI Act enforcement begins August 2, 2026. 2. Independent evidence: AISI and METR continue to publish findings that could contradict lab self-assessments. 3. Whistleblower infrastructure: Legal protections, institutional platforms, and precedent cases exist. 4. Rising capabilities: Labs have already triggered elevated (though not highest-tier) biosecurity alerts, and capability trajectories suggest further escalation. 5. Civil society accountability: Public grading, gap analyses, and media engagement create reputational costs for under-classification. The most likely external pressure pathway to a highest-tier classification would be: (a) an independent evaluator publicly identifies capabilities exceeding a lab's own threshold, creating an accountability gap the lab must address; or (b) a whistleblower discloses internal evaluations showing highest-tier capabilities that were not publicly acknowledged; or (c) model capabilities demonstrably exceed biosecurity thresholds during mandatory evaluations required by newly enforceable regulations.

Refined question Stage 2

Question Title: Will the U.S. President sign into law federal legislation mandating nucleic acid synthesis screening for all synthesis providers (not limited to federally funded orders) between March 19, 2026 and December 31, 2026 (11:59 PM UTC)? --- Background: Nucleic acid synthesis screening is a biosecurity measure in which providers of synthetic DNA and RNA check incoming orders against databases of known pathogen sequences to prevent malicious actors from obtaining dangerous biological materials. The current U.S. screening regime is governed by the "Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening," released by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) in September 2024 (https://aspr.hhs.gov/S3/Documents/OSTP-Nucleic-Acid-Synthesis-Screening-Framework-Sep2024.pdf). This Framework defines key terms including "Sequence of Concern" (broadly, a nucleotide sequence that is a best match to a sequence from a federally regulated pathogen or toxin) and establishes requirements for sequence-level and customer-level screening. Critically, the 2024 OSTP Framework applies only as a condition of receiving U.S. governmental life sciences research funding — it does not mandate screening for privately funded or commercial orders. On May 5, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14292, "Improving the Safety and Security of Biological Research" (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/05/08/2025-08266/improving-the-safety-and-security-of-biological-research), which directed OSTP to develop a strategy that "shall include actions to achieve comprehensive, scalable, and verifiable nucleic acid synthesis screening in non-federally funded" contexts. However, this executive order does not itself create a legal mandate for universal screening — it only directs the development of a strategy. On January 29, 2026, Senators Tom Cotton (R-AR) and Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) introduced S. 3741, the "Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026" (https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/3741/all-info). The bill would require the Secretary of Commerce to promulgate regulations requiring all nucleic acid synthesis providers to screen orders — not just those involving federal funding. The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on January 29, 2026. As of March 19, 2026, no further committee action (hearing, markup, or vote) has been reported. The bill has bipartisan sponsorship and endorsements from organizations including the Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI), the Federation of American Scientists (FAS), and the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. No companion bill has been identified in the House of Representatives. The FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), signed into law on December 18, 2025, included the BIOSECURE Act (restricting federal procurement from certain biotechnology companies of concern) but did not include a universal DNA synthesis screening mandate. Historically, most bills introduced in Congress do not advance beyond committee referral. However, S. 3741 has notable bipartisan support, alignment with the executive branch's stated goals in EO 14292, and endorsements from prominent biosecurity organizations. The 119th Congress (2025–2026) expires in January 2027. --- Resolution Criteria: This question resolves Yes if, between March 19, 2026 (00:00 UTC) and December 31, 2026 (23:59 UTC), the President of the United States signs into law any federal legislation that includes a legally binding requirement for nucleic acid synthesis providers operating in the United States to screen synthesis orders against sequences of concern, where this requirement applies to all orders — not solely those funded by U.S. government research funding. Specific clarifications: 1. Definition of "pass": The legislation must be signed into law by the President, or enacted through a congressional override of a presidential veto. Mere passage by one or both chambers of Congress does not suffice. 2. Definition of "DNA synthesis screening": For purposes of this question, "nucleic acid synthesis screening" refers to the practice of checking orders for synthetic nucleic acids (DNA or RNA) against databases of sequences associated with pathogens, toxins, or other biological agents of concern, and conducting follow-up screening (including customer verification) when a potential match is identified, consistent with the definition in the 2024 OSTP Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening (https://aspr.hhs.gov/S3/Documents/OSTP-Nucleic-Acid-Synthesis-Screening-Framework-Sep2024.pdf). 3. "Universal" requirement: The mandate must apply to all commercial nucleic acid synthesis providers operating in the United States (i.e., it is not limited to providers serving federally funded customers or to federally funded orders only). It is sufficient if the law requires all providers to screen all orders; it is not necessary that the law separately mandate obligations on purchasers. 4. Broader legislation: The requirement need not be enacted as a standalone bill. If the relevant DNA synthesis screening mandate is included as a provision within a broader bill (e.g., an omnibus spending bill, a National Defense Authorization Act, or any other legislative vehicle), that satisfies the resolution criteria, provided the signed law contains a legally binding universal screening requirement as defined above. 5. Regulatory delegation: If the signed legislation directs a federal agency (e.g., the Department of Commerce) to promulgate regulations establishing universal screening, this counts — even if the implementing regulations have not yet been finalized by December 31, 2026 — as long as the statute itself creates a binding legal mandate for universal screening (not merely a directive to "study" or "develop a strategy" for screening). Primary Resolution Source: The bill's status page on Congress.gov (https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/3741/all-info) or, if enacted through a different legislative vehicle, the relevant enrolled bill page on Congress.gov or the published law in the Federal Register. Credible news reporting from outlets such as Reuters, the Associated Press, or domain-specific outlets may serve as supplementary sources.

OVERALL_RISK: MEDIUM ## Edge Case Analysis for DNA Synthesis Screening Legislation Question ### Edge Case 1: Legislation Directs Agency to "Promulgate Regulations" but with Discretionary Language - SCENARIO: Congress passes and the President signs a bill (e.g., S. 3741 or a modified version) that directs the Secretary of Commerce to "promulgate regulations" for universal screening, but uses permissive language like "may" instead of "shall," or includes a clause allowing the Secretary to determine the "appropriate scope" of screening requirements — making it ambiguous whether a binding legal mandate for universal screening has been created, or merely discretionary rulemaking authority. - SEVERITY: HIGH — S. 3741 as introduced already delegates rulemaking to the Secretary of Commerce, and legislative compromises frequently introduce discretionary language. The FAS characterization of S. 3741 as focused on "assessment" and "accountability questions" rather than a binding screening mandate raises questions about whether the bill as written would clearly satisfy the resolution criteria [c5d524]. - FIX: Add language specifying: "The statute must contain language that unambiguously requires (using mandatory terms such as 'shall') the promulgation of regulations establishing universal screening. If the statute uses permissive language (e.g., 'may') or grants broad discretion to an agency to determine whether or the extent to which universal screening is required, the question resolves NO." ### Edge Case 2: Legislation Creates a "Study" or "Strategy Development" Requirement Disguised as a Mandate - SCENARIO: The President signs legislation that directs an agency to "develop a comprehensive strategy for achieving universal nucleic acid synthesis screening" and to "issue implementing guidance" — similar to the approach in EO 14292 — but frames it as a statutory directive rather than an executive order. Forecasters disagree on whether this constitutes a "binding legal mandate for universal screening" or is merely a legislatively codified directive to study/strategize, analogous to what the resolution criteria explicitly exclude. - SEVERITY: HIGH — EO 14292 already directs OSTP to develop a strategy that "shall include actions to achieve comprehensive, scalable, and verifiable nucleic acid synthesis screening in non-federally funded" contexts. If Congress codifies this same approach into statute, reasonable people could disagree about whether a statutory "develop a strategy" directive is qualitatively different from an executive "develop a strategy" directive, especially since it carries the force of law. - FIX: Add language: "The statute must impose or direct the imposition of screening obligations directly on synthesis providers (or direct an agency to do so with a mandatory compliance deadline). A statute that merely directs a federal agency to 'study,' 'develop a strategy for,' 'assess the feasibility of,' or 'issue recommendations regarding' universal screening does not resolve YES, regardless of how strongly the statute is worded." ### Edge Case 3: Universal Requirement Applies Only to DNA, Not RNA - SCENARIO: The President signs a bill that mandates screening for all synthetic DNA orders but does not explicitly cover synthetic RNA orders. The resolution criteria define "nucleic acid synthesis screening" as covering "DNA or RNA," but the enacted law's scope is limited to DNA synthesis providers. - SEVERITY: MEDIUM — Most legislative discussions and the S. 3741 bill text focus on "nucleic acid synthesis" broadly, but political compromises or drafting choices could narrow the scope to DNA only, since DNA synthesis is the more established commercial market and RNA synthesis poses somewhat different technical challenges. - FIX: Add language: "The legislation must mandate screening for synthetic nucleic acid orders broadly, covering at minimum synthetic DNA. If the legislation covers DNA synthesis but explicitly excludes RNA synthesis, the question still resolves YES, provided the DNA screening mandate is universal. However, if the legislation covers only a narrow subcategory of nucleic acid synthesis (e.g., only gene-length sequences above a certain base-pair threshold), the question resolves NO." ### Edge Case 4: Legislation Contains Exemptions That Undermine "Universal" Coverage - SCENARIO: The signed law mandates screening for all synthesis providers but includes significant exemptions — for example, exempting providers below a revenue threshold, providers of oligonucleotides below a certain length (e.g., under 200 base pairs), providers of benchtop synthesis equipment (as opposed to mail-order synthesis services), or orders placed by government agencies themselves. Forecasters disagree about whether a mandate with such carve-outs qualifies as applying to "all orders." - SEVERITY: MEDIUM — The 2024 OSTP Framework itself contains length-based thresholds and exemptions for certain types of sequences. Legislative versions are likely to include similar practical carve-outs. The California bill AB 1864 already addresses "benchtop nucleic acid synthesis equipment" separately, suggesting this is a live regulatory distinction. - FIX: Add language: "The mandate qualifies as 'universal' if it applies to all commercial nucleic acid synthesis providers regardless of whether their customers are federally funded. Reasonable technical exemptions (e.g., for sequences below a specific length threshold, consistent with the OSTP Framework) do not disqualify the mandate. However, if the exemptions are so broad as to effectively limit the mandate to a subset of the market (e.g., only providers above a certain size, or only certain types of synthesis), the question resolves NO." ### Edge Case 5: Screening Mandate Included in Broader Bill but with Delayed Effective Date Beyond 2026 - SCENARIO: The President signs an omnibus or NDAA that contains a universal synthesis screening provision, but the provision states it takes effect 24 months after enactment (i.e., in 2028 or later), or states it takes effect only after the implementing agency finalizes regulations. Forecasters disagree about whether a law signed in 2026 but not operative until years later constitutes a "binding legal mandate" within the resolution window. - SEVERITY: MEDIUM — The resolution criteria state that implementing regulations need not be finalized by December 31, 2026. However, if the statute itself has a delayed effective date, the question becomes whether the signed law "includes a legally binding requirement" at the time of signing or only at the future effective date. - FIX: Add language: "The question resolves YES upon Presidential signature of a law containing the universal screening mandate, regardless of the law's effective date or implementation timeline. A delayed effective date does not prevent resolution, as long as the law creates a binding legal obligation that will take effect at a defined future date." ### Edge Case 6: The "Universal" vs. "Federally Funded" Distinction — Mandate Applies to All Providers but Only for Certain Categories of Orders - SCENARIO: The President signs legislation requiring all synthesis providers to screen orders, but the screening obligation applies only to orders involving sequences above a certain risk threshold (e.g., "Select Agent" sequences), while routine commercial orders for common research sequences remain unscreened. The law technically applies to all providers (not just federally funded ones) but does not require screening of "all orders" — only orders matching specific risk criteria. - SEVERITY: LOW — This is essentially how any practical screening regime would work (screening against databases of known pathogens, not screening every order for every conceivable risk). The resolution criteria already reference screening "against sequences of concern," which implies a risk-based approach. However, if the enacted law's definition of "sequences of concern" is extremely narrow, it could functionally exempt most orders. - FIX: Add language: "The mandate must require providers to screen all incoming orders against a database of sequences of concern, consistent with the general approach of the 2024 OSTP Framework. It is not necessary that every order be flagged or that every possible dangerous sequence be included in the database. The key criterion is that the screening obligation applies to all orders from all customers, not that every order results in a positive match." ### Edge Case 7: Companion House Bill or Different Legislative Vehicle Passes Instead of S. 3741 - SCENARIO: Rather than S. 3741 advancing, H.R. 3029 (the "Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act") or another House bill is enacted that directs NIST to "develop technical standards" for nucleic acid synthesis screening and requires providers to comply with those standards once finalized. Forecasters disagree about whether directing NIST to develop standards (which providers must then follow) constitutes a "binding legal mandate" or is closer to a "develop a strategy" directive. - SEVERITY: MEDIUM — H.R. 3029 exists and takes a different approach (NIST standards development) compared to S. 3741 (Commerce Department rulemaking). If NIST is directed to create standards with mandatory compliance, this straddles the line between the resolution criteria's acceptance of "regulatory delegation" and its rejection of mere "study" directives. - FIX: Add language: "If the enacted legislation directs a federal agency to develop standards or regulations and separately requires providers to comply with those standards/regulations once finalized (even if finalization occurs after December 31, 2026), this resolves YES — provided the statute creates a binding compliance obligation, not merely voluntary guidance. If the statute directs development of standards but does not mandate compliance with them, the question resolves NO." --- ### Summary Assessment The resolution criteria are well-drafted and anticipate many common ambiguities (broader legislation vehicles, regulatory delegation, the study-vs-mandate distinction). However, the most significant risks center on: (1) the precise nature of the legislative mandate in S. 3741 or any successor bill — the FAS description suggests the bill may be more focused on assessment than binding mandates [c5d524]; (2) the blurry line between a statutory directive to "promulgate regulations" (which the resolution criteria accept) and a directive to "develop a strategy" (which they reject); and (3) the likelihood that any enacted legislation will contain exemptions, thresholds, or delayed effective dates that complicate the "universal" determination.

Forecast rationale

This question asks whether the U.S. President will sign into law legislation mandating universal nucleic acid synthesis screening (covering all orders, not just federally funded ones) by December 31, 2026. Here is my analysis: Current State: S. 3741, introduced January 29, 2026, by Senators Cotton and Klobuchar, is the primary legislative vehicle. As of March 19, 2026, it has been referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation with no hearings, markups, or further action reported [3539a3]. Crucially, no House companion bill exists. Base Rates Against: Historical base rates are strongly unfavorable. Only 1-4% of introduced bills become law. ~80-90% of bills referred to committee never receive a hearing. Bills introduced in the second year of a Congress in an election year face even worse odds. The absence of a House companion is a major structural bottleneck. Favorable Factors: Bipartisan sponsorship (Cotton-Klobuchar), alignment with EO 14292, institutional endorsements from NTI, FAS, and Johns Hopkins, industry support from major players wanting a level playing field [a04311], and the BIOSECURE Act precedent showing biosecurity provisions can ride must-pass bills like the NDAA [2a07a1]. Critical Negative Signal: The FY2026 NDAA (signed December 18, 2025) included the BIOSECURE Act but did NOT include a universal screening mandate, even though the concept was already being discussed. This suggests it was not considered a 'must-pass' priority for that cycle. Most Plausible Pathway: Attachment to the FY2027 NDAA or year-end omnibus. However, this requires: (1) committee action on S. 3741 or equivalent language being drafted, (2) a House process or companion, (3) surviving conference negotiations, and (4) presidential signature. The election year compresses the legislative calendar significantly. Market Signal: Manifold Markets reportedly estimates ~40% for 'Will the U.S. mandate DNA synthesis screening for all providers by 2027?' This is essentially the same timeframe. However, I believe this estimate is too high given the concrete structural obstacles—no committee action after nearly two months, no House companion, election year dynamics, and the precedent of the FY2026 NDAA excluding this provision. Key Uncertainties: 1. Will S. 3741 receive committee action? If hearings/markup occur by summer 2026, probability increases significantly (perhaps to 20-25%). If it remains stalled through September, probability drops to ~3-5%. 2. Will a House companion bill emerge? Without one, the bill must be attached to a larger vehicle. The emergence of a House companion would be a strong positive signal. 3. Will the NDAA or omnibus serve as a vehicle? If leadership prioritizes this for the FY2027 NDAA, the probability rises substantially. If it's excluded (as it was from FY2026 NDAA), standalone passage is extremely unlikely. 4. Will an external trigger (biosecurity incident, AI-bio threat) create urgency? A catalyzing event could dramatically accelerate the timeline. Synthesis: Blending the low base rates (~2-5%), the favorable but insufficient political dynamics, the concrete structural obstacles, and partially weighting the ~40% Manifold estimate (which I believe overestimates the probability given current legislative stagnation), I arrive at approximately 10%.

Importance rationale

This question tracks a pivotal transition in biosecurity governance: the move from a voluntary, funding-contingent screening regime to a universal federal mandate. Knowing the answer is highly relevant for policy and decision-making because it identifies whether a known security loophole—the 'non-federally funded' gap—will be closed. For industry, the answer determines whether synthesis providers must invest in new compliance infrastructure. For policymakers, it serves as a measure of legislative appetite for regulating the bioeconomy to prevent the illicit synthesis of pandemic-capable pathogens. The bipartisan nature of the tracked bill (S. 3741) and its alignment with Executive Order 14292 make this a critical leading indicator for the future of U.S. biological defense policy.

Detailed research

## Detailed Evidence and Analysis ### 1. Bill Introduction and Current Status (January 29, 2026 – March 19, 2026) S. 3741, the Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026, was introduced on January 29, 2026, by Senator Tom Cotton (R-AR) with Senator Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) as co-sponsor. The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. As confirmed through Congress.gov listings and multiple bill-tracking services (LegiScan, BillTrack50, TrackBill), the last recorded action on S. 3741 is its referral to the Commerce Committee. No subsequent committee action—no hearing, no markup, and no vote—has occurred as of March 19, 2026. The bill would require the Secretary of Commerce to promulgate regulations mandating nucleic acid synthesis screening by all gene synthesis providers, not limited to federally funded orders. It also directs the Department of Commerce, in coordination with other federal agencies, to compile a list of potentially dangerous genetic sequences [8b76aa]. ### 2. Senate Commerce Committee Markup and Hearing Activity in 2026 The Senate Commerce Committee, chaired by Ted Cruz (R-TX), has been active in 2026. The following is a chronological summary of known committee sessions: - February 3, 2026: Executive Session (time change announced; details suggest nominations and other measures). - February 12, 2026: Executive Session — advanced eight bipartisan measures: S. 71 (Baby Changing on Board Act), S. 1898 (ORBITS Act), S. 2585 (MAP for Broadband Funding Act), S. 3199 (988 Lifeline Location Improvement Act), S. 3266 (USMMA Athletics Act), S. 3468 (National Programmable Cloud Laboratories Network Act), S. 3639 (SAT Streamlining Act), and S. 3700 (FAA SMS Compliance Review Act). Also cleared Coast Guard promotions. S. 3741 was not among these measures [f736c9]. - February 28, 2026: Field hearing in Anchorage, Alaska on Coast Guard and Arctic security needs. - March 3, 2026: Subcommittee hearing on AI deployment (chaired by Senator Budd). - March 4, 2026: Markup of the NASA Transition Authorization Act (S. 933) and the Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2026 (a package of 17+ bipartisan bills). The NASA Authorization Act passed the committee, authorizing $24.7 billion for FY2026 and $25.3 billion for FY2027. - March 5, 2026: Hearing for NASA and NIST nominees. - March 12, 2026: Executive Session focused on nominations, including Matthew Anderson (NASA Deputy Administrator) and other nominees. - March 18, 2026: Full committee hearing — "Liability or Deniability? Platform Power as Section 230 Turns 30." - March 25, 2026 (scheduled): Full Committee Executive Session/Markup at 10:00 a.m. ET. The agenda, per the committee's announcement, includes Coast Guard Promotions (PN 622) and other items. S. 3741 is not on the agenda. Conclusion: Across at least 8-9 committee sessions in 2026 (through March 25), S. 3741 has not appeared on any agenda. ### 3. Chairman Ted Cruz's Position on S. 3741 Despite extensive searching across the Senate Commerce Committee website, Cruz's official Senate page, and news sources, no public statement, comment, or position from Chairman Ted Cruz regarding S. 3741 or nucleic acid synthesis screening was identified. Cruz's publicly articulated 2026 priorities for the committee include: - Space and NASA: Cruz led the passage of the NASA Authorization Act through committee on March 4, describing U.S. space leadership as critical to competing with China. - Aviation Safety: Cruz vowed to "keep fighting for aviation safety" (February 24, 2026). - Weather Forecasting: Cruz championed the Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act (17+ bipartisan bills). - AI Regulation: Cruz introduced the SANDBOX Act, proposing a regulatory sandbox for AI developers within OSTP, and the committee held hearings on AI's impact on workforce and industry. - Section 230: Cruz convened a hearing on March 18, 2026, examining platform power 30 years after Section 230's enactment. - Nominations: Multiple executive sessions have addressed NASA, NIST, and Coast Guard nominations. Biosecurity, biotechnology security, and nucleic acid synthesis screening do not appear among Cruz's identified priorities. This absence is significant because, as chairman, Cruz controls the committee's agenda and determines which bills receive hearings and markups. ### 4. Senate Commerce Committee Legislative Agenda for the Remainder of 2026 No comprehensive "agenda" for the remainder of 2026 has been published by the committee. However, based on observed patterns and announced priorities: - Known pipeline items: NASA authorization (already passed committee), NOAA weather bills (passed committee), additional nominations, Coast Guard matters, Section 230/tech regulation, AI regulation. - Likely upcoming areas: Aviation safety legislation, broadband/telecommunications, technology/innovation policy, continued nominations processing. - No biosecurity/biotech security items have been identified in any forward-looking committee announcements. ### 5. Senate Floor Schedule for Remainder of 2026 Per the official Senate tentative legislative schedule [a67131]: - March 30 – April 10: State Work Period (recess) - May 4–8: State Work Period - May 25–29: Memorial Day recess - June 19: Juneteenth (not in session) - June 29 – July 10: Independence Day recess - August 10 – September 11: Summer recess - October 5 – November 6: Pre-election recess - November 11–13, 23–27: Veterans Day and Thanksgiving recesses - December 21–31: Year-end recess This schedule significantly compresses available legislative time. Even if S. 3741 were to advance through committee, it would need to compete for limited floor time with major legislative priorities like government funding, reconciliation, nominations, and other must-pass legislation. ### 6. External Support for S. 3741 Despite the lack of committee action, the bill has garnered notable external support: - Federation of American Scientists (FAS): Published an analysis on February 6, 2026, calling the bill "a major step" and "a first practical step" toward modernizing biosecurity oversight [3cb56b]. - Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI): Endorsed the bill. - Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security: Commended the bill's introduction (February 5, 2026). - Reuters covered the bill's introduction on February 4, 2026 [8b76aa]. - American Enterprise Institute (AEI): Published supportive analysis on universal gene synthesis screening. - Bipartisan support: The Cotton-Klobuchar pairing represents cross-party backing. ### 7. Related Legislation - H.R. 3029 (Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act): A House companion bill referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. This bill was marked up in the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade (previously in the 118th Congress as H.R. 9194). The House Energy and Commerce Committee held a hearing on "Examining Biosecurity at the Intersection of AI and Biology" on December 17, 2025, suggesting some House-side engagement with the topic. - Executive Order: The Trump administration's AI Action Plan reportedly recommends that federally funded research institutions use vetted nucleic acid synthesis screening, and directed OSTP to revise the 2024 Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening. This executive action may either complement or reduce perceived urgency for legislative action. ### 8. Historical Context for Bills Without Early Committee Action Bills referred to Senate committees that do not receive a hearing or markup within the first few months face very low odds of advancing. In the 118th Congress, only approximately 3-5% of introduced Senate bills were enacted. Bills that never receive committee consideration have near-zero chances of passage. S. 3741 has now been pending in committee for approximately 7 weeks (January 29 to March 19, 2026) without any committee action or public signal of forthcoming consideration.

SQ2: Does a companion bill to S. 3741 exist in the U.S. House of Representatives, or is there an active effort to introduce one or attach universal DNA synthesis screening provisions to House legislation?

Summary: As of March 19, 2026, no companion bill to S. 3741 (the Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026) exists in the U.S. House of Representatives. S. 3741, introduced on January 29, 2026 by Senators Tom Cotton (R-AR) and Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), mandates that all nucleic acid synthesis providers—not just those handling federally funded orders—implement screening protocols [cb8954]. It was referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation but has not yet been advanced by that committee [fd053f]. The only House bill addressing DNA synthesis screening is H.R. 3029 (the Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act), introduced April 28, 2025, which focuses on directing NIST to develop voluntary, stakeholder-driven standards rather than mandating universal screening by all providers. H.R. 3029 was passed by the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology around April 29, 2025. The House Committee on Energy and Commerce held a hearing on biosecurity and AI on December 17, 2025 where experts urged mandatory gene synthesis screening, but no legislation has resulted. Representative Julia Brownley (D-CA), who championed the Securing Gene Synthesis Act (H.R. 4702) in the 118th Congress and led a bipartisan letter urging mandatory screening, has not publicly announced plans to introduce a companion to S. 3741 in the 119th Congress. No active efforts to attach universal DNA synthesis screening mandates to must-pass House legislation (such as the NDAA or appropriations bills) have been publicly identified. The FY2026 NDAA, signed into law on December 18, 2025, included the BIOSECURE Act but not DNA synthesis screening mandates. This absence of a House vehicle represents a critical bottleneck for enactment of universal screening legislation.
