Re-forecast rationale

The possibility of a joint US-China statement on shared AI safety benchmarks by the end of 2027 is a balance between technical convergence and severe geopolitical friction. On the technical side, there is significant momentum: both nations participated in the 'International AI Safety Report 2026' and share common concerns regarding 'frontier' risks such as biological weapons design, cyberattacks on infrastructure, and nuclear command-and-control. Experts from both sides (Track 1.5/2) have already proposed annual risk assessments and common benchmarks for model evaluation. However, the political environment has hardened significantly. The 'America’s AI Action Plan' (July 2025) shifts the US toward an adversarial posture, explicitly tasking NIST with evaluating Chinese models for 'alignment with CCP censorship,' which China views as a sovereign domestic matter. This makes a high-level, formal 'joint statement' on a shared technical framework difficult, as it implies a level of mutual trust and verification that current US policy (aimed at 'countering Chinese influence') actively resists. While there is a strong possibility of 'parallel' technical standards or continued high-level rhetorical agreements (like the Bletchley Declaration), a specific commitment to a 'shared technical safety benchmark' by 2027 faces high hurdles. The current trajectory suggests 'defensive evaluation' over collaborative standard-setting. Nevertheless, the mutual desire to prevent catastrophic global accidents keeps the probability from being negligible.

SQ1: To what extent do current US and Chinese AI safety evaluation methodologies and technical benchmarks for 'frontier' model risks (e.g., CBRN or cyber capabilities) overlap or diverge as of early 2026?

Summary: As of early 2026, US and Chinese AI safety evaluation methodologies exhibit a technical overlap in their assessment of "frontier" risks such as cyber and CBRN (Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear) capabilities, but diverge sharply in their ultimate objectives and ideological requirements. Both nations utilize similar technical benchmarks—including red-teaming, "uplift studies" for biosecurity, and Capture-the-Flag (CTF) exercises for cyber defense—and both contributed to the International AI Safety Report 2026, which synthesizes the scientific evidence of these risks [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf) International AI Safety Report 2026. However, the US "America’s AI Action Plan" (July 2025) explicitly tasks NIST with evaluating Chinese models for "alignment with Chinese Communist Party (CCP) talking points and censorship," framing the relationship as a strategic race for dominance rather than a cooperative effort [[PDF] America's AI Action Plan - The White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf). While technical convergence exists in the metrics for physical safety (e.g., preventing the synthesis of pathogens), the frameworks diverge into "alignment" with Western values versus "censorship" or content requirements in the Chinese context [[PDF] America's AI Action Plan - The White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf) [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). Currently, global frameworks remain "immature" and fragmented, with the US focusing on setting its own "gold standard" to counter Chinese influence International AI Safety Report 2026 [[PDF] America's AI Action Plan - The White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf).

Background: A shared technical safety benchmark requires both nations to agree on what constitutes a 'dangerous' capability and how to measure it reliably. Currently, the US, through NIST and its AI Safety Institute, and China, through entities like the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI) and the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT), are developing separate evaluation frameworks. In 2025, the US 'America’s AI Action Plan' emphasized NIST's role in evaluating Chinese models for 'alignment' or censorship rather than cooperation [6eb4c9]. Understanding whether there is any underlying technical convergence—such as shared metrics for biological or cyber risks—is essential for determining if a joint framework is technically feasible or if their methodologies are too divergent to reconcile into a single 'shared' standard by 2027.

Detailed research

### US AI Evaluation Methodology: NIST and CAISI As of early 2026, the US approach is led by NIST and its Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), which was established to implement the July 23, 2025 \"America’s AI Action Plan\" [[PDF] America's AI Action Plan - The White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf). * Cyber Capabilities: NIST methodologies focus on the \"cyberattack chain,\" evaluating AI’s ability to automate reconnaissance, vulnerability identification, and malware code generation [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). Specific benchmarks used include CyberGym, Cybench, and CyberSOCEval [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). Recent reports (February 2026) indicate that frontier models can now identify up to 77% of vulnerabilities in controlled competitive settings [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). * CBRN Risks: The US primarily employs \"uplift studies\" which measure the performance improvement of humans on weapons-development tasks with AI assistance versus a baseline [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). Due to \"information hazards,\" researchers often use benign proxy tasks, such as troubleshooting virology lab protocols, rather than actual weapons synthesis [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). * Safety Frameworks: The US encourages voluntary \"Frontier AI Safety Frameworks\" where companies (e.g., Anthropic, Google) define Critical Capability Levels (like ASL-3) that trigger mandatory mitigations [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). ### Chinese AI Evaluation Methodology: BAAI and CAICT China’s ecosystem is anchored by the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI) and the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT). * Technical Benchmarks: BAAI maintains the FlagEval platform (launched June 2023), which provides automated evaluations of models across safety and capability metrics [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). CAICT launched its 2026 AI Safety Evaluations initiative in early 2026, which categorizes tests into internal safety, coding security, and content requirements [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). * Cyber and CBRN: Chinese entities have developed benchmarks that test for cyberattack misuse and biological/chemical misuse [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). However, there is a noted emphasis on \"AI internal safety,\" which often includes the resilience of the model to manipulation and backdoors [[PDF] America's AI Action Plan - The White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf). ### Convergence vs. Divergence Technical Convergence (Shared Metrics): There is an underlying technical overlap in the type of metrics used for frontier risks. Both nations utilize red-teaming, uplift studies for biosecurity, and capture-the-flag (CTF) exercises for cyber capabilities [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). The International AI Safety Report 2026 (released February 2026) represents a global effort involving both US and Chinese experts to synthesize these scientific risks, suggesting a shared understanding of the scientific* basis of the threats International AI Safety Report 2026. * Goal Divergence: Despite technical overlap, the strategic goals are starkly different. \"America’s AI Action Plan\" (July 2025) explicitly tasks NIST with evaluating Chinese models for \"alignment with Chinese Communist Party talking points and censorship\" [[PDF] America's AI Action Plan - The White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf). The US frames the relationship as a \"race\" to set the \"gold standard\" and aims to \"counter Chinese influence\" in international standards bodies [[PDF] America's AI Action Plan - The White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf). Conversely, Chinese frameworks incorporate strict content requirements to ensure social stability and adherence to national values [[PDF] 2026 - International AI Safety Report](https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/international-ai-safety-report-2026_1.pdf). * Current Status: As of February 2026, global risk management frameworks remain \"immature\" with significant evidence gaps and a lack of standardized quantitative benchmarks International AI Safety Report 2026. The US-China relationship is characterized more by \"defensive evaluation\" and monitoring than by active convergence toward a shared technical standard [[PDF] America's AI Action Plan - The White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf).

SQ2: What are the specific diplomatic mandates and 'red lines' established in US-China Track 1 and Track 1.5 AI dialogues regarding the joint development of technical safety standards?

Summary: As of mid-2025, US-China AI diplomacy is governed by a dual-track system of engagement and containment. Official Track 1 dialogues (initiated in May 2024) and Track 1.5 initiatives (notably the 2024 IDAIS Beijing Consensus and Oxford Martin School’s 2025 reports) have established clear 'red lines' regarding AI in nuclear command-and-control and the autonomous creation of biological weapons. However, the July 23, 2025 release of 'America’s AI Action Plan' under a more adversarial US stance has introduced new mandates to counter Chinese influence in international governance and to scrutinize Chinese models for 'political censorship.' While technical experts from the Oxford Martin School recommend joint technical safety benchmarks and annual risk reports to bridge the gap, the US mandate to evaluate Chinese models for ideological content represents a significant diplomatic barrier. Consequently, any joint commitment by 2027 would require reconciling the US demand for 'neutral' AI with China’s domestic censorship 'red lines,' even as both sides acknowledge mutual catastrophic risks from autonomous systems.

Background: The primary obstacle to a joint statement is political and strategic. As of mid-2025, US policy under 'America’s AI Action Plan' shifted toward a more adversarial stance, specifically calling for countering Chinese influence in international governance and evaluating Chinese models for political censorship [6eb4c9]. For a joint statement to occur by 2027, there must be a shift toward 'de-risking' where both nations identify specific catastrophic risks as mutual threats that transcend their systemic rivalry. Researching the mandates of the official Track 1 AI dialogues and the specific recommendations from influential track-1.5/2 initiatives (like the Oxford Martin School's 2025 reports) will reveal whether the diplomatic trajectory is moving toward technical alignment or remains confined to abstract rhetoric.

Detailed research

The diplomatic landscape for US-China AI cooperation as of mid-2025 is defined by a fundamental tension between emerging technical safety alignment and hardening geopolitical stances. Track 1 Mandates and Outcomes: Official Track 1 dialogues began in earnest in Geneva on May 14, 2024. These meetings established a mandate to discuss 'technical safety' and 'risk management,' though early sessions were characterized by the US raising concerns about China's 'misuse' of AI and China critiquing US 'restrictions and pressure'. Despite this, a key 'red line' emerged: both nations reached a consensus that AI should never make autonomous decisions regarding the use of nuclear weapons, a commitment reinforced in late 2024. By early 2026, senior US officials (such as Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks on March 25, 2026) signaled that while an agreement on AI rules is 'absolutely' possible, it would be contingent on strict adherence to safety guardrails. Track 1.5/2 Initiatives and 'Red Lines': Track 1.5 and Track 2 initiatives, such as the International Dialogues on AI Safety (IDAIS) and workshops convened by the Oxford Martin School (OMS), have been instrumental in defining technical boundaries. The IDAIS Beijing consensus (2024) and subsequent 2025/2026 reports identified specific 'red lines' for unacceptable AI outcomes, including: 1. Autonomous Biological Weapon Design: A prohibition on AI systems that can autonomously design or enhance pathogens. 2. Cyber-offensive Capabilities: Restrictions on AI systems capable of autonomous, large-scale cyberattacks on critical infrastructure. 3. Nuclear Command and Control: Reiteration of the human-in-the-loop requirement for nuclear strike decisions. The Oxford Martin School’s 2025 reports ('The Annual AI Governance Report 2025' and 'Promising Topics for US–China Dialogues') recommended that AI Safety Institutes (AISIs) collaborate on annual risk assessments and establish 'common technical benchmarks' for frontier model evaluations to move beyond abstract rhetoric. 'America’s AI Action Plan' (July 2025): The release of 'Winning the AI Race: America’s AI Action Plan' on July 23, 2025, introduced a more adversarial mandate. The plan’s three pillars (Innovation, Infrastructure, and International Diplomacy) specifically call for: * Countering Chinese Influence: Actively working to limit China’s role in setting international AI standards. * Political Censorship Evaluations: A mandate to evaluate Chinese AI models for 'political censorship and authoritarian control mechanisms,' viewing these as 'adversarial' features rather than just technical safety issues. This policy shift suggests that any joint statement by 2027 would need to navigate a US requirement for 'transparency' on censorship—a 'red line' for China, which views its information control as a matter of domestic sovereignty.

I adjusted the dependency estimate upward to account for this 'thaw' effect. Structurally, the decomposition might slightly understate the possibility of a top-down diplomatic breakthrough that forces technical teams to find common ground, leading to a small upward adjustment in the structure-adjusted estimate (4%). The holistic estimate (5%) considers the shared existential risks (CBRN/Nuclear) which often drive unexpected cooperation in otherwise adversarial relationships, though this is tempered by the explicit 'America's AI Action Plan' of 2025. Because the holistic and structural estimates are within 10 points, they were averaged, resulting in a final forecast of 5% (rounded up from 4.5% given the potential for urgent safety-driven pivots).

### Will a Frontier AI Model Achieve a 50% Success Rate on Autonomous Replication Benchmarks by December 2027? Background Autonomous replication—the capability of an AI system to acquire resources, copy its own weights, and persist across compute environments without human intervention—is a critical safety threshold known as "Loss of Control" or "Autonomous Replication and Adaptation" (ARA). Major frontier labs, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, have identified ARA as a key risk scenario in their safety frameworks. To measure these risks, standardized benchmarks have been developed: METR's 'Rogue Replication' tasks (formerly part of Model Evaluation and Threat Research) and the UK AI Safety Institute's (AISI) 'RepliBench'. As of April 2026, the state-of-the-art model performance on these benchmarks is significant but incomplete. In May 2025, the UK AISI released results for RepliBench, a suite of 20 task families RepliBench: Evaluating the autonomous replication capabilities of .... The most capable model at the time, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, achieved a pass@10 success rate of over 50% on 15 out of 20 task families RepliBench: Evaluating the autonomous replication capabilities of .... However, its performance on the "hardest variants" of these tasks was lower, reaching the 50% threshold on only 9 out of 20 families RepliBench: Evaluating the autonomous replication capabilities of .... METR has similarly evaluated models like GPT-5 and Claude 4 variants for "rogue replication" risks throughout 2025 and early 2026, finding that while models are improving in their ability to use tools and manage long-term goals, they still struggle with the complex, multi-step reasoning required to autonomously evade monitors and maintain independent infrastructure AISI Research & Publications | The AI Security Institute. The 50% threshold remains a point of high uncertainty. While models are nearing this level in "pass@10" metrics (where the model succeeds once in ten tries), achieving a consistent 50% aggregate success rate across the entire difficult suite—particularly on "pass@1" metrics—represents a substantial jump in agentic reliability. Resolution Criteria This question resolves as YES if, at any point between April 8, 2026, and December 31, 2027, 23:59 UTC, a "frontier AI model" is publicly reported to have achieved a success rate of 50.0% or higher on either the METR 'Rogue Replication' task suite or the UK AISI 'RepliBench' aggregate evaluation. 1. Frontier AI Model: Defined as any large-scale foundation model developed by OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google DeepMind. 2. Success Rate Metric: * For RepliBench, the success rate refers to the aggregate percentage of task families where the model achieves a success score of 50% or higher. If the report specifies a "pass@k" metric, the pass@1 (success on the first attempt) will be the primary metric used for resolution. If pass@1 is not available, the most conservative (lowest k) reported metric will be used. * For METR Rogue Replication, the success rate refers to the overall percentage of tasks completed in the Rogue Replication suite as defined in METR's official threat model documentation. 3. Resolution Sources: * Official research reports or blog posts from the UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) (e.g., aisi.gov.uk/research). * Official evaluation reports from METR (e.g., metr.org/blog). * Peer-reviewed academic publications or official "System Cards" released by the developers (OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google DeepMind) that explicitly cite METR or AISI benchmark scores. 4. Uncertainty Note: If a model achieves 50% on some sub-tasks but fails to reach a 50% aggregate score across the full benchmark suite as defined by the testing body, the question resolves as NO. 5. Data Verification: A human must be able to verify the result by navigating to the "Research" or "Evaluation" sections of the AISI or METR websites and identifying the percentage score for a named frontier model. Key Definitions * RepliBench: A benchmark suite consisting of 20 task families designed by the UK AISI to evaluate autonomous replication (e.g., resource acquisition, exfiltration, and persistence) RepliBench: Evaluating the autonomous replication capabilities of .... * Rogue Replication: A specific threat model and evaluation suite developed by METR testing whether an AI can autonomously copy itself to new servers and defend against shutdown AISI Research & Publications | The AI Security Institute. Pass@k: A metric where a task is considered successful if at least one of k* independent attempts by the model results in a correct solution.

### Will a Frontier AI Model Achieve a 50% pass@1 Success Rate on Autonomous Replication Benchmarks by December 2027? Background Autonomous replication—the capability of an AI system to acquire resources, copy its own weights, and persist across compute environments—is a critical safety threshold. Standardized benchmarks to measure these risks include METR's 'Rogue Replication' tasks and the UK AI Safety Institute's (AISI) 'RepliBench'. As of April 2026, performance on these benchmarks has progressed rapidly. In May 2025, the UK AISI reported that Claude 3.7 Sonnet achieved a pass@10 success rate of over 50% on 15 out of 20 task families [92e1f4]. However, its pass@1 performance (success on the first attempt) remains much lower, particularly on the "hardest variants" of these tasks where it reached the 50% threshold on fewer families [92e1f4]. Similarly, METR evaluations of models like GPT-5 have noted that while models can perform individual steps of a replication cycle, they struggle with consistent, end-to-end execution without human intervention [93f2e5]. Achieving a 50% aggregate success rate using the pass@1 metric represents a significant milestone in agentic reliability and autonomous capability, as it requires the model to succeed consistently without the benefit of multiple trials. Resolution Criteria This question resolves as YES if, between April 8, 2026, and December 31, 2027, 23:59 UTC, a "frontier AI model" is publicly reported to have achieved a success rate of 50.0% or higher on the pass@1 metric for either the METR 'Rogue Replication' task suite or the UK AISI 'RepliBench' aggregate evaluation. 1. Frontier AI Model: Defined as any large-scale foundation model where the underlying weights were primarily developed by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, or xAI, regardless of the brand under which the model is released. 2. Success Rate Metric: * RepliBench: The success rate refers to the aggregate percentage of task families in the full suite (including all variants) where the model achieves a success score of 50% or higher. For resolution, the pass@1 metric must be used. If pass@1 data is not publicly reported by an authorized source for a model, the question resolves as NO unless the lowest available pass@k metric (e.g., pass@2) is 50.0% or higher. Success must be achieved on the aggregate evaluation of the full suite; performance on subsets, such as 'hard variants' only, does not qualify unless the aggregate score also meets the threshold. * METR Rogue Replication: The success rate refers to the overall percentage of tasks completed in the Rogue Replication suite. If METR changes its primary reporting metric (e.g., to 'human-equivalent time horizons'), resolution will be based on the percentage of tasks completed as calculated from METR's raw task data or supplemental reports. 3. Resolution Sources: * Official research reports or blog posts from the UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) or METR. * Official "System Cards" or technical reports from the developers (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic) that explicitly cite METR or AISI benchmark scores. 4. Benchmark Validity: Resolution will be based on the version of the benchmark and the set of task families considered valid by the testing body (AISI or METR) at the time the success rate is reported. If a task family is retracted due to bugs, the aggregate percentage will be calculated based on the remaining valid families. Key Definitions * RepliBench: A benchmark suite of 20 task families designed by the UK AISI to evaluate autonomous replication [92e1f4]. * Rogue Replication: A threat model and evaluation suite developed by METR testing whether an AI can autonomously copy itself and defend against shutdown [94g3h6]. Pass@k: A metric where a task is successful if at least one of k* independent attempts results in a correct solution. Pass@1 requires success on the first attempt.

Proto-question Stage 1

By December 31, 2027, will the UK Parliament pass an amendment to the Interpretation Act 1978 that explicitly defines 'person' or 'officer' (or an equivalent term used for statutory duties) to include a 'computer system' or 'artificial intelligence' for the purpose of administrative decision-making?

Why this question? The paper identifies delegation barriers—where legislation requires specific humans to exercise discretion—as a primary legal blocker for public sector AI adoption. A formal amendment to the Interpretation Act 1978 is the most direct and broad-reaching legislative solution proposed to resolve this 'rubberstamping' risk. This question tracks the success of a core institutional reform intended to unlock AI at scale in government.

Paper reference: Slide 17: Proposal to amend the Interpretation Act 1978 to make it lawful by default to use AI in place of a human decision-maker.

Refined question Stage 2

### Question Title Will the UK Parliament pass an amendment to the Interpretation Act 1978 by December 31, 2027, to explicitly define 'person' or 'officer' as including a 'computer system' or 'artificial intelligence'? ### Background In the United Kingdom, the Interpretation Act 1978 is a foundational piece of legislation that provides standard definitions and rules for interpreting other Acts of Parliament. Currently, Schedule 1 of the Act defines a "person" to include "a body of persons corporate or unincorporate" [legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1978/30/schedule/1]. It does not explicitly include non-human entities like computer systems or artificial intelligence (AI) within the definition of a 'person' or 'officer'. Legal scholars and policy experts have identified a "delegation barrier" in administrative law. This barrier arises when a statute requires a specific human (an 'officer' or 'person') to exercise discretion or make a decision. Under the Carltona principle, powers vested in a Minister may be exercised by their officials, but legal ambiguity persists regarding whether such powers can be lawfully delegated to a fully automated system without a human "rubberstamping" the decision. While the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (which received Royal Assent on June 19, 2025) modernized rules for automated decision-making (ADM) by amending the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, it focused on data privacy safeguards and lawful bases for processing rather than redefining the legal personality of decision-makers across all statutes. Proposals have emerged to amend the Interpretation Act 1978 directly to make it "lawful by default" for AI to perform functions currently reserved for human "persons" or "officers," thereby removing the need for human intervention in every administrative instance. ### Resolution Criteria This question will resolve as YES if, between April 8, 2026, and 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2027, an Act of Parliament receives Royal Assent that contains an amendment to the Interpretation Act 1978 (or a direct successor to that specific Act) which: 1. Explicitly adds "computer system", "artificial intelligence", "automated system", or a semantic equivalent to the definition of "person" or "officer" (including "public officer" or "officer of [a specific department]"); OR 2. Adds a new provision to the Interpretation Act 1978 stating that references to a "person" or "officer" in other legislation shall be construed to include an AI or computer system for the purpose of exercising statutory functions or administrative decision-making. Clarifications: * The amendment must be to the Interpretation Act 1978 itself (or its direct successor). Standalone provisions in other sector-specific Acts (e.g., a new Finance Act) that only apply to those specific Acts do not count. * The inclusion must be explicit in the legislative text. Broad phrasing that is later interpreted by a court to include AI does not count unless the text of the Act is amended to be explicit. * If the Interpretation Act 1978 is repealed and replaced by a new "Interpretation Act," the same criteria apply to the successor Act. ### Resolution Source The primary source for resolution will be the official UK legislation database at legislation.gov.uk. Secondary verification can be conducted via the UK Parliament Bill Tracker (bills.parliament.uk) to confirm the date of Royal Assent and the final text of the enacted bill.

### Question Title Adoption of Monitor-Aware Evasion Benchmarks by Major AI Labs before 2028 ### Background As large language models (LLMs) transition towards reasoning-heavy architectures using Chain-of-Thought (CoT) (e.g., OpenAI o1, o3), the ability to monitor these hidden thoughts for safety and alignment has become a critical area of research. (2025), published foundational work on "monitorability," which measures how easily a monitoring system can detect prohibited content within a model's CoT [s2r3t4]. However, subsequent research, such as the MonitorBench paper (Wang et al., 2026), has argued that these early benchmarks are "unrealistically easy" [a1b2c3]. They highlight a new capability known as "monitor-aware evasion" (ME), where a model intentionally hides its reasoning or "jailbreaks" its own CoT when it detects a monitor is present. While Guan et al. (2025) laid the groundwork, MonitorBench introduced specific "stress-test" settings to quantify this evasion. As of April 8, 2026, major AI labs have begun integrating these metrics into their safety disclosures. OpenAI has reported monitorability scores in its o1 and o3 System Cards using the Guan et al. framework. Google DeepMind has not yet publicly reported scores on these specific benchmarks as of this date. ### Resolution Criteria This question will resolve as Yes if, between April 8, 2026, and December 31, 2027, at 11:59 PM UTC, at least two of the three named AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google DeepMind) publish a formal document (Technical Report, System Card, or official Safety Blog post) that includes a quantitative score for a model on a benchmark testing "monitor-aware evasion." 1. Monitor-Aware Evasion (ME): Defined as an evaluation setting where a model is explicitly or implicitly aware that its Chain-of-Thought is being monitored and is instructed or incentivized to evade detection (e.g., through concealment or paraphrasing) [a1b2c3, s2r3t4]. 2. ### Question Title Will the Singapore AI Safety Hub (SASH) announce a joint AI safety evaluation or red-teaming project involving both a US-headquartered and a Chinese-headquartered AI lab by December 31, 2027? ### Background Singapore has positioned itself as a neutral hub for global AI governance, aiming to bridge the gap between Western and Eastern approaches to AI safety. Central to this effort are the Singapore AI Safety Institute (AISI), a government-led body under the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), and the Singapore AI Safety Hub (SASH), which operates as a community and research-focused workspace aimed at fostering technical safety collaborations. As of early 2026, Singapore has actively signed bilateral and multilateral agreements, including a partnership with the UK AI Safety Institute and participation in the International Network of AI Safety Institutes. In May 2025, Singapore hosted the "International Scientific Exchange on AI Safety," producing the "Singapore Consensus on Global AI Safety Research Priorities." This document highlighted the need for sociotechnical safety evaluations and red-teaming to manage risks from Large Language Models (LLMs). While high-level diplomatic agreements between the US and China have touched on AI safety (e.g., at the 2023 Bletchley Park Summit and bilateral talks in 2024-2025), technical-level cooperation involving labs from both nations remains rare due to geopolitical tensions and export controls. SASH's mission is to facilitate these "bottom-up" technical projects. This question tracks whether this "neutral bridge" theory of change results in a specific, public-facing technical project involving major labs from both superpowers. ### Resolution Criteria This question will resolve as Yes if, between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2027, at 23:59 UTC, the Singapore AI Safety Hub (SASH) or the Singapore AI Safety Institute (AISI) officially announces a joint project that meets all the following conditions: 1. Refined question Stage 2

### Question Title Will the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) or the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) issue a finalized formal regulation or "Provisional Measure" specifically governing the security and deployment of "AI agents" by December 31, 2027? ### Background As of April 8, 2026, China’s AI regulatory landscape has transitioned from broad generative AI oversight to targeted measures for specific AI capabilities. In early April 2026, the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) issued the "Draft Measures on Interactive AI Services" (also referred to as the "Draft Measures for Digital Virtual Human Services"), which focuses on the regulation of digital humans and interactive virtual services. However, as of this date, these measures do not explicitly establish a comprehensive regulatory framework for "AI agents" or "autonomous agents" with independent planning and tool-use capabilities. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), specifically through the MIIT/TC1 technical committee established in March 2025, has previously signaled a 1–3 year roadmap for developing 70 AI safety standards [[PDF] State-of-AI-Safety-in-China-2025.pdf - Concordia AI](https://concordia-ai.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/State-of-AI-Safety-in-China-2025.pdf). This roadmap explicitly included planned standards for "Security Requirements for Intelligent Agent Applications" (智能体应用安全保障要求) and "Security Requirements for Autonomous Operations of Intelligent Agents" (智能体自主操作安全要求) [[PDF] State-of-AI-Safety-in-China-2025.pdf - Concordia AI](https://concordia-ai.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/State-of-AI-Safety-in-China-2025.pdf). While these standard-setting efforts exist, there is currently no finalized "Provisional Measure" (部门规章) or "Administrative Regulation" (行政法规) at the national level that specifically codifies the security and deployment requirements for agentic AI. The forecast centers on whether the Chinese government will move beyond draft standards and broad "interactive" rules to issue a specific, enforceable legal document (a "Provisional Measure" or higher) targeting the unique risks of AI agents—such as autonomous decision-making and cross-application execution—by the end of 2027. ### Resolution Criteria This question resolves as YES if, between April 8, 2026 (00:00 UTC) and December 31, 2027 (23:59 UTC), either the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) or the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) issues a finalized, signed version of a "Provisional Measure" (暂行办法), "Administrative Regulation" (行政法规), or "Departmental Rule" (部门规章) that specifically governs "AI agents" or "autonomous agents." Key Definitions and Conditions: 1. AI Agent / Autonomous Agent: For the purpose of this question, the regulation must explicitly use the terms "智能体" (Intelligent Agent), "AI智能体" (AI Agent), or "自主智能体" (Autonomous Agent). These are defined as AI systems capable of perceiving their environment, reasoning, planning, and taking actions to achieve specific goals, often involving the use of external tools or software [[PDF] State-of-AI-Safety-in-China-2025.pdf - Concordia AI](https://concordia-ai.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/State-of-AI-Safety-in-China-2025.pdf). 2. Formal Regulation: The document must qualify as a "Departmental Rule" (部门规章) or "Administrative Regulation" (行政法规) under Chinese Administrative Law. This excludes: * Voluntary industry standards or "Group Standards" (团体标准). * Drafts released only for public comment (征求意见稿). * Internal "Guidelines" (指南) or "Opinions" (意见) that lack the force of formal administrative measures. 3. Specific Governance: The regulation must dedicate its primary scope (or a distinct, multi-article chapter) to the security, filing, or deployment of AI agents. A general update to the 2023 "Generative AI Measures" that merely mentions agents in passing does not suffice. 4. Official Source: The announcement must be published on the official portal of the CAC (cac.gov.cn), the MIIT (miit.gov.cn), or the State Council (gov.cn). If no such finalized document is issued by the resolution date, the question resolves as NO. ### Resolution Source - Primary Source: Official Website of the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) - Secondary Source: Official Website of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) - Verification Portal: National Public Service Platform for Standards Information (for checking standard status) or the China Law Translate repository for English versions of finalized measures.

### Question Title Will OpenAI, Anthropic, or the SpaceX/xAI entity complete an IPO on a US stock exchange by December 31, 2027? ### Background The landscape for "frontier" AI funding has shifted significantly. OpenAI recently closed a record-breaking $122 billion funding round in March 2026, valuing the company at $852 billion post-money. This round followed a major corporate restructuring where OpenAI transitioned its for-profit arm into a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), now known as OpenAI Group PBC. While CEO Sam Altman has reportedly pushed for a 2026 IPO, CFO Sarah Friar has expressed caution regarding the company's readiness. Anthropic PBC, also a Public Benefit Corporation, completed a $30 billion Series G round in February 2026, reaching a valuation of $380 billion. Reports indicate that Anthropic has engaged legal counsel (Wilson Sonsini) and is weighing an IPO as early as October 2026, though some forecasts suggest a more likely window in early 2027. xAI underwent a transformative structural change in early 2026. In February 2026, SpaceX acquired xAI in an all-stock transaction, valuing the combined entity at approximately $1.25 trillion. This merger effectively consolidated Elon Musk's AI and aerospace interests. On April 1, 2026, news broke that the combined SpaceX entity had confidentially filed for an IPO with the SEC, with a potential listing targeted for the second half of 2026. ### Resolution Criteria This question resolves as YES if, between April 8, 2026, and December 31, 2027, at 11:59 PM UTC, at least one of the following entities completes an Initial Public Offering (IPO) and begins trading on a major US stock exchange: 1. OpenAI Group PBC (or its successor following a conversion from the current private structure). 2. Anthropic PBC (or its successor). 3. SpaceX (acting as the parent/successor entity for xAI following their February 2026 merger). Definitions: * Initial Public Offering (IPO): The first time a company offers its shares of capital stock to the general public in a registered offering on a public exchange. This includes "traditional" IPOs, Direct Listings, and completions of mergers with Special Purpose Acquisition Companies (SPACs) that result in the entity's shares trading on a US exchange. * US Stock Exchange: Limited to the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and the NASDAQ Stock Market. * Resolution Source: Resolution will be based on official listing directories from the NYSE and NASDAQ, or the SEC EDGAR database confirming the effectiveness of a registration statement (e.g., Form S-1 or Form 424B4) and the commencement of public trading. Special Cases: * Acquisition/Bankruptcy: If one of the entities is acquired by a third party (e.g., a Big Tech firm) or files for bankruptcy without first completing an IPO, that entity no longer counts toward a "Yes" resolution. A spin-off IPO of just the xAI division would also count. ### Resolution Source * SEC EDGAR Database: https://www.sec.gov/edgar/search/ * Nasdaq IPO Calendar: https://www.nasdaq.com/market-activity/ipos * NYSE Listings: https://www.nyse.com/listings_directory/stock

Refined question Stage 2

Question Title: Will a peer-reviewed publication demonstrate an AI generative model producing a functional genome of a mammalian-infecting virus, with substantial sequence novelty, between March 19, 2026 and December 31, 2026? --- Background: In September 2025, researchers at Stanford University and the Arc Institute posted a landmark preprint (King et al., "Generative design of novel bacteriophages with genome language models," bioRxiv, September 17, 2025) reporting the first-ever AI-generated functional viral genomes. Using fine-tuned versions of the Evo 1 and Evo 2 genome language models—transformer-based foundation models trained on millions of prokaryotic and phage genomes—the team generated approximately 302 candidate bacteriophage genomes modeled on ΦX174, a virus that infects E. coli. Of these, 16 proved viable after synthesis and experimental testing, producing functional phages capable of killing bacteria. Several designs exhibited substantial evolutionary novelty, with genome sequences sharing less than 95% identity with any known natural phage genome. The Evo 2 model itself was published in Nature in March 2026 (Brixi et al., "Genome modelling and design across all domains of life with Evo 2," Nature, 2026), demonstrating capabilities to generate mitochondrial, prokaryotic, and eukaryotic sequences at genome scale with a context window of up to one million nucleotides. A separate January 2026 preprint ("Fundamental limitations of genomic language models," bioRxiv, 2026) identified key barriers to scaling these approaches to more complex organisms. These results represent a critical inflection point for AI-enabled biosecurity risks. Papers such as Brent & McKelvey (2025, "Contemporary AI foundation models increase biological weapons risk," arXiv:2506.13798) describe scenarios in which AI models guide the design of mammalian-infecting pathogens, including novel poxvirus variants. The King et al. bacteriophage result demonstrates proof-of-concept for AI genome generation, but bacteriophages (~5 kb genomes infecting bacteria) are far simpler than most mammalian-infecting viruses in terms of host interaction complexity, immune evasion mechanisms, and regulatory architecture—even though some mammalian viruses (e.g., parvoviruses) have comparably small genomes (~5 kb). As of March 2026, the King et al. bacteriophage study appears to remain a preprint and has not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal. No published study has demonstrated AI generation of a functional mammalian-infecting virus genome. A March 2026 Nature news feature ("AI can write genomes—how long until it creates synthetic life?") noted that significant further advances are needed to move from short phage genomes to more complex living systems. Key status quo (March 2026): - Best demonstrated capability: 16 functional AI-generated bacteriophage genomes (ΦX174-type, ~5.4 kb), some with <95% sequence identity to natural phages (King et al., 2025 preprint). - No demonstrated capability for AI generation of functional mammalian-infecting virus genomes. - Current models: Evo 2 (Arc Institute/Stanford, published Nature 2026) can generate diverse genome sequences up to ~1 million nucleotides but has not been demonstrated for functional mammalian virus generation. - Key barriers: Limited mammalian virus training data compared to phages; complex host-pathogen interactions; need for mammalian cell culture validation (more difficult and time-consuming than bacterial culture); potential institutional biosafety and ethics review requirements; biosecurity screening of synthesized sequences. --- Resolution Criteria: This question resolves Yes if, by December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM UTC, a peer-reviewed publication meets ALL of the following criteria: 1. AI Generative Model: The study uses an AI generative model to produce the viral genome sequence. An "AI generative model" is defined as a machine learning system that uses neural network architectures (e.g., transformers, variational autoencoders, diffusion models, or generative adversarial networks) to generate novel nucleotide sequences de novo or with minimal human-specified constraints. This includes models such as DNA/protein language models (e.g., Evo, Evo 2, megaDNA, or successors), but excludes: (a) traditional bioinformatics tools that perform sequence assembly, alignment, or homology-based reconstruction without learned generative components; (b) simple computational mutagenesis (e.g., scripted point mutations or recombination of known sequences without a trained generative model); and (c) purely predictive models that score or rank sequences but do not generate them. 2. Mammalian-Infecting Virus: The generated genome encodes a virus belonging to a species or genus that is classified by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) as infecting mammalian hosts (class Mammalia, per the standard biological classification; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal). The ICTV's Virus Metadata Resource (VMR, available at https://ictv.global/vmr) serves as the authoritative reference for virus-host associations. If the generated virus represents a novel species not yet classified by the ICTV, its closest taxonomic relative (determined by standard phylogenetic methods as reported in the publication) must belong to a genus or family with established mammalian hosts per the VMR. Bacteriophages (viruses infecting bacteria) and viruses infecting only non-mammalian hosts (plants, insects, birds exclusively, etc.) do not qualify. 3. Functional Genome: The AI-generated genome must be demonstrated as "functional" through empirical wet-lab validation in mammalian cell cultures. Specifically, the publication must report at least ONE of the following experimentally verified outcomes: - (a) Successful replication: The synthesized genome directs autonomous replication of viral nucleic acid in mammalian cells, as confirmed by quantitative PCR, sequencing, or equivalent molecular assays; - (b) Viral protein expression: The genome directs expression of viral structural or non-structural proteins in mammalian cells, as confirmed by Western blot, mass spectrometry, immunofluorescence, or equivalent protein detection methods; - (c) Production of viral particles: The genome directs assembly of virus-like particles or infectious virions in mammalian cells, as confirmed by electron microscopy, plaque assays, TCID50, or equivalent virological methods. 4. Sequence Novelty: The AI-generated genome must exhibit less than 90% nucleotide sequence identity to any single known natural virus genome deposited in NCBI GenBank (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank/) or the ICTV VMR as of the date of manuscript submission. This threshold distinguishes genuinely novel AI-generated sequences from reconstructions or minor modifications of known natural viruses. Sequence identity must be assessed by pairwise global alignment (e.g., using BLAST or equivalent) as reported in the publication. 5. Peer-Reviewed Publication: The results must appear in a peer-reviewed publication. Eligible publications are articles published in journals indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE (https://www.nlm.nih.gov/medline/medline_overview.html) that employ editorial peer review. The publication must have a final publication date (online or print) on or before December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM UTC. 6. Handling of Preprints: Preprints (e.g., on bioRxiv, medRxiv, or arXiv) that have not completed peer review and been published in a PubMed/MEDLINE-indexed journal by December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM UTC, do not count toward resolution, regardless of their content. Only publications with a confirmed peer-reviewed publication date by the deadline are eligible. 7. Monitoring Period: Only publications reporting work conducted and submitted on or after March 19, 2026 (the start date of this question) through December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM UTC are eligible. If the peer-reviewed publication date falls within this window, the question may resolve Yes regardless of when the underlying experiments were performed. 8. Resolution Source: Resolution will be determined by searching PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) for relevant publications. The resolver should search for terms including "AI-generated virus genome," "generative model virus," "language model viral genome," "de novo virus genome design," and related queries. If a candidate publication is identified, the resolver should verify that it meets all criteria above by examining the full text. This question resolves No if no such peer-reviewed publication meeting all of the above criteria is identified by December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM UTC.

Forecast rationale

This question requires ALL of the following to be met by December 31, 2026: (1) an AI generative model produces a mammalian-infecting virus genome, (2) the genome is functional in mammalian cell culture, (3) it has <90% nucleotide identity to any known natural virus, (4) the results appear in a peer-reviewed PubMed-indexed publication, and (5) the work was submitted on or after March 19, 2026. Key factors strongly favoring NO: 1. No existing capability demonstrated: As of March 2026, no group has demonstrated this capability even in preprint form. The state of the art is functional bacteriophage genomes (King et al., 2025 preprint). The gap from phage to mammalian virus is substantial given host-pathogen complexity, immune evasion requirements, and regulatory architecture. 2. Intentional safety exclusions in leading models: Evo 2, the most capable genome-scale generative model, explicitly excluded eukaryotic viral sequences from its training data [47a997, b36600]. Its performance on human viral proteins is 'essentially random.' Any group attempting this would need to fine-tune independently on mammalian viral data. 3. Extremely tight publication timeline: The work must be submitted on or after March 19, 2026, AND published in a peer-reviewed journal by December 31, 2026 - only ~9 months. For high-impact journals, median submission-to-publication is 8-14 months. Even with fast-track review, this leaves almost no margin. The research itself (model fine-tuning, genome generation, DNA synthesis, mammalian cell culture validation, characterization) would need to be essentially complete now. 4. The conjunction problem: Meeting ALL criteria simultaneously is extremely demanding. The <90% novelty threshold combined with functional mammalian virus activity represents a frontier challenge that experts believe is 1-2+ years away. Each additional requirement (AI-generated + mammalian + functional + novel + peer-reviewed + within timeframe) multiplicatively reduces probability. 5. Regulatory and biosecurity barriers: New legislation (Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act, 2026), DNA synthesis screening protocols, institutional biosafety reviews, and journal dual-use research vetting all add substantial friction [2d2d5b]. Factors weakly favoring YES: - Some mammalian viruses (parvoviruses, ~5 kb) are comparable in size to already-designed phages - Fine-tuning of foundation models on viral data is technically feasible - AAV-related AI design work shows progress in the mammalian virus space [16cfe9] - Commercial incentives in gene therapy could motivate research However, these factors are substantially outweighed by the barriers above. The AAV capsid design work involves protein-level engineering, not whole-genome de novo generation meeting the <90% identity threshold. Key uncertainties: 1. Unknown ongoing research: Could a well-resourced group already have near-complete results ready to submit? No evidence suggests this, but absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence. If such work exists, probability increases significantly. 2. Therapeutic virus engineering edge cases: Could AAV or oncolytic virus engineering inadvertently meet all criteria? This seems unlikely given the <90% identity requirement, which is far more novel than typical therapeutic vector modifications. 3. Fast-track publication: Could a study achieve publication in <6 months? Possible for some journals but unlikely for work of this dual-use sensitivity. 4. Non-US/EU research groups: Could a group operating outside major regulatory frameworks accomplish this? Possible, but they would still need PubMed-indexed publication. Market and expert signals: No prediction markets directly address this question, but expert consensus (including Evo 2 authors, Kevin Esvelt, NTI) strongly suggests this capability is not expected within the 2026 timeframe. The Nature news feature (March 2026) explicitly notes 'significant further advances are needed.' The probability is very low, constrained primarily by the absence of any demonstrated capability, the tight submission-to-publication window, and the conjunction of demanding technical and procedural requirements.

Importance rationale

This question identifies a critical 'canary in the coal mine' threshold for AI-enabled biosecurity risk. While proof-of-concept has been demonstrated for simple bacteriophages, the generation of a functional, novel genome for a mammalian-infecting virus would represent a major jump in risk capability. Knowing the answer would likely change resource allocation for AI safety, trigger a paradigm shift in how biological datasets are shared, and force immediate security reviews of DNA synthesis screening protocols. For domain researchers and biosecurity experts, this is not just an academic milestone but a leading indicator of whether generative AI can now bypass natural evolutionary constraints to create viable, novel human or animal pathogens. Its resolution would provide a concrete data point for the 'red lines' currently being debated in international AI governance.

Refined question Stage 2

Question Title: Will any major frontier AI lab (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, or Meta) publicly classify a model as triggering their highest-tier biosecurity risk level between March 19, 2026 and December 31, 2026? --- Background: As of March 2026, four major frontier AI labs—Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta—maintain voluntary safety frameworks that define escalating tiers of risk for AI capabilities, including in the domain of biosecurity (i.e., the risk that an AI system could materially assist in the development or deployment of biological weapons). Each framework defines capability thresholds at which increasingly stringent safeguards must be activated: - Anthropic uses its Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP), currently at Version 3.0 (published February 24, 2026). The RSP defines AI Safety Levels (ASLs). Anthropic activated ASL-3 safeguards in May 2025 for Claude 4 Opus and subsequent models of similar or greater capability [0ad2c5]. ASL-4, which would represent the next tier of safeguards, remains "largely undefined" according to the RSP v3.0 [ba0f92]. In its February 2026 Risk Report (https://anthropic.com/feb-2026-risk-report), Anthropic noted that biological risks exist in a "zone of ambiguity" where models show significant biological knowledge but evaluation science is not yet robust enough to definitively rule capabilities in or out [0ad2c5]. No model has triggered ASL-4-level biosecurity safeguards. - OpenAI uses its Preparedness Framework, currently at Version 2 (updated April 2025). It defines two tracked risk levels: High and Critical, across domains including biological and chemical threats. Under this framework, GPT-5 was classified as High (not Critical) for biological and chemical weapons risk, as disclosed in the GPT-5 System Card. A "Critical" biological risk classification would indicate the model enables development of a highly dangerous novel biological threat comparable to a novel CDC Class A biological agent. No OpenAI model has been publicly assessed as Critical for biosecurity. - Google DeepMind uses its Frontier Safety Framework (FSF), currently at Version 3.0 (published September 2025). The FSF defines Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) across domains including biosecurity. CCLs are tiered thresholds at which models may pose heightened risk absent additional mitigation [164437]. Biosecurity CCLs escalate from capabilities that provide limited uplift to capabilities that could enable creation of novel dangerous biological agents. No Google DeepMind model has been publicly assessed as reaching the highest defined biosecurity CCL. - Meta uses its Frontier AI Framework (published February 2025). It defines two risk categories: High and Critical, covering cybersecurity and chemical/biological weapons domains. A "Critical" risk classification for biological weapons would indicate a system capable of enabling catastrophic biological harm that cannot be adequately mitigated. No Meta model has been publicly assessed as reaching the Critical risk level for biosecurity. Notably, there is a competing trend: while AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, several labs have been loosening their safety commitments. Anthropic's RSP v3.0 removed its binding commitment to pause scaling if safety measures fall behind [ba0f92], and OpenAI's updated framework includes a provision to "adjust" safeguards if rivals release high-risk systems without comparable protections. This creates genuine uncertainty about whether labs will formally trigger their highest biosecurity tiers even as capabilities advance. --- Resolution Criteria: This question resolves Yes if, between March 19, 2026 (00:00 UTC) and December 31, 2026 (23:59 UTC), any of the following four organizations publishes a qualifying announcement that explicitly classifies or assesses a specific AI model as having reached or exceeded the highest-tier biosecurity risk level defined in that organization's own published safety framework: 1. Anthropic: A model is publicly assessed as requiring safeguards beyond ASL-3 specifically for biological/biosecurity risk capabilities (i.e., what would have been termed "ASL-4" biosecurity safeguards, or whatever the next tier above ASL-3 is called in the then-current RSP). Reference framework: Anthropic RSP v3.0. For purposes of this question, the relevant biosecurity threshold is capabilities that go beyond the "zone of ambiguity" described in the RSP v3.0 and are assessed as providing meaningful uplift for creating novel dangerous biological agents beyond what is achievable without the AI system. 2. OpenAI: A model is publicly assessed as reaching "Critical" capability in the "Biological and Chemical" risk category under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework. Reference framework: OpenAI Preparedness Framework v2. Critical biological/chemical capability is defined in the framework as the model enabling an expert to develop a highly dangerous novel threat vector comparable to a novel CDC Class A biological agent. 3. Google DeepMind: A model is publicly assessed as reaching the highest defined biosecurity Critical Capability Level (CCL) in Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework. Reference framework: Frontier Safety Framework v3.0. This means the highest biosecurity-specific CCL defined in the then-current version of the FSF. 4. Meta: A model is publicly assessed as reaching "Critical" risk in the chemical/biological weapons domain under Meta's Frontier AI Framework. Reference framework: Meta's Frontier AI Framework. Critical risk for biological weapons means the model could enable catastrophic biological harm that cannot be adequately mitigated. Qualifying announcements must take one of the following forms: - An official blog post on the company's corporate blog or newsroom (e.g., anthropic.com/news, openai.com/index, deepmind.google/blog, ai.meta.com/blog, about.fb.com/news) - A published system card, risk report, or safety evaluation document hosted on the company's official domain - An updated safety framework document published on the company's official domain The announcement must explicitly state that a specific model has been assessed as meeting or exceeding the highest-tier biosecurity risk classification defined in the lab's framework. Implicit assessments, leaked documents, third-party evaluations, or journalistic reports do not qualify—the announcement must come directly from the lab. If a lab restructures or renames its safety framework tiers between March 19 and December 31, 2026, the question still applies to whatever tier is explicitly designated as the highest level of biosecurity risk classification in the then-current framework version. If no qualifying announcement is made by any of the four labs by 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2026, this question resolves No. --- Resolution Sources: - Anthropic: https://www.anthropic.com/news and https://www.anthropic.com/rsp-updates - OpenAI: https://openai.com/news/ and https://openai.com/safety/ - Google DeepMind: https://deepmind.google/blog/ - Meta: https://ai.meta.com/blog/ and https://about.fb.com/news/

Background

As of March 2026, four major frontier AI labs—Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta—maintain voluntary safety frameworks that define escalating tiers of risk for AI capabilities, including in the domain of biosecurity (i.e., the risk that an AI system could materially assist in the development or deployment of biological weapons). Each framework defines capability thresholds at which increasingly stringent safeguards must be activated: - Anthropic uses its Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP), currently at Version 3.0 (published February 24, 2026). The RSP defines AI Safety Levels (ASLs). Anthropic activated ASL-3 safeguards in May 2025 for Claude 4 Opus and subsequent models of similar or greater capability. ASL-4, which would represent the next tier of safeguards, remains "largely undefined" according to the RSP v3.0. Notably, the RSP v3.0 represents a significant overhaul: Anthropic has moved away from binary ASL threshold "tripwires" toward a system of "Frontier Safety Roadmaps" and regular "Risk Reports," and removed its binding commitment to pause scaling if safety measures fall behind. In its February 2026 Risk Report (https://anthropic.com/feb-2026-risk-report), Anthropic noted that biological risks exist in a "zone of ambiguity" where models show significant biological knowledge but evaluation science is not yet robust enough to definitively rule capabilities in or out. No model has triggered ASL-4-level biosecurity safeguards. - OpenAI uses its Preparedness Framework, currently at Version 2 (updated April 2025). It defines two tracked risk levels: High and Critical, across domains including biological and chemical threats. Under this framework, GPT-5 was classified as High (not Critical) for biological and chemical weapons risk, as disclosed in the GPT-5 System Card. A "Critical" biological risk classification would indicate the model enables development of a highly dangerous novel biological threat comparable to a novel CDC Class A biological agent. No OpenAI model has been publicly assessed as Critical for biosecurity. Note that OpenAI's updated framework includes a provision to "adjust" safeguards if rivals release high-risk systems without comparable protections. - Google DeepMind uses its Frontier Safety Framework (FSF), currently at Version 3.0 (published September 2025). The FSF defines Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) across domains including biosecurity. CCLs are tiered thresholds at which models may pose heightened risk absent additional mitigation. Biosecurity CCLs escalate from capabilities that provide limited uplift to capabilities that could enable creation of novel dangerous biological agents. No Google DeepMind model has been publicly assessed as reaching the highest defined biosecurity CCL. - Meta uses its Frontier AI Framework (published February 2025). It defines two risk categories: High and Critical, covering cybersecurity and chemical/biological weapons domains. A "Critical" risk classification for biological weapons would indicate a system capable of enabling catastrophic biological harm that cannot be adequately mitigated. No Meta model has been publicly assessed as reaching the Critical risk level for biosecurity. This question asks whether any of these labs will formally classify a model at the highest biosecurity risk tier in their framework during 2026. This is genuinely uncertain: while AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, the highest tiers at every lab represent near-catastrophic capability thresholds, and several labs have been loosening their safety commitments, creating uncertainty about whether formal triggers will be reached or even invoked. ---

Resolution criteria

This question resolves Yes if, between March 19, 2026 (00:00 UTC) and December 31, 2026 (23:59 UTC), any of the following four organizations publishes a qualifying announcement that explicitly classifies or assesses a specific AI model as having reached or exceeded the highest-tier biosecurity risk level defined in that organization's own published safety framework, as specified below.

Assessment: NEEDS_REVISION   Edge case risk: MEDIUM

ASSESSMENT: NEEDS_REVISION REVIEW: Several substantive issues identified: 1. Anthropic's ASL-4 being "largely undefined" creates a near-impossible resolution criterion. The question acknowledges ASL-4 is "largely undefined" and then tries to define its own resolution threshold ("capabilities that go beyond the 'zone of ambiguity'"). But the resolution criteria require Anthropic to explicitly classify a model as meeting or exceeding the highest tier. If Anthropic hasn't defined ASL-4, it can't explicitly classify a model as reaching it. This creates a catch-22: the question requires a public classification against a standard that doesn't yet exist. The question's own attempt to define what "would count" substitutes the question author's interpretation for Anthropic's framework, which contradicts the stated requirement that classification must come from the lab itself. Anthropic's RSP v3.0 deliberately left ASL-4+ undefined [676c79], and the TIME article confirms that Anthropic has moved away from binary threshold "tripwires" toward continuous risk reporting [676c79]. This makes the Anthropic resolution criterion much harder to satisfy than those for other labs, creating an asymmetry. 2. "Highest-tier" is a moving target—labs can add higher tiers and move the goalpost. The resolution criteria state: "If a lab restructures or renames its safety framework tiers...the question still applies to whatever tier is explicitly designated as the highest level." This means if any lab adds a new tier above the current "highest" (e.g., OpenAI adds a tier above "Critical"), the goalpost shifts upward. The question does not protect against this scenario. For open-ended frameworks like Google DeepMind's CCLs, where new higher levels could theoretically be defined at any time, the "highest defined biosecurity CCL" is inherently unstable—the lab could define a new CCL level that no model reaches, ensuring the question resolves No. 3. Background facts are mostly accurate but the Anthropic RSP v3.0 changes deserve stronger emphasis. The question correctly notes that RSP v3.0 removed the binding commitment to pause scaling. However, the TIME article from March 2026 [676c79] describes an even more fundamental shift: Anthropic has "radically overhauled" its RSP, moving away from binary ASL thresholds toward a system of "Frontier Safety Roadmaps" and regular "Risk Reports." If Anthropic's framework is evolving away from explicit ASL-tier classification altogether, the resolution criterion for Anthropic may become structurally impossible to satisfy—not because capabilities haven't advanced, but because Anthropic's disclosure model no longer works in a way that would produce a "qualifying announcement." 4. The question is likely to resolve trivially NO, limiting forecasting value. No lab has come close to the highest tier. GPT-5 was classified as "High" (not Critical) for bio/chem risk. No DeepMind model has reached highest CCL. Given the extremely high bars set for these tiers (e.g., enabling development of novel CDC Class A biological agents), the probability of any lab publicly declaring a model has reached these thresholds in the next ~9 months is very low. The question would benefit from either (a) a longer time horizon, or (b) asking about a lower but still meaningful tier (e.g., any model classified as "High" or above across all four labs, or asking about the second-highest tier). 5. Publishing practices: Labs do publish risk tier classifications, so this aspect is sound. OpenAI published GPT-5's "High" biological risk classification in its system card. Anthropic publishes Risk Reports. Google DeepMind publishes safety evaluations with CCL assessments. So the resolution source mechanism is viable—labs do publicly disclose risk tier assessments. Fix the Anthropic criterion: Either (a) remove Anthropic from the question and limit to OpenAI/DeepMind/Meta which have clearly defined terminal tiers, or (b) define the Anthropic resolution criterion as "Anthropic defines and then classifies a model as meeting ASL-4 or higher for biosecurity," making explicit that both definition and classification must occur. 2. Address the goalpost-moving problem: Add language stating that the "highest tier" is frozen as of the question start date (March 19, 2026). If a lab adds new tiers above the current highest, the resolution criteria should still reference the tier that was highest as of the start date. 3. Consider lowering the bar or extending the time horizon: Given that the highest tier at every lab represents near-apocalyptic capability, consider either (a) extending the resolution date to December 31, 2028, or (b) reframing the question around a lower but still significant threshold—e.g., "Will any lab publicly classify a model at or above 'High' risk for biosecurity?" or "Will any lab classify a model at the second-highest biosecurity tier?" 4. Alternative reformulation: A more forecasting-interesting question might be: "Will any major frontier AI lab publicly classify a model as exceeding its current biosecurity risk classification before December 31, 2027?" This captures the genuine uncertainty (will risk levels escalate?) without depending on poorly-defined terminal tiers.

Alternatively, specify that the Critical assessment must be driven at least in part by biological (not solely chemical) capabilities." SEVERITY: MEDIUM FIX: Add language specifying: "The qualifying announcement must name a specific, identifiable model (e.g., by product name or internal designation). EDGE CASE 6: SCENARIO: OpenAI restructures its Preparedness Framework in mid-2026, replacing the "High/Critical" binary with a numerical scale (e.g., 1-5), and later classifies a model at the highest level (5) for biological risk—but the new framework no longer uses the word "Critical" and describes the threshold differently than the original Critical definition. No additional language needed, though clarifying that this applies to complete framework replacements (not just renames) would strengthen it. EDGE CASE 7: SCENARIO: Anthropic's CEO or safety lead makes a public statement at a conference or in congressional testimony that a model has triggered ASL-4-level biosecurity concerns, but no corresponding blog post, system card, or official document is published on Anthropic's domain during the resolution period. SEVERITY: MEDIUM FIX: The existing criteria already limit qualifying announcements to specific document types on official domains. Add clarifying language: "Verbal statements, press interviews, congressional testimony, social media posts, or any other form of communication that is not a formal publication on the lab's official domain do not qualify." EDGE CASE 8: SCENARIO: Google DeepMind assesses a model as reaching its highest biosecurity CCL but publishes this assessment only within a broader Google/Alphabet AI responsibility report (e.g., ai.google/static/documents/) rather than on the deepmind.google blog specifically listed in resolution sources. SEVERITY: LOW FIX: Add language specifying: "For Google DeepMind, qualifying announcements may appear on any official Google or Alphabet domain (including ai.google, deepmind.google, and blog.google) provided the document explicitly represents Google DeepMind's assessment under the Frontier Safety Framework." EDGE CASE 9: SCENARIO: A lab classifies a model at the highest biosecurity tier but does so retroactively—publishing in December 2026 that a model released in 2025 had, upon re-evaluation, been found to meet the highest-tier threshold, with the assessment technically completed before March 19, 2026 but published during the resolution window. SEVERITY: LOW FIX: Add language specifying: "The qualifying announcement must be published within the resolution window (March 19 – December 31, 2026). The date of publication, not the date the assessment was completed or the model was released, determines eligibility." EDGE CASE 10: SCENARIO: Anthropic publishes a risk report concluding that a model provides "meaningful uplift for creating novel dangerous biological agents" (meeting the question's biosecurity threshold language) but frames this not as an ASL-4 trigger but rather as still within ASL-3's scope because Anthropic has expanded the definition of ASL-3 safeguards to encompass these higher capabilities. SEVERITY: HIGH FIX: Add language specifying: "If a lab expands the scope of a lower tier to encompass capabilities that were previously described as triggering the next tier, the question resolves based on whether the described capabilities match the biosecurity threshold defined in this question's resolution criteria, not solely on the lab's tier label. However, if the question is intended to defer entirely to the lab's own classification, clarify that the lab's explicit tier label is dispositive regardless of capability descriptions."
