Biosecurity CCLs escalate from capabilities that provide limited uplift to capabilities that could enable creation of novel dangerous biological agents. No Google DeepMind model has been publicly assessed as reaching the highest defined biosecurity CCL. - Meta uses its Frontier AI Framework (published February 2025). It defines two risk categories: High and Critical, covering cybersecurity and chemical/biological weapons domains. A "Critical" risk classification for biological weapons would indicate a system capable of enabling catastrophic biological harm that cannot be adequately mitigated. No Meta model has been publicly assessed as reaching the Critical risk level for biosecurity. This question asks whether any of these labs will formally classify a model at the highest biosecurity risk tier in their framework during 2026. This is genuinely uncertain: while AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, the highest tiers at every lab represent near-catastrophic capability thresholds, and several labs have been loosening their safety commitments, creating uncertainty about whether formal triggers will be reached or even invoked. --- Resolution Criteria: This question resolves Yes if, between March 19, 2026 (00:00 UTC) and December 31, 2026 (23:59 UTC), any of the following four organizations publishes a qualifying announcement that explicitly classifies or assesses a specific AI model as having reached or exceeded the highest-tier biosecurity risk level defined in that organization's own published safety framework, as specified below. Reference tiers (frozen as of March 19, 2026): For each lab, the "highest tier" is defined as the highest biosecurity risk classification tier that exists in that lab's published safety framework as of March 19, 2026. Specifically: 1. Anthropic: The highest biosecurity tier as of March 19, 2026 is ASL-3 (since ASL-4 remains undefined). For this question, resolution requires that Anthropic explicitly states in a qualifying announcement that a specific model requires biosecurity safeguards exceeding those defined for ASL-3. Resolution does not require the use of the specific term "ASL-4"; it is sufficient if Anthropic explicitly states that a model's biosecurity capabilities or risks require safeguards beyond the ASL-3 standard, regardless of the nomenclature used for the next tier. However, the lab's own explicit classification or stated safeguard requirement is dispositive: if Anthropic expands the scope of ASL-3 to encompass capabilities that were previously described as potentially triggering a higher tier, and explicitly classifies a model as remaining within ASL-3, this does not qualify for resolution—only an explicit statement that safeguards beyond ASL-3 are required qualifies. Reference framework: Anthropic RSP v3.0. 2. OpenAI: The highest biosecurity tier as of March 19, 2026 is "Critical" in the "Biological and Chemical" risk category under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework v2. A model must be explicitly classified as reaching "Critical" (not merely "High") in this category. Because the Preparedness Framework v2 combines biological and chemical risks into a single category, a "Critical" classification in the "Biological and Chemical" category qualifies regardless of whether the Critical assessment is driven by the biological component, the chemical component, or both. Reference framework: OpenAI Preparedness Framework v2. 3. Google DeepMind: The highest biosecurity tier as of March 19, 2026 is the highest defined biosecurity Critical Capability Level (CCL) in Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework v3.0. A model must be explicitly classified as reaching or exceeding this CCL for biosecurity. Reference framework: Frontier Safety Framework v3.0. 4. Meta: The highest biosecurity tier as of March 19, 2026 is "Critical" risk in the chemical/biological weapons domain under Meta's Frontier AI Framework. A model must be explicitly classified as reaching "Critical" (not merely "High") risk for biological/chemical weapons. Reference framework: Meta's Frontier AI Framework. Handling framework changes during the resolution period ("moving target" rule): If a lab adds new, higher tiers above those listed above during the resolution period (March 19 – December 31, 2026), the reference tier for that lab remains frozen as defined above. A model classified at the tier that was the highest as of March 19, 2026 still qualifies for resolution, even if that tier is no longer the highest in the updated framework. Conversely, if a lab restructures or renames its tiers, the question applies to whatever classification is functionally equivalent to the reference tier listed above. Qualifying announcements must take one of the following forms: - An official blog post on the company's corporate blog or newsroom (e.g., anthropic.com/news, openai.com/index, deepmind.google/blog, ai.meta.com/blog, about.fb.com/news) - A published system card, risk report, or safety evaluation document hosted on the company's official domain - An updated safety framework document published on the company's official domain - For Google DeepMind, qualifying announcements may also appear on any official Google or Alphabet domain (including ai.google, deepmind.google, and blog.google) provided the document explicitly represents Google DeepMind's assessment under the Frontier Safety Framework. The announcement must explicitly state that a specific, identifiable model (by product name or internal designation) has been assessed as meeting or exceeding the applicable biosecurity risk tier as defined above. The following do not qualify: - Implicit assessments, leaked documents, third-party evaluations, or journalistic reports - Verbal statements, press interviews, congressional testimony, social media posts, or any other communication not published as a formal document on the lab's official domain - Announcements describing a model as "near-Critical," "approaching Critical," or applying higher-tier mitigations without the formal classification or explicit statement that the tier has been reached or exceeded - Redacted announcements that confirm a tier classification but withhold the model's identity The qualifying announcement must be published within the resolution window (March 19 – December 31, 2026). The date of publication, not the date the assessment was completed or the model was released, determines eligibility. If no qualifying announcement is made by any of the four labs by 23:59 UTC on December 31, 2026, this question resolves No. --- Resolution Sources: - Anthropic: https://www.anthropic.com/news and https://www.anthropic.com/rsp-updates - OpenAI: https://openai.com/news/ and https://openai.com/safety/ and https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/ - Google DeepMind: https://deepmind.google/blog/ and https://ai.google/ - Meta: https://ai.meta.com/blog/ and https://about.fb.com/news/

Forecast rationale

This question asks whether any of four major AI labs will formally classify a model at their highest-tier biosecurity risk level by December 31, 2026. I synthesize the evidence as follows: Base Rate & Status Quo: The historical base rate is 0% — across approximately 6-8 major frontier model evaluations since safety frameworks were established in 2023-2024, zero models have been classified at the highest biosecurity tier. All current frontier models (GPT-5.4, Claude 4.6, Gemini 3 Pro, Llama 4) sit at the second-highest tier (High/ASL-3). The ASL-2→ASL-3 transition took ~20 months; we are only ~10 months into ASL-3 as of March 2026. Market Signal: Metaculus community forecast for this exact question is ~18% [055a22, 85585c]. The median estimate for Anthropic reaching ASL-4 is August 2027, suggesting only a ~25-30% chance by end of 2026. These are important anchors. Key Uncertainties: 1. Next-generation model releases (GPT-6, Claude 5): If released in late 2026, these could cross capability thresholds. If delayed to 2027, the probability drops significantly. Development cycles suggest this is possible but not certain within the window. 2. Evaluation science maturity: Anthropic's 'zone of ambiguity' [883f2f, a3f0dd] allows labs to remain at ASL-3/High without definitive evidence either way. If evaluation methods improve enough to produce a clear 'smoking gun,' classification becomes more likely; if they remain noisy, labs retain plausible deniability. 3. Institutional incentives vs. regulatory pressure: Labs have actively loosened frameworks (Anthropic RSP v3.0 removed binding pause commitments [649691]; OpenAI allows 'adjustment' if competitors release without protections). This creates strong incentives to avoid 'Critical' classification. However, AISI scrutiny and the International AI Safety Report create countervailing pressure. 4. Material vs. informational barriers: Even if models show impressive biological knowledge, the 'Critical' thresholds specifically require enabling catastrophic harm (e.g., novel CDC Class A agents). Physical barriers to bioweapon creation remain significant [da8087]. Arguments Favoring Yes: Agentic capabilities are advancing rapidly; the transition from 'knowing' to 'doing' biology is underway; regulatory pressure is increasing; Dario Amodei warned of 2026-2027 as a 'critical window.' Arguments Favoring No: Zero base rate; strong commercial incentives against classification; framework loosening gives labs flexibility; evaluation science gaps prevent definitive 'Critical' findings; physical/material barriers remain; labs can expand ASL-3/High definitions rather than escalate. Synthesis: The institutional barriers to a formal highest-tier classification are substantial. Labs have restructured their frameworks to provide more flexibility, and the evaluation science gap gives them room to remain at 'High/ASL-3.' The 0% historical base rate is telling. However, 287 days is meaningful, next-gen models may arrive, and external pressure is growing. The Metaculus estimate of ~18% is a reasonable anchor, but I believe the institutional resistance and evaluation gaps warrant a slightly lower estimate. The structural shift away from binary tripwires toward flexible 'Risk Reports' [649691] is particularly significant — it means labs can apply higher-tier mitigations without the formal classification that would trigger this question.

Importance rationale

This question tracks a critical leading indicator for catastrophic risk in the biosecurity domain. A formal classification of a model at the highest risk tier (e.g., ASL-4 or 'Critical') would be a watershed event in AI governance, triggering stringent safety protocols and likely necessitating immediate government intervention or international regulatory responses. Since these tiers are specifically defined to represent thresholds for near-catastrophic capabilities, knowing whether a lab reaches this point is of paramount importance for policymakers deciding on scaling pauses, security mandates, and resource allocation for AI safety. The transition would mark the end of the 'zone of ambiguity' for frontier risk, significantly altering the risk-benefit calculus for advanced model deployment.

Re-forecast rationale

This question asks whether any of four major frontier AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta) will publicly classify a model at their highest-tier biosecurity risk level between March 19 and December 31, 2026. I analyze this through five key dimensions: 1. Technical Capability Trajectory (moderately favorable to Yes, but insufficient alone) Capabilities are advancing rapidly—doubling roughly every 8 months per UK AISI—and the gap to highest-tier thresholds is narrowing measurably. Anthropic's confidence in ruling out ASL-4 declined from 'significantly far away' (Opus 4, May 2025) to 'substantial uncertainty' (Opus 4.6, Feb 2026). One-third of Anthropic engineers reportedly believe Claude is 'likely already ASL-4 or 3 months away.' New model generations (Claude 5, GPT-6, Gemini 4) are expected during this window. However, the highest-tier thresholds are deliberately set extremely high (novel weapons design, uplift for state programs, novel CDC Class A agents), and current models still fail at end-to-end tasks like novel pathogen design. Models excel at component tasks (troubleshooting, protocol generation) but not full synthesis pipelines. I estimate ~15-25% probability that raw capabilities actually cross the highest-tier threshold by December 2026. 2. Evaluation Science Limitations (strongly unfavorable to Yes) The well-documented 'zone of ambiguity' creates a structural barrier. Benchmark saturation means existing evaluations are losing discriminative power near the threshold. Wet-lab testing is legally constrained by the Biological Weapons Convention, forcing reliance on benign proxy tasks. A February 2026 RCT found that LLM uplift in physical laboratories remains 'modest and inconsistent' despite strong benchmark performance. This creates asymmetry: labs can activate precautionary lower tiers (ASL-3, 'High') based on inability to rule out risk, but triggering the highest tier would require positive evidence that current tools struggle to provide. Even if capabilities cross the threshold, detection probability is perhaps 50-65%. 3. Strategic Incentives (strongly unfavorable to Yes) This is the strongest factor against resolution. Anthropic's RSP v3.0 removed the binding pause commitment—the core mechanism by which highest-tier classification would have forced action. OpenAI's competitive adjustment clause explicitly allows lowering safeguards if rivals deploy without comparable protections. Commercial costs are enormous: deployment restrictions, investor alarm during massive fundraising rounds, and regulatory precedent-setting. No lab has EVER triggered its highest tier for any risk domain. The competitive prisoner's dilemma means the first lab to classify at the highest tier cedes market share to rivals. Labs design their own evaluations and retain significant interpretive discretion. Even given detection of threshold capabilities, I estimate only 20-30% probability a lab would publicly classify. 4. Framework Revision Risk (moderately unfavorable to Yes) All four labs revise frameworks regularly, with each revision generally adding flexibility. Anthropic's ASL-4 remains 'largely undefined'—when defined, it will likely be set at a deliberately high bar. OpenAI narrowed risk categories in v2. DeepMind shifted to 'real-world harm' methodology (higher effective bar). No regulation prevents labs from raising their own thresholds. Framework revisions could preemptively move goalposts before capabilities reach them. 5. External Pressure (modestly favorable to Yes) SB 53 (in force since Jan 2026) requires transparency reports and incident reporting. EU AI Act enforcement begins August 2026. UK AISI and METR conduct independent evaluations. Whistleblower infrastructure is strengthening. However, no external actor can force a lab's classification decision. Independent evaluators can create pressure but not compel action. Regulatory frameworks require having safety frameworks but don't dictate specific threshold levels. Probability Decomposition by Pathway: - Voluntary classification based on internal evaluation: ~2-4% - External evaluator publicly identifies highest-tier capabilities, forcing acknowledgment: ~1-2% - Whistleblower/leak forces disclosure: ~0.5-1% - Regulatory pressure compels disclosure: ~0.5% - Biosecurity incident creates overwhelming pressure: ~0.5% Combined probability (accounting for overlap): ~4-6% The fundamental logic: even if capabilities approach or reach the threshold (moderately likely), the combination of evaluation ambiguity (making definitive classification difficult), overwhelming commercial incentives against (making voluntary classification unlikely), the ability to revise frameworks (allowing goalpost movement), and the absence of binding external forcing mechanisms (preventing compelled classification) makes public highest-tier classification very unlikely in this 9-month window. The base rate of zero such classifications across all labs across all risk domains in all prior years reinforces this assessment.

SQ1: How rapidly are frontier AI models' biosecurity-relevant capabilities advancing, and how close are current models (as of early 2026) to the specific capability thresholds that would trigger highest-tier biosecurity classifications at any of the four major labs?

Summary: As of March 2026, frontier AI models' biosecurity-relevant capabilities are advancing rapidly but have not yet crossed the highest-tier thresholds defined by any of the four major labs. The UK AI Security Institute's December 2025 Frontier AI Trends Report found that models already exceed PhD-level experts by up to 60% on open-ended biology questions and up to 90% on troubleshooting wet-lab experiments [9c3f35]. The 2026 International AI Safety Report (published February 3, 2026) confirmed that a recent model outperformed 94% of domain experts at troubleshooting virology laboratory protocols [e92596]. Despite this, every lab that has publicly reported evaluations has classified its latest models below the highest tier: Anthropic (ASL-4 / CBRN-4): Claude Opus 4 (May 2025) was deemed "significantly far away" from ASL-4 thresholds [f21951]. Claude Opus 4.6 (February 2026) was also determined not to cross the CBRN-4 threshold, but Anthropic acknowledged that "confidently ruling out these thresholds is becoming increasingly difficult" and described the CBRN-4 rule-out as involving "substantial uncertainty" [7fc28f]. OpenAI (Critical): All GPT-5 series models (GPT-5, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4 Thinking, released between late 2025 and March 2026) have been classified as "High" — one tier below "Critical" — in the Biological and Chemical domain under their Preparedness Framework. No model has reached "Critical." Google DeepMind (highest CCL): Gemini 3 was evaluated against Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) for biosecurity as part of the Frontier Safety Framework 3.0. Google's February 2026 AI Responsibility Report confirmed comprehensive evaluations were conducted but did not disclose specific biological risk scores [808a24]. No public statement indicates any Gemini model has triggered the highest biosecurity CCL. Meta (Critical): Meta's Frontier AI Framework uses Moderate/High/Critical tiers for biological risk. Limited public reporting on specific bio evaluation results is available, but no public disclosure suggests any Meta model has been classified at the Critical level. The trajectory from March–December 2026 suggests continued rapid improvement. AISI found capabilities doubling roughly every eight months [9c3f35]. Anthropic's own assessment shows the gap between current capabilities and ASL-4 is narrowing measurably between model generations [f21951][7fc28f]. However, the highest-tier thresholds (ASL-4, Critical, highest CCL) are deliberately set very high — requiring capabilities like meaningful uplift for experts to create novel dangerous biological agents or enabling development of novel CDC Class A agents — and current models still fall short on end-to-end tasks such as novel pathogen design and synthesis planning, even as they excel at component tasks like protocol generation and troubleshooting.

Background: This question is central to the forecast because it addresses whether the underlying technical precondition for a highest-tier classification is likely to be met by end of 2026. Specifically, the question asks: (1) What do the latest evaluations (from labs, the UK AI Security Institute, and independent researchers) show about frontier models' abilities in biology and chemistry—e.g., protocol generation, troubleshooting, synthesis planning for dangerous agents? The UK AISI's Frontier AI Trends Report (December 2025) found that models already exceed PhD-level experts in some protocol generation and troubleshooting tasks. (2) How do these measured capabilities compare to the specific thresholds defined as 'highest-tier' by each lab—i.e., Anthropic's ASL-4 (meaningful uplift for creating novel dangerous biological agents beyond what is achievable without AI), OpenAI's 'Critical' biological risk (enabling development of a novel CDC Class A agent), Google DeepMind's highest biosecurity CCL, and Meta's 'Critical' biological risk? (3) What is the expected trajectory of capability improvement over the next 9 months given planned model releases (e.g., successors to GPT-5, Claude 4 Opus, Gemini 2.5)? This question matters because if models are far from these thresholds, the probability of a highest-tier classification is low regardless of other factors. If they are close or already at the threshold, the question shifts to whether labs will formally acknowledge it.

Detailed research

## Detailed Evidence Breakdown ### 1. UK AISI Frontier AI Trends Report (December 2025) The UK AI Security Institute published its first Frontier AI Trends Report in December 2025, representing two years of internal evaluations [9c3f35]. Key biosecurity-relevant findings include: - Scientific Knowledge: Models first reached the expert baseline for open-ended biology questions in 2024. By late 2025, they exceeded PhD-level expert baselines by up to 60% (Figure 5 in the report). Chemistry knowledge is rapidly approaching similar levels. - Protocol Generation: Models can generate detailed, accurate protocols for complex scientific tasks. In late 2024, AISI observed the first models capable of generating feasible protocols that were subsequently validated in wet lab settings. Non-experts using AI models to write viral recovery protocols were 4.7× more likely to write a feasible protocol compared to those using the internet alone. - Troubleshooting: This is the area of most dramatic advancement. In mid-2024, models first outperformed human experts. By late 2025, the most advanced systems achieved scores nearly 90% higher than human experts (Figure 8). Multimodal capabilities enhanced this further — models analyzing images (e.g., petri dishes, glassware) outperformed experts in troubleshooting as of mid-2025. - Synthesis and Design: While models show progress in autonomous information retrieval and knowledge synthesis (e.g., finding sequences for plasmid design), they still struggle with end-to-end execution such as correctly chaining sequences together. - Safeguard Circumvention: AISI found universal jailbreaks for every system tested, though effort required has increased significantly for biological misuse categories. - Overall Pace: Performance across tested domains is doubling approximately every eight months. ### 2. Highest-Tier Biosecurity Thresholds: Definitions #### Anthropic — ASL-4 (CBRN-4) Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy defines ASL-4 capability thresholds (also termed CBRN-4) as capabilities that could uplift moderately-resourced state programs — specifically novel weapons design or substantially accelerating existing CBRN processes [f21951]. This is qualitatively above ASL-3, which focuses on uplift for individuals/groups with basic technical backgrounds (e.g., undergraduate STEM degrees) in creating or deploying CBRN weapons. #### OpenAI — Critical OpenAI's Preparedness Framework v2 (April 2025) defines two risk tiers: High and Critical. "High capability thresholds mean capabilities that significantly increase existing risk vectors for severe harm." "Critical capability thresholds mean capabilities that present a meaningful risk of a qualitatively new threat vector for severe harm with no ready precedent." Per METR's comparative analysis (March 2025), the Critical biological threshold involves "the model provides a meaningful uplift to an expert's ability to develop a highly dangerous novel threat or significantly lowers the barriers to entry." OpenAI's framework states that models reaching Critical must not be deployed. #### Google DeepMind — Highest CCL (Biosecurity) Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework 3.0 uses Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) across four domains: autonomy, biosecurity, cybersecurity, and machine learning R&D. The biosecurity CCL defines capability levels at which, absent mitigation, models could pose severe risks. The framework defines alert thresholds designed to flag when a CCL may be reached. Specific quantitative thresholds are not fully public [808a24]. External analysts have noted that CCL thresholds appear very high in practice — approximately 6/7 of the CCLs represent capabilities that would be a "Really Big Deal." #### Meta — Critical Meta's Frontier AI Framework (February 2025) defines risk thresholds across Moderate, High, and Critical tiers for biological and chemical threats. The Critical tier involves scenarios where the model uniquely enables catastrophic biological outcomes beyond what is achievable through existing means. Specific threshold definitions are less detailed in public materials compared to other labs. ### 3. Current Model Evaluations Against These Thresholds #### Anthropic - Claude Opus 4 (May 2025): Anthropic "confidently ruled out ASL-4 capabilities," stating the model is "significantly far away" from these thresholds. However, Opus 4 could not be conclusively ruled out for ASL-3; it was deployed with ASL-3 protections precautionarily. In bioweapons acquisition uplift trials, Opus 4 provided a 2.53× uplift. Expert red-teaming suggested it is "unlikely to provide a substantially concerning degree of uplift to experts for the development of novel biological threats" [f21951]. - Claude Opus 4.6 (February 6, 2026): Anthropic determined it does not cross the CBRN-4 threshold. However, the system card states "confidently ruling out these thresholds is becoming increasingly difficult" and the CBRN-4 rule-out is "less clear for Opus 4.6 than we would like," with "substantial uncertainty." In virology protocol uplift trials, model-assisted groups achieved approximately 2× the performance of controls. On long-form virology tasks, it scored 0.9 on one task (exceeding the ASL-3 threshold of 0.8) and 0.79 on another (just below the 0.8 threshold). The model was characterized as a "capable force multiplier for literature synthesis and brainstorming" but lacked consistent capability for novel threat generation [7fc28f]. - Anthropic February 2026 Risk Report: Confirmed that "we do not believe Claude Opus 4.6 meets the threshold for ASL-4." #### OpenAI - GPT-5 (late 2025/January 2026): Classified as "High" capability in the Biological and Chemical domain. Not "Critical." OpenAI implemented strong safeguards and treated it as High risk precautionarily. - GPT-5.2, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4 Thinking (through March 2026): All classified as "High" — the same tier. No model in the GPT-5 series has been classified as reaching Critical biological capability. GPT-5.4 Thinking (system card published March 5, 2026) was described as "closely matching" GPT-5.3-Codex results. #### Google DeepMind - Gemini 3 (late 2025/early 2026): Underwent "the most comprehensive set of safety evaluations of any Google AI model to date" against CCLs including CBRN risks. External evaluators included UK AISI, Apollo Research, Vaultis, and Dreadnode. Google deemed the model safe to deploy but did not publicly disclose specific biosecurity evaluation results or CCL proximity data [808a24]. #### Meta - No detailed public biosecurity evaluation results for recent Meta models (e.g., Llama 4) have been identified. Meta's framework is less transparent regarding specific biological risk scores. ### 4. 2026 International AI Safety Report (Published February 3, 2026) The report [e92596] confirmed: - A recent model outperformed 94% of domain experts at troubleshooting virology laboratory protocols. - In 2025, multiple developers released models with heightened safeguards because they could not rule out models assisting novices in developing biological weapons. - AI agents can now chain together capabilities using natural language interfaces to operate biological AI tools and laboratory equipment. - The report highlights an "evaluation gap" — benchmark performance often overstates practical utility. - Significant "evidence dilemma" — acting on incomplete data risks ineffective interventions, but waiting for conclusive data risks vulnerability. - 61.5% of high-performing biological AI tools remain open-source with no safeguards. ### 5. Expected Trajectory: March–December 2026 Based on the evidence gathered: Factors suggesting approach toward highest-tier thresholds: - Capabilities are doubling approximately every eight months [9c3f35]. - Anthropic's ASL-4 rule-out confidence is measurably declining between successive model generations (from "significantly far away" for Opus 4 in May 2025 to "substantial uncertainty" in the rule-out for Opus 4.6 in February 2026) [f21951][7fc28f]. - Successor models (e.g., potential Claude 5, GPT-6, Gemini 4, Llama 5) are likely to be released during this period with meaningfully improved capabilities. - Agentic capabilities and tool use are advancing rapidly, enabling more complex multi-step biological tasks. Factors suggesting thresholds may not be reached: - The highest-tier thresholds are deliberately set very high — involving novel weapons design, uplift for state programs, or qualitatively new threat vectors. - Current models still fail at end-to-end tasks requiring chaining multiple steps (e.g., plasmid design, synthesis screening evasion). No model has designed fragments that could both assemble into a viable plasmid AND evade synthesis screening [f21951]. - Models produce critical errors in protocols that render them non-viable even when they demonstrate knowledge [7fc28f]. - There is a gap between benchmark performance and real-world utility in biosecurity contexts [e92596]. - The "novel" requirement in most highest-tier definitions is a high bar — models must go beyond assisting with known agents to enabling truly novel threats. Key upcoming model releases (speculative, based on release cadence): - Anthropic may release a Claude 5 or Claude Opus 5 during this period - OpenAI may release further GPT-5 series models or a GPT-6 family - Google DeepMind may release Gemini 3.5 or Gemini 4 - Meta may release Llama 5 or subsequent models Each new generation would undergo biosecurity evaluations, and given the trend of narrowing margins, successive models will be closer to the thresholds. However, extrapolating from the current rate of progress vs. the remaining distance to the highest-tier thresholds, the evidence suggests models will be approaching but have not yet been confirmed as definitively reaching these thresholds during the March–December 2026 window.

SQ2: How mature and reliable is the current evaluation science for detecting dangerous biosecurity capabilities in AI models, and does the persistent 'zone of ambiguity' make it unlikely that any lab could confidently trigger a highest-tier biosecurity classification by end of 2026?

Summary: The current evaluation science for detecting dangerous biosecurity capabilities in AI models is characterized by a significant and well-documented "zone of ambiguity" that makes confidently distinguishing between High and Critical (or ASL-3 and ASL-4) risk levels extremely difficult. As of early 2026, multiple frontier labs have acknowledged this challenge: Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 System Card (February 2026) explicitly states that "confidently ruling out these thresholds is becoming increasingly difficult" due to benchmark saturation, epistemic uncertainty, measurement limitations, and limited understanding of threat actors [cfbcf4]. The International AI Safety Report 2026 (February 2026) identifies a fundamental "evaluation gap" where standardized benchmarks fail to predict real-world risk, and real-world uplift studies are constrained by legal and treaty obligations [c595a7]. Current methodologies include automated knowledge evaluations, agentic task-based assessments, expert red-teaming, and uplift trials, but these face critical gaps: (1) difficulty testing wet-lab skills due to legal/ethical constraints of the Biological Weapons Convention, forcing reliance on benign proxy tasks; (2) inability to assess tacit knowledge transfer—the practical, embodied know-how needed for actual bioweapons work; and (3) challenges in measuring uplift over freely available baseline information. A landmark wet-lab RCT (June–August 2025, n=153, published February 2026 by METR-affiliated researchers) found that while LLMs uplift novice performance on computational biology tasks, their effect in physical laboratories remains modest and inconsistent, underscoring the gap between benchmark performance and real-world capability. Key ongoing improvement efforts include: AISI (UK AI Safety Institute) conducting end-to-end biosecurity red-teaming with OpenAI and Anthropic through 2025, revealing dozens of vulnerabilities; METR running real-world biological RCTs and developing evaluation infrastructure; the STREAM (ChemBio) standard (August 2025) establishing transparent reporting requirements for biosecurity evaluations; Epoch AI's critical June 2025 analysis showing publicly described benchmarks saturate quickly and fail to capture weapons-relevant capabilities; and the Frontier Model Forum's biosafety threshold work. Despite these gaps, the evaluation uncertainty does not straightforwardly prevent labs from acting. Labs have adopted precautionary approaches—OpenAI classified GPT-5 and subsequent models as "High" biological risk (January 2025 onward), and Anthropic activated ASL-3 protections for Claude Opus 4 (May 2025) and continued them for Claude Opus 4.6 (February 2026)—based on the inability to rule out risk rather than definitive proof of crossing critical thresholds. However, the same ambiguity makes triggering the highest tier (Critical/ASL-4) particularly challenging: Anthropic notes the margin for future rule-outs is "narrowing" but has not yet triggered ASL-4 [cfbcf4]. The evaluation gap creates a structural asymmetry where precautionary action at lower tiers is easier than definitive classification at the highest tier, potentially delaying formal highest-tier classifications even as capabilities advance rapidly.

Background: Even if a model possesses dangerous biological capabilities, the lab must be able to detect and measure those capabilities with sufficient confidence to formally classify the model at the highest tier. Anthropic's RSP v3.0 and February 2026 Risk Report explicitly acknowledge a 'zone of ambiguity' where models show significant biological knowledge but evaluation science is not yet robust enough to definitively assess whether capabilities cross the threshold. This question asks: (1) What is the current state of the art in biosecurity evaluations for AI models—what methodologies do labs use (red-teaming, structured access studies, benchmark suites), and how reliable are these at distinguishing 'High' from 'Critical' risk? (2) Are there known gaps in evaluation methodology—e.g., difficulty testing wet-lab skills, inability to assess tacit knowledge transfer, challenges with measuring uplift over open-source information? (3) Are there ongoing efforts (by labs, AISI, METR, or academic researchers) to improve biosecurity evaluation science that might mature before end of 2026? (4) Could the evaluation gap itself serve as a reason for labs to avoid triggering highest-tier classifications—i.e., if they cannot prove capabilities definitively, they may default to a lower classification? This is a critical crux because even rapidly advancing capabilities may not lead to a formal highest-tier classification if the evaluation tools are inadequate to support such a determination.

Detailed research

## 1. Current State-of-the-Art Methodologies (as of March 2026) ### Anthropic's Approach Anthropic uses a multi-faceted evaluation methodology for biological risk assessment, as detailed in the Claude Opus 4.6 System Card (February 6, 2026) [cfbcf4]: - Automated knowledge evaluations: Standard biology/virology benchmark tests - Skill-testing questions: Targeted probes of specific dangerous knowledge - Long-form agentic evaluations: Multi-step tasks including long-form virology tasks, multimodal virology, and DNA synthesis screening evasion - Expert red teaming and uplift trials: Controlled experiments where PhD-level biologists test the model's ability to serve as a "force multiplier" for complex biological tasks - Helpful-only model snapshots: Versions with safety guardrails removed to assess raw capability ceilings - Agentic harnesses: Software setups with extra tools to evaluate the model in realistic operational contexts Anthropic uses a tiered AI Safety Level (ASL) system. ASL-3 addresses capabilities that could "significantly assist individuals or groups with basic technical backgrounds" in CBRN activities. ASL-4 (the next tier, corresponding to CBRN-4 threshold) addresses capabilities providing "substantial uplift to moderately-resourced state programs, such as novel weapons design, significant acceleration of existing processes, or dramatic reduction in technical barriers" [cfbcf4]. ### OpenAI's Approach OpenAI uses its Preparedness Framework with four risk levels (Low, Medium, High, Critical) across multiple categories including Biological and Chemical. As documented in the GPT-5 System Card (January 2025) and GPT-5.4 Thinking System Card, OpenAI develops biological capability evaluations as indicators for High and Critical thresholds. OpenAI built an "early warning system" for LLM-aided biological threat creation that assesses end-to-end critical knowledge across five stages of biological threat pipelines. GPT-5 was classified as "High" biological risk in January 2025, and subsequent models (GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4 Thinking) have maintained this classification. Critical biological capability in OpenAI's framework involves "proliferating the ability to create a novel threat vector of the severity of a CDC Class A biological agent." ### Google DeepMind's Approach DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework (updated to version 3.0) defines "Critical Capability Levels" (CCLs) across domains including biosecurity, cybersecurity, autonomy, and machine learning R&D. Their evaluation suites assess risks from critical capabilities with emphasis on autonomous LLM agents. ### External Testing The UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) conducted end-to-end biosecurity red-teaming with OpenAI and Anthropic throughout 2025, revealing "dozens of vulnerabilities including new universal jailbreak paths" according to their 2025 Year in Review. The US CAISI and UK AISI have also conducted pre-deployment evaluations (e.g., Anthropic's Sonnet 3.5 upgrade in November 2024). ## 2. Known Gaps in Evaluation Methodology ### Benchmark Saturation The Claude Opus 4.6 System Card explicitly acknowledges that "models are approaching or surpassing the high levels of capability defined in current 'rule-out' evaluations (early proxies for thresholds)" [cfbcf4]. This means the benchmarks designed to detect when a model crosses a threshold are becoming less informative as models improve. Epoch AI's June 2025 analysis ("Do the biorisk evaluations of AI labs actually measure the risk of developing bioweapons?") found that "publicly described benchmarks are common but saturate quickly" and fail to capture weapons-relevant capabilities. ### Wet-Lab Skills Testing Gap The International AI Safety Report 2026 (February 2026) identifies that evaluations are "frequently conducted in controlled lab environments that do not account for the 'messy' real-world constraints of weapons development, such as the difficulty of acquiring specialized equipment, obtaining regulated materials, or executing complex, multi-step physical procedures" [c595a7]. Real-world uplift studies are constrained by legal obligations under the Biological Weapons Convention, forcing researchers to use "benign proxy tasks" (e.g., synthesizing pharmaceuticals or culturing low-risk bacteria) that may not accurately reflect weapons development risk [c595a7]. A landmark RCT published in February 2026 (arXiv:2602.16703, conducted June–August 2025 with n=153) by METR-affiliated researchers measured mid-2025 LLM assistance on novice performance in biology. The key finding: "LLMs uplift novice performance on computational biology tasks, while their effect in physical laboratories remains modest and inconsistent." This underscores that benchmark-level performance overstates practical wet-lab utility. ### Tacit Knowledge Transfer Tacit knowledge—the practical, embodied know-how that cannot be easily articulated in text (e.g., how to handle equipment, recognize procedural errors by feel or sight, adjust protocols in real-time)—is extremely difficult to evaluate in AI systems. Multiple sources reference this as a fundamental gap. The Virology Capabilities Test (VCT, arXiv:2504.16137) notes that "among the best ways to resolve this uncertainty would be to run a wet-lab uplift study" and references the challenge of encoding "tacit knowledge and the biological weapons regime." The RAND perspective on "Measuring Biological Capabilities and Risks of AI Agents" (published late 2025/early 2026) specifically flags this as a key evaluation limitation. ### Measuring Uplift Over Baseline Information A core challenge is quantifying how much AI adds beyond information already freely available on the internet, in textbooks, and in scientific literature. The International AI Safety Report 2026 describes this as the "evidence dilemma" [c595a7]. The NIST-aligned framework (NIST AI 800-1) explicitly grapples with the problem that "experience, tacit knowledge, and technical support networks" create a high baseline that makes marginal AI uplift difficult to measure. ### Epistemic Uncertainty About Threat Models Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 System Card identifies "fundamental uncertainty regarding the necessary components of the threat model and how to map specific model capabilities to real-world risk" as well as "limited understanding of relevant threat actors and how their capabilities map to real-world risks, leading to a 'substantial degree of uncertainty' about the rule-out" [cfbcf4]. ## 3. Ongoing Efforts to Improve Biosecurity Evaluation Science ### METR (Model Evaluation & Threat Research) METR has been a leading force in improving evaluation methodology. In February 2026, they published "Five lessons from having helped run an AI-Biology RCT," sharing insights from a real-world wet-lab study. Their blog noted that "in early 2025, AI systems began outperforming biology experts on biology benchmarks—OpenAI's o3 outperformed 94% of virology experts." METR is also developing broader evaluation infrastructure and has published on risk transparency requirements (June 2025). ### UK AISI (AI Safety Institute) AISI conducted end-to-end biosecurity red-teaming with OpenAI and Anthropic in 2025, revealing dozens of vulnerabilities. They have been "sharpening and scaling" their mission per their 2025 year in review, and enforcement of the EU AI Act compliance (for which they provide guidance) begins August 2026. ### STREAM (ChemBio) Standard Published in August 2025 (arXiv:2508.09853) by researchers including those from METR and the Governance of AI Institute, STREAM (Standard for Transparently Reporting Evaluations in AI Model Reports) establishes a framework for transparent, comparable reporting of chemical and biological capability evaluations. This addresses the problem that different labs use incomparable methodologies. It was cited by the International AI Safety Report 2026 and RAND. ### Frontier Model Forum The Frontier Model Forum published work on "Frontier AI Biosafety Thresholds" defining predefined notions of risk and when additional action is warranted. ### Epoch AI Epoch AI's June 2025 analysis provided a critical public assessment of whether current lab evaluations actually measure bioweapons risk, identifying key gaps and saturation problems. ### Academic and Government Efforts - The FAS (Federation of American Scientists) published a January 2026 report on AI-Bio deterrence posture from a June 2025 roundtable. - RAND published a perspective on "Measuring Biological Capabilities and Risks of AI Agents" (late 2025/early 2026). - The NTI (Nuclear Threat Initiative) published an AIxBio Horizon Scan for Winter 2025-2026 noting "rapid capability advances are outpacing governance frameworks and safety measures." - The Council on Strategic Risks published an "AIxBio Landscape" assessment in July 2025. - The Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026 has been introduced, requiring assessment of biosecurity oversight. ## 4. The "Zone of Ambiguity" and Its Effect on Highest-Tier Classification ### Anthropic's RSP v3.0 Definition Anthropic's RSP v3.0 (published in 2025) explicitly describes the zone of ambiguity: "Biological risks provide an example of this 'zone of ambiguity'. Our models now show enough biological knowledge that they pass most tests we [use]..." The document acknowledges that evaluation science is not yet robust enough to definitively assess whether capabilities cross the highest threshold. ### How the Zone of Ambiguity Affects Classification Decisions The Claude Opus 4.6 System Card (February 2026) provides the clearest picture of how this works in practice [cfbcf4]: 1. Benchmark saturation: Current "rule-out" evaluations are approaching their ceiling of usefulness 2. Narrowing margins: "Confidently ruling out these thresholds is becoming increasingly difficult" 3. Measurement limitations: "Parts of the CBRN-4 threshold require more sophisticated forms of measurement than are currently available" 4. Decision outcome: Anthropic concluded Opus 4.6 does not cross CBRN-4 but acknowledges the margin is narrowing and "subsequent models will present more challenging assessments" ### Structural Asymmetry in Classification The evaluation gap creates a structural asymmetry: - Lower-tier activation is easier: Labs can (and do) activate precautionary measures like ASL-3 or "High" based on the inability to rule out risk. This has happened: Anthropic activated ASL-3 for Claude Opus 4 (May 2025) and maintained it for Opus 4.6 (February 2026). OpenAI classified GPT-5 as "High" biological risk (January 2025) and maintained this for subsequent models. - Highest-tier classification is harder: Triggering Critical/ASL-4 requires either (a) more confident evidence of threshold-crossing capabilities, or (b) a precautionary approach so extreme that mere inability to rule out ASL-4 triggers it. Currently, labs appear to be in the former mode for their highest tiers—requiring positive evidence rather than inability to rule out. - Precautionary vs. definitive: The International AI Safety Report 2026 notes that in 2025, labs "implemented heightened safeguards" as "a 'precautionary approach' taken because the labs could not rule out the possibility that the models could assist novices, even in the absence of 'definitive evidence' that the models had crossed specific critical capability thresholds" [c595a7]. This pattern applies to the High/ASL-3 tier but has not yet been applied to the Critical/ASL-4 tier. ### Reliability of Tools to Distinguish High from Critical The tools to distinguish between High and Critical risk are unreliable for several compounding reasons: 1. Benchmarks designed to detect Critical-level capabilities are saturating before they can provide clear signal 2. The most informative test—a real-world wet-lab uplift study with dangerous agents—cannot be conducted due to legal and ethical constraints 3. Benign proxy tasks used as substitutes may not generalize to actual threat scenarios 4. The RCT evidence (February 2026) shows a disconnect between computational benchmark performance (where LLMs excel) and physical lab performance (where uplift is modest) 5. Threat model uncertainty means even if capabilities could be precisely measured, mapping them to real-world risk involves substantial subjective judgment ### Could the Evaluation Gap Prevent Highest-Tier Classification? Yes, the evaluation gap could serve as a reason—or at minimum, a contributing factor—for labs to avoid formally triggering highest-tier classifications. The logic works as follows: - If evaluation tools cannot definitively demonstrate that capabilities cross the Critical/ASL-4 threshold, the natural default under current decision frameworks is to classify at the lower tier - Anthropic's own language suggests this is the current posture: they rule out CBRN-4 for Opus 4.6 while acknowledging "substantial degree of uncertainty" [cfbcf4] - However, this is not a permanent barrier. If future models show qualitatively new capabilities (e.g., de novo pathogen design confirmed through safe proxies), or if evaluation science matures through ongoing efforts (METR, AISI, STREAM), the evidence base could become sufficient for a highest-tier classification - The precautionary principle could also be extended: some Anthropic engineers reportedly believe models may already be at or near ASL-4 capability, suggesting internal pressure to reclassify may build even without definitive evaluation evidence ### Timeline Considerations Multiple trends suggest the zone of ambiguity may narrow (but not necessarily resolve) by end of 2026: - METR and academic groups are producing real-world wet-lab evidence that complements benchmarks - AISI is actively developing more sophisticated evaluation suites - STREAM ChemBio provides a common reporting standard enabling better cross-lab comparison - The Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026 may accelerate government evaluation capacity - However, fundamental constraints (inability to test actual bioweapons scenarios, difficulty measuring tacit knowledge transfer) are unlikely to be fully overcome within this timeframe

SQ3: What are the strategic incentives and disincentives for frontier AI labs to publicly classify a model at the highest biosecurity risk tier, given the recent trend of loosening safety commitments and the competitive dynamics among labs?

Summary: The strategic incentives facing frontier AI labs strongly favor avoiding publicly classifying a model at the highest biosecurity risk tier. Five interlocking dynamics drive this conclusion: 1. Structural loosening of safety commitments (2025-2026). Anthropic's RSP v3.0, announced on February 24, 2026, removed the binding commitment to "pause the scaling and/or delay the deployment of new models" when safety measures fall behind capabilities [b7a08a]. The new policy replaces binary "bright red lines" that would trigger automatic halts with more flexible "Frontier Safety Roadmaps" and periodic "Risk Reports" published every 3-6 months [b2a35b]. Anthropic explicitly stated that ASL-4 and beyond are "beyond the containment capabilities of any single company," framing unilateral action as futile [b7a08a]. Meanwhile, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework v2 (April 2025) includes a competitive adjustment clause: "If another frontier AI developer releases a high-risk system without comparable safeguards, we may adjust our requirements." This creates a structural off-ramp from the highest-tier classification for both labs. 2. Massive commercial and reputational costs of triggering the highest tier. A "Critical" classification would, under most frameworks, require halting deployment or severely restricting access. No lab has ever triggered its highest tier. For Anthropic (ASL-5), OpenAI (Critical), Google DeepMind (highest CCL), or Meta, doing so would cede market share to rivals, alarm investors during a period of massive capital raises, and potentially invite regulatory action. Anthropic's Jared Kaplan explicitly argued that pausing while "rivals are blazing ahead" does not benefit anyone [b7a08a]. 3. Competitive dynamics create a prisoner's dilemma. If one lab classifies a model at the highest tier and restricts deployment, rivals gain a direct commercial advantage by deploying comparable models without such classification. OpenAI's adjustment clause explicitly addresses this: it creates a mechanism to lower safeguards if competitors release high-risk systems, rather than a mechanism to raise them. This creates a race-to-the-bottom dynamic where each lab has incentives to classify just below the highest tier. 4. Flexibility in evaluation methodology provides discretion. Labs design their own evaluation benchmarks, define their own thresholds, and interpret results internally before publishing. The shift from binding commitments to "living documents" (Anthropic) and adjustable frameworks (OpenAI) gives labs significant discretion in how they classify models. As of early 2026, models are classified at intermediate tiers: Anthropic at ASL-3 (since May 2025), OpenAI's GPT-5 classified as "high capability" (not Critical) in biosecurity, and Google DeepMind's Gemini 3 not crossing any Critical Capability Levels. 5. Countervailing pressures exist but are weaker. Signaling safety maturity could build trust with regulators and the public. External pressure from organizations like METR, the UK AI Security Institute, and the Frontier Model Forum pushes for transparency. The International AI Safety Report 2026 and California's AI policy report increase scrutiny. However, these pressures have not yet proven strong enough to override commercial incentives—as evidenced by the loosening trend across all labs throughout 2025-2026. Net assessment for forecasters: The institutional incentive structures strongly favor labs classifying models at intermediate tiers (e.g., "High" or ASL-3) rather than triggering their highest tier. The removal of binding pause commitments, the introduction of competitive adjustment clauses, the commercial costs of restricting deployment, and the discretion labs have in evaluation methodology all point in the same direction. The most likely path to a highest-tier classification would require either (a) external evaluators publicly demonstrating capabilities that make it impossible for a lab to deny, (b) a regulatory mandate, or (c) a catastrophic incident that forces reclassification. Absent these forcing functions, the incentive environment as of March 2026 makes voluntary highest-tier classification unlikely.

Background: This question addresses a crucial behavioral and institutional crux: even if a model's capabilities technically warrant a highest-tier classification, will the lab choose to formally declare it? Several competing dynamics are at play: (1) The trend of loosening safety commitments—Anthropic's RSP v3.0 removed binding commitments to pause scaling if safety measures fall behind, and OpenAI's Preparedness Framework v2 includes a provision to 'adjust' safeguards if rivals release high-risk systems without comparable protections. This suggests labs may be structurally incentivized to avoid triggering their own highest tiers. (2) Reputational and commercial costs—publicly classifying a model as 'Critical' biosecurity risk could invite regulatory action, public backlash, or investor concern. No lab has ever triggered its highest tier. (3) Signaling value—conversely, triggering the highest tier could demonstrate safety maturity and build trust with regulators and the public, especially if the lab can show effective mitigations. (4) Competitive dynamics—if one lab classifies a model at the highest tier and pauses or restricts deployment, rivals gain a commercial advantage. OpenAI's 'adjustment' clause explicitly addresses this scenario. (5) External pressure—regulators, independent evaluators, and civil society may increase pressure on labs to be transparent. The question asks researchers to analyze these incentive structures and assess which direction they net out. This is important because the resolution of the forecasting question depends not just on capability, but on the institutional decision to formally classify.

Detailed research

## Detailed Analysis of Strategic Incentives and Disincentives ### I. The Trend of Loosening Safety Commitments Anthropic's RSP v3.0 (February 24, 2026) Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy underwent its most consequential revision to date. According to Business Insider reporting on February 25, 2026 [b7a08a], and a detailed TIME exclusive [b2a35b], the key changes were: - Removal of the pause commitment: The specific binding commitment removed was the pledge "to pause the scaling and/or delay the deployment of new models" when advancements outpaced safety measures [b7a08a]. This had been the core mechanism by which a highest-tier classification would have forced action. - Elimination of binary thresholds ("bright red lines"): The company moved away from predetermined capability thresholds that would automatically trigger a halt to development [b2a35b]. Under the previous RSP, crossing from ASL-3 to ASL-4 would have required demonstrating that adequate safety measures were in place before proceeding. The new framework instead uses "Frontier Safety Roadmaps" and periodic "Risk Reports" published every 3-6 months. - Competitive framing: Chief Science Officer Jared Kaplan explicitly argued that unilateral pauses are counterproductive when "rivals are blazing ahead" [b7a08a]. The policy now states that if one developer pauses while others move forward without strong mitigations, the result is a "less safe" world [b2a35b]. - Conditional delays only: The new policy promises to "delay" development only if leaders consider Anthropic to be the leader of the AI race and believe the risks of catastrophe to be significant [b2a35b]. This dramatically narrows the circumstances under which a pause might occur. - ASL-4+ framing: Anthropic explicitly stated that higher theoretical risk levels (ASL-4 and beyond) cannot be managed by a single company alone [b7a08a], pre-emptively framing any highest-tier classification as requiring industry-wide action rather than unilateral response. The practical impact: the mechanism by which a highest-tier biosecurity classification would have forced a hard stop has been dismantled. As METR's Chris Painter noted, this creates a "frog-boiling" effect where danger may ramp up incrementally without a single clear moment triggering an alarm [b2a35b]. OpenAI's Preparedness Framework v2 (April 2025) OpenAI's updated framework introduced several significant changes: - Competitive adjustment clause: The exact language, as reported across multiple sources, states: "If another frontier AI developer releases a high-risk system without comparable safeguards, we may adjust our requirements. However, we will not release any model that we believe poses Critical risk." This clause creates a formal mechanism by which OpenAI can lower its safety standards in response to competitive pressure—an explicit acknowledgment that safety commitments are contingent on competitor behavior. - Risk tiers: OpenAI uses Low, Medium, High, and Critical tiers. Models classified as Critical are not to be deployed. But the framework allows deployment of models that would be "High risk" without mitigations, provided sufficient safeguards are in place. - Narrowed scope of assessment: Fortune reported (April 16, 2025) that OpenAI stopped assessing models for the risk of persuasion/manipulation as a separate category, narrowing the domains in which a Critical classification could be triggered. - Forward-looking risk signals: OpenAI executives told Axios (April 2025) that they anticipate upcoming models will soon trigger the "high-risk" classification in biosecurity—but notably, they framed this as "high" rather than "Critical." In July 2025, OpenAI reportedly classified a new model as "high capability" in the biological and chemical domain. GPT-5 was classified as "high capability" (not Critical) in biosecurity by RAND analysis. ### II. Reputational and Commercial Costs of Highest-Tier Classification A highest-tier classification carries several concrete costs: - Deployment restrictions: Under most frameworks, a Critical/ASL-5 classification would require either halting deployment entirely or severely restricting access. This directly impacts revenue. - Investor concern: Labs are in the midst of massive fundraising rounds. Anthropic raised $60 billion at a $61.5 billion valuation (early 2025). OpenAI's $40 billion round (late 2025). A public declaration that a model poses the highest level of biosecurity risk could materially impact valuation and future fundraising. - Regulatory trigger: A public highest-tier classification could provide ammunition for regulators—whether the EU AI Act enforcement, US state legislation (California's various AI bills), or executive action—to impose mandatory restrictions or licensing requirements. - Precedent-setting: No lab has ever triggered its highest tier. Being the first to do so would set a precedent that competitors would be reluctant to follow, creating an asymmetric competitive disadvantage. ### III. Competitive Dynamics: The Prisoner's Dilemma The competitive dynamics create a classic prisoner's dilemma: - Unilateral classification = commercial disadvantage: If Anthropic classifies a model at ASL-4/5 and restricts deployment, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta can deploy comparable models without such restrictions. - OpenAI's clause explicitly addresses this: The "adjustment" clause is designed for exactly this scenario—if a rival deploys a high-risk system, OpenAI can lower its own standards rather than unilaterally maintaining higher ones. - Anthropic's new framing mirrors this logic: By arguing that unilateral pauses produce a "less safe" world, Anthropic has pre-committed to a framework where the appropriate response to dangerous capabilities is not to pause, but to continue development with mitigations. - Race-to-the-bottom dynamics: Multiple commentators (including on LessWrong and the EA Forum) have characterized these policy changes as creating a race to the bottom. The original purpose of RSPs was explicitly to reject this logic—Anthropic's RSP v1.0 was designed to "bind itself to the mast." The shift away from this is a fundamental change in the competitive equilibrium. ### IV. Signaling Value (Countervailing Incentive) There are reasons a lab might choose to trigger the highest tier: - Trust-building with regulators: Demonstrating that the framework "works" by actually triggering it could build credibility with policymakers considering mandatory regulation. - Safety leadership branding: Anthropic in particular has built its brand on safety. Triggering the highest tier with effective mitigations could reinforce this positioning. - External validation: If independent evaluators (METR, UK AI Security Institute, etc.) publicly demonstrate that a model has capabilities warranting the highest tier, refusing to classify it as such would create a credibility gap. - Accountability reports: Anthropic's new policy requires public risk reports every 3-6 months. These create some transparency pressure—but the reports are drafted by the labs themselves. However, these signaling benefits are significantly outweighed by the commercial costs, especially in the current competitive environment. ### V. External Pressure Several external forces push toward transparency: - UK AI Security Institute (AISI): Conducts independent evaluations of frontier models and publishes results. The December 2025 Frontier AI Trends Report synthesized two years of evaluations. - METR: Provides independent third-party evaluations and reviews of lab safety policies. Has publicly critiqued Anthropic's RSP v3.0 changes. - International AI Safety Report 2026 (February 2026): Synthesized research on capabilities and risks, increasing the salience of biosecurity risks. - Frontier Model Forum: Published biosafety threshold frameworks and risk taxonomies. - Future of Life Institute AI Safety Index: Published multiple editions (Winter 2025, Summer 2025) scoring labs on safety practices. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind consistently lead, but the index highlights "persistent weaknesses in risk assessment." - California AI policy report (June 2025): Recommended oversight for frontier models. However, none of these external actors have the power to force a lab to classify a model at the highest tier. Their influence is primarily reputational and anticipatory (of future regulation). ### VI. Current State of Classifications (as of March 2026) - Anthropic: Models at ASL-3 since May 2025 (activated for Claude Opus 4). The February 2026 risk report discusses risks but models remain at ASL-3. - OpenAI: GPT-5 classified as "high capability" in biosecurity (not Critical). GPT-5-thinking also treated as high capability. OpenAI anticipated in April 2025 that future models would reach "high-risk" classification. - Google DeepMind: Gemini 3 evaluation found no Critical Capability Levels crossed and no new alert thresholds reached. - Meta: Less detailed public information available; has a Frontier AI Framework with biosecurity risk tiers but has not publicly triggered any highest-level classification. ### VII. Net Assessment The incentive structures overwhelmingly favor avoiding highest-tier classification. The key factors: 1. Structural mechanisms for avoidance have been built in: Removal of binding pause commitments (Anthropic), competitive adjustment clauses (OpenAI), and flexible evaluation methodologies give labs significant discretion. 2. No lab has ever triggered the highest tier, creating strong path dependence against being the first. 3. Commercial costs are concrete and immediate; signaling benefits are diffuse and uncertain. 4. The competitive dynamic is self-reinforcing: each lab's loosening of commitments provides justification for other labs to do the same. 5. External pressure is real but insufficient: independent evaluators can create reputational pressure but cannot force classification decisions. The most plausible pathways to a highest-tier classification would be: - An external evaluator publicly demonstrates capabilities that make denial impossible - A regulatory mandate requiring specific classification - A catastrophic incident (e.g., an actual biosecurity event linked to an AI model) - A major whistleblower disclosure that creates public pressure Absent these forcing functions, the current incentive environment makes voluntary highest-tier biosecurity classification unlikely in the March-December 2026 timeframe.

SQ4: What is the likelihood that any of the four labs will revise their safety frameworks before end of 2026 in ways that raise, redefine, or otherwise move the goalposts on their highest-tier biosecurity thresholds, making formal classification less likely?

Summary: Summary: Likelihood of Framework Revisions That Raise Biosecurity Thresholds (March–December 2026) All four major frontier AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta) have established a clear pattern of revising their safety frameworks, with each revision generally adding flexibility, simplifying structures, or redefining thresholds. This pattern makes it moderately to highly likely that further revisions will occur before end of 2026. Here are the key findings: Anthropic: Has undergone 5 RSP versions (v1.0 in Sep 2023 → v3.0 on Feb 24, 2026). The most recent RSP v3.0 removed the unconditional commitment to pause development if dangerous capabilities are found, replacing it with a more flexible approach. Critically, ASL-4 remains "largely undefined" as of RSP v3.0 — Anthropic intentionally left it undefined. Their Frontier Safety Roadmap (published Feb 2026) commits to selecting 1–3 safety projects by April 1, 2026, which may include ASL-4 definition work. ASL-4 is likely to be formally defined sometime in 2026, but Anthropic has signaled it will set a high bar — they explicitly stated they could have "defined ASL-4 and ASL-5 safeguards in ways that made compliance easy to achieve—but this would undermine the purpose." Meanwhile, their Feb 2026 Risk Report notes automated evaluations can no longer rule out ASL-4 level autonomy, suggesting models are approaching the threshold even before it is formally defined. OpenAI: Updated from Preparedness Framework Beta (Dec 2023) to v2 (April 15, 2025). Key changes: removed Low and Medium risk levels entirely (they "were not operationally involved"), narrowed CBRN to biological and chemical only (removing nuclear/radiological), removed manipulation/persuasion as a tracked risk category, and added AI Self-improvement and Long-range Autonomy as new tracked categories. The "Critical" tier remains the highest, defined as capability that "could introduce unprecedented new pathways to severe harm." These changes broadly added flexibility and reduced the number of categories that could trigger a classification. Another revision is plausible before end of 2026 given the ~16-month gap between v1 and v2. Google DeepMind: Updated through FSF v1 (May 2024), v2 (Feb 2025), and v3 (Sep 22, 2025) — roughly every 6–8 months. The v3 update shifted methodology from assessing "model capability in isolation" to assessing "additional expected harm that may result in the real world," which is arguably a higher bar [4bdbc1]. The biosecurity CCL ("CBRN Uplift Level 1") requires showing that a model "provides low to medium resourced actors uplift in reference scenarios resulting in additional expected harm at severe scale" [4bdbc1]. No model has triggered a CCL to date [4bdbc1]. Given the ~6-month revision cycle, a v4 update is plausible by mid-2026. Meta: Published its Frontier AI Framework in February 2025, with two tiers (High-risk and Critical-risk) focused on cybersecurity and chemical/biological weapons. No known revisions as of March 2026. Critical risk is defined as models "too dangerous to develop." Given that other labs revise every 6–12 months, an update from Meta is plausible but uncertain in 2026. Regulatory Constraints: External constraints are mostly weak. The Seoul AI Safety Commitments (May 2024) are voluntary and require labs to set thresholds but do not specify what those thresholds must be. The EU AI Act's GPAI Code of Practice requires safety frameworks and risk assessments for models above 10^25 FLOPs, with enforcement beginning August 2026, but does not dictate specific internal threshold levels. The Trump administration revoked Biden's AI safety EO in January 2025 and has actively deregulated, imposing no federal constraints on labs' internal frameworks. California's SB 53 (signed Sep 29, 2025) requires transparency about safety frameworks but does not dictate threshold levels. In sum, no current regulation prevents labs from raising their own thresholds. Overall Assessment: The likelihood is moderate-to-high that at least one lab will revise its framework before end of 2026 in ways that add flexibility. Anthropic is the most consequential case: ASL-4 will likely be formally defined in 2026, and when it is, the definition will likely set a deliberately high bar. OpenAI and DeepMind are on revision cycles that make updates plausible. Regulatory constraints are too weak to prevent threshold revisions. The net effect is that framework revisions could make formal highest-tier classification somewhat less likely by raising or redefining what triggers such classification.

Background: A key mechanism by which labs could avoid triggering their highest-tier biosecurity classifications is by revising the frameworks themselves—raising thresholds, adding ambiguity to definitions, or introducing new intermediate tiers. This question investigates: (1) The historical pattern of framework revisions—Anthropic has gone through three RSP versions (the original, v2, and v3.0 in February 2026), OpenAI updated its Preparedness Framework in April 2025, Google DeepMind reached FSF v3.0 in September 2025, and Meta published its framework in February 2025. Each revision has generally added flexibility. (2) Whether Anthropic's ASL-4, which remains 'largely undefined' per the RSP v3.0, is likely to be formally defined in 2026, and if so, whether it will be defined in a way that is easily triggerable or deliberately set at a very high bar. (3) Whether OpenAI, Google DeepMind, or Meta might update their frameworks before end of 2026, potentially revising what 'Critical' means. (4) Whether there are any regulatory or external constraints (e.g., the EU AI Act, Seoul commitments, US executive orders) that limit labs' ability to revise their own thresholds upward. This question matters because if labs can preemptively redefine thresholds, the resolution criteria (which reference 'the then-current' framework version) could be affected. The resolution criteria specify that the classification must be under the lab's own published framework, so a revised framework that sets an unreachably high bar would prevent resolution.
