Detailed research

1. FY2027 NDAA: Timeline and Historical Precedent The NDAA is the single most important must-pass legislative vehicle for the remainder of 2026. It has been enacted annually for over 60 consecutive years. The typical NDAA process follows a well-established pattern: - February: President submits budget request (statutory deadline: first Monday in February) - Spring/Summer: Armed Services Committees hold hearings and markups - Summer/Fall: House and Senate floor votes on respective versions - Fall/Winter: Conference committee negotiations - December: Conference report passed and signed into law Historical signing dates for recent NDAAs: - FY2026 NDAA: Signed December 18, 2025 (P.L. 119-60) - FY2025 NDAA: Signed December 23, 2024 (P.L. 118-159) - FY2024 NDAA: Signed December 22, 2023 (P.L. 118-31) - FY2023 NDAA: Signed December 23, 2022 (P.L. 117-263) - FY2022 NDAA: Signed December 27, 2021 (P.L. 117-81) - FY2021 NDAA: Signed January 1, 2021 (P.L. 116-283, after a veto override) - FY2020 NDAA: Signed December 20, 2019 (P.L. 116-92) This record shows that in 6 of the last 7 years, the NDAA was signed by December 27. The one exception (FY2021) involved a presidential veto and override, with enactment on January 1. This strongly suggests the FY2027 NDAA can be expected to be enacted by late December 2026, well within the December 31, 2026 deadline. Current FY2027 NDAA status (as of March 19, 2026): - The FY2027 President's budget request has been delayed; the White House targets release for the week of March 30, 2026 (Roll Call, March 4, 2026). - Individual House members have already begun accepting FY2027 NDAA and appropriations requests, with deadlines as early as February-March 2026. - The House Armed Services Committee typically marks up the NDAA in June-July; the Senate Armed Services Committee follows a similar timeline. - For the FY2026 NDAA, HASC markup was July 15, 2025, SASC markup was July 9-11, 2025, and the bill was signed December 18, 2025. The late budget submission (approximately 8 weeks behind schedule) may compress the committee markup timeline but is unlikely to prevent December enactment, as similar delays have occurred in prior years. 2. FY2026 Appropriations Status As of March 19, 2026: - 11 of 12 FY2026 appropriations bills have been enacted. The timeline was: - Three bills (Commerce-Justice-Science, Energy-Water, Interior-Environment) were passed as part of the November 2025 CR package. - Agriculture, Military Construction-VA, and Legislative Branch were enacted in subsequent packages. - H.R. 7148 (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026) was signed February 3, 2026, covering 5 additional bills: Defense; Labor-HHS-Education; Transportation-HUD; Financial Services; and others. - Total: 11 of 12 enacted. - Homeland Security is the only remaining bill. A partial DHS shutdown began approximately February 14, 2026. The House passed H.R. 7744 (DHS Appropriations Act, 2026) on March 5, 2026, but the Senate rejected it on March 12, 2026. The DHS bill will eventually be resolved (either through a full-year bill, another CR, or a negotiated package), but as a single-agency appropriation, it is an unlikely vehicle for biosecurity policy provisions unrelated to homeland security. That said, DHS does include CISA and other agencies with some biosecurity relevance, making it a theoretical but unlikely carrier. 3. Iran War Defense Supplemental A major new development: as of mid-March 2026, the U.S. is engaged in military operations in Iran. Key developments: - The Pentagon is seeking supplemental funding estimated at $50-200+ billion (Washington Post, March 18, 2026; Breaking Defense, March 2026; NBC News). - Speaker Johnson called a supplemental funding bill "inevitable" (The Hill, Politico, March 2026). - Senate Democrats are split on supplemental funding. - The Pentagon comptroller has not specified when the formal request will be sent to Congress. A defense supplemental is a must-pass bill that could move through Congress in 2026. Historically, wartime supplementals have served as vehicles for additional legislative provisions. However, the timing is highly uncertain — the formal request hasn't been submitted yet, and congressional debate could take months. This represents a significant new legislative vehicle that didn't exist when the forecasting question was initially framed. 4. Second Reconciliation Bill ("Reconciliation 2.0") Following the enactment of the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act" (signed July 4, 2025, P.L. 119-21), House Republicans are discussing a second reconciliation package: - House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington indicated interest in targeting fraud, waste, and abuse, as well as healthcare, housing, and energy costs (Politico, March 10, 2026). - The Republican Study Committee published a "Reconciliation 2.0 Framework" in January 2026. - Some have suggested using reconciliation for defense spending related to the Iran conflict. - Timeline: Very early stages as of March 2026. Even if pursued aggressively, reconciliation takes 3-6 months from budget resolution to final passage. However, reconciliation bills are subject to the Byrd Rule, which limits provisions to those with budgetary impact. A regulatory mandate for nucleic acid synthesis screening — which is primarily a regulatory/policy provision — would likely be ruled out under the Byrd Rule unless it could be framed as having a direct and significant budgetary impact. This makes reconciliation an extremely unlikely vehicle for a synthesis screening mandate. 5. FY2027 Appropriations The FY2027 appropriations process is just beginning. With the President's budget not yet submitted, committee hearings and markups are months away. Full-year FY2027 appropriations bills are virtually certain not to be enacted by December 31, 2026. Historically, full-year appropriations are almost never enacted before the start of the fiscal year (October 1), and usually require CRs extending into the following calendar year. A CR to extend FY2026 funding levels past September 30, 2026, is highly likely, but CRs typically don't include new policy provisions like screening mandates. 6. Standalone Biosecurity Legislation Two relevant bills have been introduced: - S.3741 (Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026): Introduced January 29, 2026, by Senators Cotton (R-AR) and Klobuchar (D-MN). The bill directs the Commerce Department to require gene synthesis labs to screen orders and customers, and to compile a list of dangerous genetic sequences. It has bipartisan support and endorsements from organizations like NTI and FAS. Referred to the Senate Commerce Committee. No committee action as of March 2026. - H.R. 3029 (Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act): Introduced by Rep. Salinas (D-OR). Authorizes $5M/year through NIST for screening standards. More limited in scope — focuses on standards development rather than a universal mandate. Neither bill has progressed beyond introduction. Standalone biosecurity bills face significant hurdles: they must compete for limited floor time, may face industry opposition, and lack the urgency of must-pass legislation. Their most realistic path to enactment is attachment to a must-pass vehicle such as the FY2027 NDAA. The FY2026 NDAA precedent is instructive: it included the BIOSECURE Act (addressing Chinese biotech companies) but did NOT include a universal DNA synthesis screening mandate, suggesting that while biosecurity provisions can be attached to the NDAA, a synthesis screening mandate specifically was not prioritized in the most recent cycle. 7. Congressional Calendar and Lame-Duck Session Key dates for the remainder of 2026: - March 30 (approx.): Expected release of FY2027 President's budget - June-July: Expected Armed Services Committee markups of FY2027 NDAA - August 10 – September 11: Senate State Work Period (recess) - September 30: End of FY2026; likely need for CR to fund FY2027 - October 5 – November 6: Senate State Work Period (pre-election recess) - November 3, 2026: Midterm elections - November 9 – December 18/20: Lame-duck session - December 18, 2026: Target adjournment for both chambers - December 21-31: Non-legislative period - January 3, 2027: 119th Congress expires The lame-duck session (approximately 5-6 weeks post-election) is the critical window for: - FY2027 NDAA conference report and final passage - Potential year-end legislative packages - Defense supplemental (if not already enacted) - Any remaining must-pass legislation Historically, the lame-duck period is when the most consequential year-end legislation moves, often under time pressure. This creates both opportunities (attachment of additional provisions to must-pass bills) and constraints (limited floor time, leadership prioritization). SQ4: What is the Trump administration's current position on mandatory universal nucleic acid synthesis screening legislation, and would the President likely sign such a bill if it reached his desk?

Summary: The Trump administration has signaled strong interest in extending nucleic acid synthesis screening beyond federally funded orders through Executive Order 14292 (signed May 5, 2025), which directed OSTP to revise the 2024 Framework within 90 days (~August 3, 2025) and develop a broader strategy—including legislative proposals—within 180 days (~November 1, 2025). However, as of March 2026, there is no public evidence that either the revised framework or the broader strategy has been released, meaning both deadlines appear to have been missed. The administration's AI Action Plan (July 2025) addressed nucleic acid synthesis screening but only proposed requirements tied to federally funded institutions, not universal mandates for all providers [b2247e]. S. 3741, the Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026, introduced January 29, 2026 by Senators Cotton (R-AR) and Klobuchar (D-MN), would mandate universal screening by all synthesis providers regardless of funding source [049632], but the Trump administration has not explicitly endorsed this bill. Multiple endorsements have come from organizations like the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology and NTI, but not the White House. A separate House bill, H.R. 3029 (the Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act), takes a lighter voluntary-standards approach. A tension exists between the administration's general deregulatory philosophy and the biosecurity imperative: the EO's language about "comprehensive, scalable, and verifiable" screening in non-federally funded contexts suggests support for extending regulation, but the AI Action Plan's narrower focus on federal funding conditions and the missed deadlines for the broader strategy suggest bureaucratic or philosophical friction in translating that aspiration into concrete action or legislative proposals.

Background: On May 5, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14292, which directed OSTP to develop a strategy that 'shall include actions to achieve comprehensive, scalable, and verifiable nucleic acid synthesis screening in non-federally funded' contexts. This signals executive branch interest in extending screening beyond federally funded research. The EO also required OSTP to revise the 2024 Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening within 90 days and to develop a broader strategy including legislative proposals within 180 days (approximately by early November 2025). Research should determine: (1) Has OSTP released the revised framework or the broader strategy as directed by EO 14292? (2) Did the strategy include specific legislative proposals for universal screening? (3) Has the Trump administration explicitly endorsed S. 3741 or similar legislation? (4) Are there any signals that the administration prefers an executive/regulatory approach over a legislative mandate, or vice versa? (5) Given the current administration's general stance on deregulation, are there tensions between biosecurity goals and anti-regulation philosophy? The likelihood of a presidential signature is a necessary condition for resolution, and executive branch alignment with Congress is a key factor.

Detailed research

## 1. Executive Order 14292: Provisions and Deadlines President Trump signed Executive Order 14292, "Improving the Safety and Security of Biological Research," on May 5, 2025. Based on the Federal Register text, multiple legal analyses, and the White House fact sheet, the EO included two critical provisions regarding nucleic acid synthesis screening: 90-day deadline (~August 3, 2025): The Director of OSTP was directed to "revise or replace" the 2024 Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening. The revised framework was to include "enforcement mechanisms prescribed by this order to ensure compliance." 180-day deadline (~November 1, 2025): The Director of OSTP, in coordination with national security agencies, was directed to "implement a strategy" that "shall include actions to achieve comprehensive, scalable, and verifiable nucleic acid synthesis screening in non-federally funded" settings. This language explicitly contemplated extending screening beyond the federal funding lever. The White House fact sheet accompanying EO 14292 criticized the Biden-era 2024 Framework as one of the "inadequate policies that rely on self-reporting and fail to protect" against biosecurity threats. ## 2. Status of OSTP Deliverables: Framework Revision and Broader Strategy Revised Framework: Multiple sources indicate the revised framework has NOT been publicly released as of early 2026: - An SSRN paper (ADAPT programme) states: "The revised Framework has not been released at the time of writing." - A Frontiers in Bioengineering article refers to the 2024 framework as "later rescinded by Executive Order 14292 in 2025." - Penn State's research support page notes: "An Executive Order released on May 5, 2025 has paused implementation of the Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening." - EBRC (September 2025) urged: "OSTP should continue its development and implementation of a revised Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening." - The Arms Control Association article (November 24, 2025) discussed "regulatory gaps" in the context of the administration having "indicated that it would revise or replace the framework within 90 days." - ARI's July 2025 recommendations document referred to looking forward to "the legislative proposals that will emerge from the 180-day strategy," suggesting it had not yet been released at that time. 180-day Strategy: There is no public evidence that the broader strategy, which was supposed to include legislative proposals for non-federally funded screening, has been released. The 180-day deadline (approximately November 1, 2025) appears to have passed without a public deliverable. A December 2025 year-in-review article from the Council on Strategic Risks did not mention the strategy's release. ## 3. America's AI Action Plan (July 2025) and Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening The White House released "America's AI Action Plan" in July 2025. According to the document itself [b2247e], the plan addresses nucleic acid synthesis screening under its biosecurity provisions but takes a narrower approach than EO 14292 contemplated: - It requires "all institutions receiving Federal funding for scientific research to use nucleic acid synthesis tools and synthesis providers that have robust nucleic acid sequence screening and customer verification procedures" [b2247e]. - It calls for "enforcement mechanisms for this requirement rather than relying on voluntary attestation" [b2247e]. - It directs OSTP to "convene government and industry actors to develop a mechanism to facilitate data sharing between nucleic acid synthesis providers to screen for potentially fraudulent or malicious customers" [b2247e]. Crucially, the AI Action Plan does NOT call for mandatory universal screening of all providers regardless of funding source. Its requirements are explicitly limited to federally funded institutions [b2247e]. This is a significantly narrower scope than what EO 14292 contemplated with its language about "non-federally funded" contexts. ## 4. S. 3741: Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026 Introduced January 29, 2026, by Senators Tom Cotton (R-AR) and Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), S. 3741 would mandate universal nucleic acid synthesis screening [049632]: Key provisions [049632]: - Defines "covered provider" as any person who synthesizes and sells synthetic nucleic acids to persons in the United States, or produces/distributes benchtop synthesis equipment—regardless of funding source. - Requires covered providers to implement screening protocols for "sequences of concern" and verify customer identity and legitimacy. - Directs the Secretary of Commerce to promulgate regulations implementing these requirements. - Requires persons receiving federal funds to purchase only from compliant covered providers. - Establishes conformity assessment including adversarial "red-teaming" and auditing. - Authorizes civil enforcement by the Attorney General with statutory damages up to $750,000. - Creates a "biotechnology governance sandbox." - Requires OSTP to assess and streamline existing federal biosecurity authorities. The bill was referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Endorsements: The bill has been endorsed by the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology (NSCEB), the Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI), the Advancing Research Institute (ARI), and the Engineering Biology Research Consortium (EBRC), among others. A bipartisan companion effort appears to be in development in the House, with Rep. Kiley reportedly urging the House Energy and Commerce Committee to hold a hearing. ## 5. Has the Trump Administration Explicitly Endorsed S. 3741? No. Despite extensive searching, I found no evidence of explicit White House, OSTP, or Trump administration endorsement of S. 3741 or any similar legislative bill mandating universal screening. The Reuters article on the bill's introduction [dc39e8] does not mention any administration position. No White House statements of administration policy (SAPs) regarding the bill were found. The fact that S. 3741 was introduced by Senator Tom Cotton, a close ally of the Trump administration on national security matters, is notable but does not constitute an administration endorsement. ## 6. Other Relevant Congressional Activity H.R. 3029 - Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act (introduced April 28, 2025 by Rep. Andrea Salinas): This bill takes a lighter approach. The House Science, Space, and Technology Committee described it as strengthening "biosecurity without regulation by supporting voluntary" standards. It directs NIST to establish a public-private consortium to develop technical standards for nucleic acid screening. The committee voted to favorably report it. This bill does NOT mandate universal screening. Export control efforts: In December 2025, a bipartisan group of lawmakers introduced a bill requiring export licenses before sending gene sequence data to China, reflecting a separate but related biosecurity concern. ## 7. Tension Between Deregulation Philosophy and Biosecurity Goals Several indicators point to a genuine tension: Signals favoring regulation/legislation: - EO 14292 explicitly called for "comprehensive, scalable, and verifiable nucleic acid synthesis screening in non-federally funded" contexts, signaling intent to go beyond existing federal funding conditions. - The White House fact sheet criticized the Biden-era framework for relying on "self-reporting," implying a desire for stronger enforcement. - Senator Cotton (a Trump ally) introduced legislation mandating universal screening with civil penalties. - The administration framed biosecurity as a national security issue, an area where the Trump administration has historically been willing to impose regulatory requirements. Signals favoring a lighter approach: - The AI Action Plan (July 2025) only proposed requirements tied to federal funding, not universal mandates [b2247e]. - H.R. 3029, advanced with apparent bipartisan support in the House Science Committee, explicitly supports "voluntary" standards. - The missed deadlines for the revised framework and the broader strategy suggest either bureaucratic capacity issues (OSTP has been significantly reduced under the current administration's DOGE-related restructuring) or lack of prioritization. - The administration's broader deregulatory agenda, including executive orders to reduce regulatory burdens, could create philosophical resistance to a new mandatory screening regime imposed on private industry. Assessment: The administration appears genuinely interested in biosecurity as a national security priority but has not yet reconciled this with its general opposition to new federal regulations on private industry. The path of least resistance—attaching requirements to federal funding—has been the approach taken in the AI Action Plan. Whether the administration would actively support or sign into law a broader mandate applying to all private sector synthesis providers (as S. 3741 would require) remains uncertain. The fact that the 180-day strategy with potential legislative proposals has not been publicly released adds significant uncertainty about the administration's preferred approach.

SQ5: What are the key political, industry, and practical obstacles that could prevent universal nucleic acid synthesis screening legislation from being enacted by December 31, 2026?

Summary: S. 3741, the Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026, was introduced on January 29, 2026, by Senators Tom Cotton (R-AR) and Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, where it remains in "Introduced" status as of March 19, 2026 [c82b0c]. The bill would mandate the Secretary of Commerce to require all synthesis providers to screen orders for sequences of concern and verify customer identities [c82b0c]. Multiple obstacles stand between this bill and enactment by December 31, 2026: Industry Stances: Major providers—Twist Bioscience, IDT, GenScript, and Thermo Fisher—all voluntarily screen orders under the IGSC Harmonized Screening Protocol and have submitted self-attestation documents to comply with the Biden-era Framework. Twist Bioscience, through VP James Diggans's December 17, 2025 congressional testimony, has been a vocal proponent of strengthened screening. The ARI's January 2026 paper "Competitive Compliance" argues mandatory uniform standards support innovation and prevent regulatory arbitrage, suggesting some industry actors favor a mandate. However, no public statements from IDT, GenScript, or Thermo Fisher explicitly endorsing or opposing S. 3741's mandatory approach were identified. GenScript faces separate national security scrutiny over its China ties. Base Rate Data: According to GovTrack, only about 2-3% of bills introduced in Congress are enacted into law, and only approximately 11% make it past committee. The BIOSECURE Act—a comparable biosecurity measure—took roughly two full congressional sessions (first introduced in 2023, enacted December 18, 2025) and ultimately passed only by being attached to the must-pass FY2026 NDAA, illustrating that standalone biosecurity bills face steep odds without a legislative vehicle. Trump Administration's Deregulatory Stance vs. Biosecurity: The Trump administration's general posture is strongly deregulatory (10-to-1 deregulation executive order, January 31, 2025). However, Trump's May 5, 2025 Executive Order on "Improving the Safety and Security of Biological Research" explicitly calls for a strategy to "achieve comprehensive, scalable, and verifiable nucleic acid synthesis screening in non-federally funded" contexts, signaling some openness to expanded screening. This creates a tension: the administration appears sympathetic to biosecurity goals but may prefer executive/voluntary pathways over congressional mandates on private industry. Competing Legislative Priorities: The 119th Congress's first session was dominated by the "One Big Beautiful Bill" reconciliation act (signed July 4, 2025) and the FY2026 NDAA (signed December 18, 2025). The second session (2026) faces midterm election pressures, government funding battles (FY2027 appropriations and potential continuing resolutions), and implementation oversight of the reconciliation law. The Senate's 2026 calendar includes significant recess periods [010255], and the bill must still receive a committee hearing, markup, floor votes in both chambers, and presidential signature—all within roughly 9 months. Alternative Legislative Approaches: H.R. 3029, the Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act (passed House Science Committee April 2025), takes a voluntary, NIST-led standards approach rather than a Commerce Department mandate, representing a competing and less prescriptive vision. This alternative could dilute momentum for mandatory screening or serve as a compromise vehicle. Key Pathway: The most plausible route to enactment would be attachment to a must-pass vehicle like the FY2027 NDAA (typically finalized in late 2026), mirroring the BIOSECURE Act's path. However, this would require the bill's provisions to gain sufficient bipartisan momentum and committee advancement in a compressed timeline.

Background: While S. 3741 has bipartisan sponsorship and endorsements from prominent biosecurity organizations (NTI, FAS, Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security), multiple factors could impede its enactment. Research should investigate: (1) Industry opposition or concerns: Do major DNA synthesis providers (e.g., Twist Bioscience, IDT, GenScript, Thermo Fisher) or biotech trade associations (e.g., BIO, PhRMA) oppose or have reservations about mandatory universal screening? The ARI published a paper titled 'Competitive Compliance: Why Uniform Screening Standards Support Innovation' suggesting some industry actors favor mandatory standards, but are there dissenters, particularly among smaller providers or international companies? (2) Political obstacles: Are there key senators on the Commerce Committee or House members who oppose the mandate? Is the current Congress focused on other priorities (e.g., budget reconciliation, tax policy, immigration) that crowd out biosecurity legislation? (3) Regulatory philosophy concerns: Does the Trump administration's general deregulatory stance create tension with imposing new mandates on private industry? (4) Technical/practical objections: Are there concerns about the feasibility, cost, or scope of universal screening that could lead to prolonged negotiation? (5) Base rate considerations: What percentage of bills referred to committee in recent Congresses have been enacted into law, and what is the typical timeline for biosecurity-related legislation? Understanding these obstacles is essential for calibrating the probability of enactment within the ~9-month window.

Detailed research

## 1. Bill Status and Sponsors S. 3741, the Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026, was introduced on January 29, 2026, by Senator Tom Cotton (R-AR) with Senator Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) as cosponsor [c82b0c]. It was referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and remains in "Introduced" status with no committee hearings or markups scheduled as of March 19, 2026 [c82b0c]. The bill mandates the Secretary of Commerce to promulgate regulations requiring "covered providers" (those who synthesize or sell synthetic nucleic acids or related equipment) to implement screening protocols for "sequences of concern" and verify customer identity and legitimacy [c82b0c]. Reuters reported on February 4, 2026, that the bill was introduced to "create new rules around the sale of synthetic gene sequences that could be used to create bioweapons" [6606ea]. The Reuters article noted the bill's bipartisan sponsorship but did not identify specific industry or political reactions [6606ea]. Endorsements have come from NTI, FAS, and the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. FAS characterized the bill as a "major step" for U.S. biosecurity but noted the 90-day interagency assessment timeline was "ambitious" [2fa60e]. FAS focused on the bill's broad governance reform aspects rather than nucleic acid screening specifically [2fa60e]. ARI also endorsed the bill. ## 2. Industry Positions on Mandatory Screening ### Twist Bioscience Twist Bioscience is the most publicly vocal major provider supporting strengthened screening. James Diggans, VP of Policy and Biosecurity, testified before the House Energy & Commerce Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations on December 17, 2025. From Google search snippets, Twist "screen[s] every order to prevent misuse, serving as a frontline defense." Twist submitted comments to BIS in May 2025 supporting synthesis screening. Twist has published research in Science (October 2, 2025) examining biosecurity screening practices. While direct access to Diggans's testimony was unavailable due to timeouts, the snippets indicate Twist made specific policy recommendations supporting comprehensive screening. The Google snippet of a Twist-authored BIS comment states that "U.S. government guidance specifically asks commercial DNA synthesis providers to screen not just sequences but the customers and institutional" context. ### IDT (Integrated DNA Technologies) IDT follows the IGSC Harmonized Screening Protocol and has published a self-attestation document committing to biosecurity compliance with the Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening. IDT's website states: "IDT takes the steps set out in the Harmonized Screening Protocol to screen the sequences of ordered genes and the prospective customers who submit those orders." No public statement was found where IDT explicitly endorses or opposes mandatory universal screening legislation like S. 3741. ### GenScript GenScript has published a public letter addressing concerns about the BIOSECURE Act and its China ties. The company has been under heightened scrutiny from Congress—the House Select Committee on China sent a letter to the FBI on July 8, 2025, regarding GenScript's ties to the PRC. GenScript's biosecurity screening stance is complicated by the broader national security questions surrounding the company. No direct statement on S. 3741 was found. ### Thermo Fisher Scientific Thermo Fisher's GeneArt division has published a self-attestation document committing to following the guidelines in the Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening. Their conditions of sale reserve the right to refuse orders of potential dual-use concern. No public statement was found explicitly endorsing or opposing mandatory universal screening legislation. ### ARI "Competitive Compliance" Paper (January 2026) The ARI paper argues that "mandatory" screening standards "support innovation and thwart regulatory capture." The snippet states: "By implementing a gene synthesis screening mandate, the U.S. government could further minimize the costs of synthesis screening compliance." This represents a think-tank argument that some industry players benefit from mandatory standards because they level the playing field. ### IGSC Members Broadly Members of the International Gene Synthesis Consortium (including Twist, IDT, GenScript, and Thermo Fisher's GeneArt) have voluntarily screened orders since 2009. A 2025 academic paper in PMC notes that "Industry leaders have recognised for nearly 20 years that some sequences... Synthesis Screening Can Create Conflict Between Biosecurity and Business." IBBIS has noted industry calls for stronger EU leadership on screening, with the message that "mandatory, interoperable screening across the EU Single Market" is needed. ### Key Uncertainty While the largest providers already voluntarily screen and some (especially Twist) appear to favor mandatory standards, no definitive public positions endorsing or opposing S. 3741 specifically from IDT, GenScript, or Thermo Fisher were identified. The voluntary screening by IGSC members suggests alignment with screening principles, but support for voluntary standards ≠ support for a legislative mandate. Smaller and international providers who do not screen—and whose competitive advantage comes from lower compliance costs—may oppose mandates, though no specific opposition was documented. ## 3. Base Rate Data for Bill Enactment According to GovTrack's analysis methodology (snippets from search results, as the page itself timed out): - Only about 2-3% of bills introduced in Congress are enacted into law. - Approximately 11% of bills make it past committee. - GovTrack's own estimate for a randomly selected bill (H.R. 7480) stated: "15% chance of getting past committee. 3% chance of being enacted." For context on biosecurity-specific legislation timelines: - The BIOSECURE Act was first introduced in the 118th Congress (2023-2024), passed the House in September 2024, but failed to advance in the Senate. It was reintroduced in the 119th Congress (December 11, 2025) and enacted on December 18, 2025 as Section 851 of the FY2026 NDAA—requiring approximately two full years and attachment to a must-pass defense authorization bill. - The Biden-era Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening (September 2024) took approximately one year from conception to publication and applied only to federally funded orders—a narrower scope than S. 3741's universal mandate. S. 3741 was introduced on January 29, 2026—meaning it would need to complete the entire legislative process (committee hearing, markup, floor votes in both chambers, conference/reconciliation, presidential signature) within approximately 11 months. Given base rates and the BIOSECURE Act precedent, this is an extremely compressed timeline for a standalone bill. ## 4. Trump Administration Deregulatory Stance vs. Biosecurity Mandate Deregulatory posture: President Trump signed Executive Order "Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation" on January 31, 2025, establishing a 10-to-1 deregulation ratio (ten rules removed for every new one). This is the most aggressive deregulatory mandate in modern presidential history and creates a philosophical tension with S. 3741, which imposes new regulatory obligations on private industry. Biosecurity exception: However, Trump's May 5, 2025 Executive Order on "Improving the Safety and Security of Biological Research" explicitly addresses synthesis screening. Multiple sources confirm the EO includes language directing development of a "strategy" that "shall include actions to achieve comprehensive, scalable, and verifiable nucleic acid synthesis screening in non-federally funded" contexts. This suggests the administration recognizes the biosecurity gap but may prefer executive action (revising/replacing the Biden framework) over statutory mandates. NTI's assessment: NTI characterized the May 2025 EO as holding "promise but leav[ing] crucial gaps," advocating for congressional action to close them. Tension: The administration's approach appears to be: support expanded screening in principle, but implement it through executive/voluntary pathways (consistent with deregulatory philosophy) rather than congressional mandates on private industry. This creates a potential conflict if S. 3741 reaches the President's desk—though the bill's bipartisan framing and national security rationale could potentially overcome deregulatory objections. ## 5. Competing Legislative Priorities ### Already completed in the first session (2025): - One Big Beautiful Bill Act: Signed July 4, 2025—a massive budget reconciliation bill that consumed enormous legislative bandwidth in the first session. - FY2026 NDAA: Signed December 18, 2025 (included BIOSECURE Act). ### Expected priorities for the second session (2026): - FY2027 appropriations: Government funding for the fiscal year beginning October 1, 2026. This typically dominates the fall legislative calendar and may result in continuing resolutions or omnibus packages. - FY2027 NDAA: The annual defense authorization bill, typically debated in summer/fall—this could serve as a potential legislative vehicle for biosecurity provisions. - 2026 midterm election pressures: The November 2026 midterms will compress the legislative calendar as members campaign. Congress typically accomplishes less in election years. - Implementation oversight: The OBBBA's implementation will require congressional attention. - Debt ceiling/fiscal issues: Ongoing fiscal policy debates. - Other policy priorities: Immigration enforcement, trade/tariffs, and potential foreign policy crises could consume floor time. ### Senate 2026 Calendar [010255]: The Senate's tentative schedule includes extensive recess periods: March 30–April 10, May 4–8, May 25–29, June 29–July 10, August 10–September 11 (summer recess), October 5–November 6 (pre-election recess), and December 21–31. These recesses significantly limit available session days for advancing new legislation. ## 6. Alternative Legislative Vehicle: H.R. 3029 H.R. 3029, the Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act, was introduced on April 28, 2025, and passed the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee on April 24, 2025. Unlike S. 3741, this bill takes a voluntary, NIST-led standards approach rather than mandating screening through Commerce Department regulations. The House Science Committee description states it "Strengthens biosecurity without regulation by supporting voluntary, stakeholder-driven nucleic acid synthesis standards." This bill represents a competing, less prescriptive legislative vision that could either complement or undercut S. 3741's mandatory approach. CBO issued a cost estimate on June 24, 2025. ## 7. NDAA as Potential Vehicle The most plausible pathway for S. 3741's provisions to become law in 2026 would be attachment to the FY2027 NDAA, following the BIOSECURE Act's precedent. However, this typically occurs in late fall/winter—potentially at the very end of the 2026 window. The bill's provisions would need to gain sufficient bipartisan support and committee-level advancement to be included in a conference report. Given that S. 3741 was only introduced in late January 2026 and has not yet received a committee hearing, the timeline is extremely tight. ## Summary of Key Obstacles 1. Low base rate: Only ~2-3% of introduced bills become law; ~11% clear committee. 2. Early stage: S. 3741 has not had a committee hearing as of March 2026, with ~9 months remaining. 3. No companion House bill: S. 3741 lacks a House companion mandating universal screening; H.R. 3029 takes a voluntary approach. 4. Deregulatory tension: The Trump administration's 10-to-1 deregulation stance conflicts with new private-sector mandates, even if biosecurity goals align. 5. Competing priorities: FY2027 appropriations, NDAA, midterm elections, and other policy fights will crowd the legislative calendar. 6. Limited session days: The Senate's 2026 schedule includes extensive recess periods [010255]. 7. Industry ambiguity: While major providers voluntarily screen, explicit public endorsements of mandatory legislation from IDT, GenScript, and Thermo Fisher were not identified. 8. Alternative approaches: H.R. 3029's voluntary standards framework competes with S. 3741's mandatory approach. 9. Historical precedent: The BIOSECURE Act required ~2 years and attachment to a must-pass NDAA to be enacted.

Proto-question Stage 1

Will the BWC Working Group on Strengthening the Convention produce a consensus final report recommending a formal verification or compliance mechanism by December 31, 2026?

Why this question? The paper emphasizes that the BWC 'does not have a formal verification process' as a major gap enabling covert state bioweapons programs. The BWC Working Group has its 8th session (Feb 2026) and 9th session (Aug 17-21, 2026) scheduled. Whether it achieves consensus on verification is genuinely uncertain given geopolitical tensions between Russia, China, and Western states. This is a critical institutional indicator of whether the international community can constrain the state-level risks the paper models.

Paper reference: The paper notes that '184 states are party to the BWC' but that 'the BWC does not have a formal verification process and no state has publicly acknowledged a current offensive bioweapon programme' (Section 1). Section 5 discusses attribution as a key deterrent and notes the 'absence of verification mechanisms within the BWC.'

Refined question Stage 2

Title: Will the BWC Working Group on Strengthening the Convention adopt a consensus final report recommending establishment of a new subsidiary body dedicated to verification or compliance measures by December 31, 2026? Background: The Biological Weapons Convention (BWC; full title: Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production and Stockpiling of Bacteriological (Biological) and Toxin Weapons and on their Destruction) is a multilateral disarmament treaty banning biological weapons. As of 2025, the BWC has 189 States Parties and 4 Signatory States (Egypt, Haiti, Somalia, and Syria). Unlike the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), which is overseen by the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) and includes a comprehensive verification regime with routine inspections, the BWC does not have a formal verification process or a standing organizational body dedicated to monitoring compliance. This absence has been widely identified as a major gap in the international biosecurity regime. The Ninth Review Conference of the BWC (November–December 2022) established a Working Group on the Strengthening of the Convention (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_Weapons_Convention). Under paragraph 16, Part II of the Final Document (BWC/CONF.IX/9, available at https://docs.un.org/en/BWC/CONF.IX/9), the Working Group is mandated to "identify, examine and develop specific and effective measures, including possible legally-binding measures, and to make recommendations to strengthen and institutionalize the Convention in all its aspects." The Working Group is tasked with submitting a final report including "conclusions and recommendations" to the Tenth Review Conference (scheduled for 2027), or earlier at a Special Conference or Meeting of States Parties. The Working Group operates under the Rules of Procedure of the Ninth Review Conference (BWC/CONF.IX/2, available at https://docs.un.org/en/BWC/CONF.IX/2) applied mutatis mutandis, as confirmed in its organizational document BWC/WG/1/2 (available at https://docs.un.org/en/BWC/WG/1/2). Under these rules, the Working Group's final report—including any conclusions and recommendations—must be adopted by consensus. Through its first seven sessions (2023–2025), the Working Group developed a "rolling text" addressing various aspects of BWC strengthening. The Working Group was urged by the Ninth Review Conference to complete its tasks by the end of 2025 but did not achieve this. At its 7th session (December 2025), the Working Group adopted its procedural report by consensus but did not finalize its substantive report. At the 8th session (February 9–13, 2026, Geneva), the Working Group adopted a procedural report by consensus on February 13, 2026, and continued work on the rolling text, including discussion of verification-related provisions (e.g., "methods, procedures and techniques that could contribute to verification"), but did not adopt a final substantive report. The documents from this session are available at https://meetings.unoda.org/meeting/79376/documents, including the draft procedural report (BWC/WG/8/CRP.1/Rev.3) and a revised draft final report (BWC/WG/8/CRP.1). Reports from the session indicate growing support among delegations for recommending that the Tenth Review Conference establish an Open-Ended Working Group (OEWG) specifically dedicated to compliance and verification, though formal consensus on this point has not been reached and significant disagreements remain on the substance. Three remaining sessions are scheduled in 2026: - 9th session: August 17–21, 2026 - 10th session: December 7–11, 2026 - BWC Meeting of States Parties: December 14–16, 2026 Geopolitical tensions significantly complicate consensus-building. Russia—which has been assessed by some states as maintaining an active offensive bioweapons program—has historically resisted binding verification measures. China and other states have expressed concerns about intrusiveness. Western states and a majority of States Parties generally support stronger verification measures. However, the consensus requirement gives any single State Party present an effective veto over the final report. Resolution Criteria: This question resolves Yes if, between March 19, 2026 (00:00 UTC) and December 31, 2026 (23:59 UTC), the BWC Working Group on the Strengthening of the Convention adopts by consensus a final report that contains an explicit recommendation to establish a new subsidiary body—such as an Open-Ended Working Group (OEWG), Ad Hoc Committee, Ad Hoc Group, or equivalent institutional arrangement—with a specific mandate to develop, negotiate, or implement measures for verification of compliance with the BWC, or to develop a legally binding compliance or verification instrument. This question resolves No if any of the following conditions hold as of December 31, 2026 (23:59 UTC): - The Working Group does not adopt a consensus final report by that date; - The Working Group adopts a consensus final report that does not contain a recommendation to establish a new subsidiary body with a specific mandate focused on verification or compliance; or - The final report mentions verification or compliance only in general or aspirational terms (e.g., "States Parties should consider further discussions on verification") without recommending the establishment of a specific new dedicated body or institutional process. Key Definitions: 1. "Consensus" means adoption without any State Party present at the relevant session formally objecting to the adoption, consistent with the practice under Rule 28 of the Rules of Procedure of the Ninth Review Conference (BWC/CONF.IX/2), as applied to the Working Group per BWC/WG/1/2. As stated in BWC/WG/1/2: "If the Working Group decides so by consensus, it will prepare the report." 2. "Formal verification or compliance mechanism" means, for purposes of this question, any proposed institutional arrangement—whether a new subsidiary body, standing committee, Open-Ended Working Group (OEWG), Ad Hoc Committee, Ad Hoc Group, or legally binding protocol—that would be specifically mandated to develop, negotiate, assess, monitor, or implement measures for verification of compliance with the obligations of the BWC (Articles I–IV). This definition draws on: - The Ninth Review Conference mandate (BWC/CONF.IX/9, Part II, paragraph 16), which charges the Working Group with identifying "specific and effective measures, including possible legally-binding measures"; - The concept of verification as described in NTI's analysis of the BWC verification protocol (https://www.nti.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Creating-a-Verification-Protocol_FINAL_June2022.pdf), defining verification as "the collective evaluation of intent to adhere to both the positive ('to do') and negative ('not to do') provisions of the Convention"; - The U.S. State Department's characterization that "the BWC does not establish a formal international mechanism for verifying compliance" (https://2001-2009.state.gov/t/vci/rls/prsrl/58267.htm). A general recommendation for "further discussions" on verification, or a recommendation that merely reaffirms existing provisions, without establishing or recommending a dedicated new body, does not meet this threshold. 3. "Recommendation" means language that appears in the conclusions and recommendations section of the Working Group's final report (as described in BWC/WG/1/2 and the mandate in BWC/CONF.IX/9), using formulations such as "recommends," "recommends that," "decides to recommend," or "recommends that the [Tenth Review Conference / Meeting of States Parties / States Parties] establish." The recommendation must be a formal part of the adopted consensus text, not merely a proposal, working paper, or Chair's summary that was not adopted. 4. "Final report" means the substantive report of the Working Group containing conclusions and recommendations as mandated by the Ninth Review Conference (BWC/CONF.IX/9, Part II, paragraph 16), as distinguished from procedural session reports adopted at individual sessions. This is the report described in the Working Group's mandate as being submitted to the Tenth Review Conference, or earlier at a Special Conference or Meeting of States Parties. Resolution Source: The official documents of the BWC Working Group, as published on the United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs (UNODA) Meetings Place at https://meetings.unoda.org/. The specific documents pages for relevant sessions include: - 9th session: https://meetings.unoda.org/bwc-/biological-weapons-convention-working-group-on-the-strengthening-of-the-convention-ninth-session-2026 - 10th session: https://meetings.unoda.org/bwc-/biological-weapons-convention-working-group-on-the-strengthening-of-the-convention-tenth-session-2026 - Meeting of States Parties 2026: https://meetings.unoda.org/bwc-msp/biological-weapons-convention-meeting-of-states-parties-2026 If the final report is adopted at any of these sessions, the adopted text published on the corresponding UNODA documents page will serve as the primary resolution source. The BWC documents library at https://docs-library.unoda.org/ may also be consulted. If no final report is published on any of these pages by December 31, 2026, the question resolves No.

Background

The Biological Weapons Convention (BWC; full title: Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production and Stockpiling of Bacteriological (Biological) and Toxin Weapons and on their Destruction) is a multilateral disarmament treaty banning biological weapons. As of 2025, the BWC has 189 States Parties and 4 Signatory States (Egypt, Haiti, Somalia, and Syria). Unlike the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), which is overseen by the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) and includes a comprehensive verification regime with routine inspections, the BWC does not have a formal verification process or a standing organizational body dedicated to monitoring compliance. This absence has been widely identified as a major gap in the international biosecurity regime. The Ninth Review Conference of the BWC (November–December 2022) established a Working Group on the Strengthening of the Convention (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_Weapons_Convention). Under paragraph 16, Part II of the Final Document (BWC/CONF.IX/9, available at https://docs.un.org/en/BWC/CONF.IX/9), the Working Group is mandated to "identify, examine and develop specific and effective measures, including possible legally-binding measures, and to make recommendations to strengthen and institutionalize the Convention in all its aspects." The Working Group is tasked with submitting a final report including "conclusions and recommendations" to the Tenth Review Conference (scheduled for 2027), or earlier at a Special Conference or Meeting of States Parties. The Working Group operates under the Rules of Procedure of the Ninth Review Conference (BWC/CONF.IX/2, available at https://docs.un.org/en/BWC/CONF.IX/2) applied mutatis mutandis, as confirmed in its organizational document BWC/WG/1/2 (available at https://docs.un.org/en/BWC/WG/1/2). Under these rules, the Working Group's final report—including any conclusions and recommendations—must be adopted by consensus. Through its first seven sessions (2023–2025), the Working Group developed a "rolling text" addressing various aspects of BWC strengthening. The Working Group was urged by the Ninth Review Conference to complete its tasks by the end of 2025 but did not achieve this. At its 7th session (December 2025), the Working Group adopted its procedural report by consensus but did not finalize its substantive report. At the 8th session (February 9–13, 2026, Geneva), the Working Group adopted a procedural report by consensus on February 13, 2026, and continued work on the rolling text, including discussion of verification-related provisions (e.g., "methods, procedures and techniques that could contribute to verification"), but did not adopt a final substantive report. The documents from this session are available at https://meetings.unoda.org/meeting/79376/documents, including the draft procedural report (BWC/WG/8/CRP.1/Rev.3) and a revised draft final report (BWC/WG/8/CRP.1). Reports from the session indicate growing support among delegations for recommending that the Tenth Review Conference establish an Open-Ended Working Group (OEWG) specifically dedicated to compliance and verification, though formal consensus on this point has not been reached and significant disagreements remain on the substance. Three remaining sessions are scheduled in 2026: - 9th session: August 17–21, 2026 - 10th session: December 7–11, 2026 - BWC Meeting of States Parties: December 14–16, 2026 Geopolitical tensions significantly complicate consensus-building. Russia—which has been assessed by some states as maintaining an active offensive bioweapons program—has historically resisted binding verification measures. China and other states have expressed concerns about intrusiveness. Western states and a majority of States Parties generally support stronger verification measures. However, the consensus requirement gives any single State Party present an effective veto over the final report.

Resolution criteria

This question resolves Yes if, between March 19, 2026 (00:00 UTC) and December 31, 2026 (23:59 UTC), the BWC Working Group on the Strengthening of the Convention adopts by consensus a final report that contains an explicit recommendation to establish a new subsidiary body—such as an Open-Ended Working Group (OEWG), Ad Hoc Committee, Ad Hoc Group, or equivalent institutional arrangement—with a specific mandate to develop, negotiate, or implement measures for verification of compliance with the BWC, or to develop a legally binding compliance or verification instrument. This question resolves No if any of the following conditions hold as of December 31, 2026 (23:59 UTC): - The Working Group does not adopt a consensus final report by that date; - The Working Group adopts a consensus final report that does not contain a recommendation to establish a new subsidiary body with a specific mandate focused on verification or compliance; or - The final report mentions verification or compliance only in general or aspirational terms (e.g., "States Parties should consider further discussions on verification") without recommending the establishment of a specific new dedicated body or institutional process.

Three sessions remain: 9th (Aug 17-21), 10th (Dec 7-11), and MSP (Dec 14-16). The question is genuinely open. 2. Background is largely accurate but slightly understates OEWG consensus: The CBW Events report from the 8th session states "There is a clear consensus that there should be an Open-Ended Working Group (OEWG) on compliance and verification established by the Tenth BWC Review Conference" [c70740]. The question's background characterizes this as merely "growing support," which may slightly understate the level of agreement on the OEWG concept itself. However, the same report confirms that significant disagreements remain on substance—specifically on the scope of verification (whether it covers only Articles I-II or broader provisions like Article X) and the legal nature of verification measures (legally-binding vs. non-legally-binding) [c70740]. This means the real uncertainty is less about whether an OEWG will be recommended and more about whether the entire final report can achieve consensus given these unresolved substantive disputes. 4. Resolution criteria are well-calibrated: The criteria properly distinguish between (a) adoption of a consensus final report (not just procedural reports), (b) containing an explicit recommendation for a new subsidiary body, (c) with a specific mandate on verification/compliance. The draft rolling text (BWC/WG/8/CRP.1/Rev.2) already contains language about an "Open-Ended Working Group on Compliance and Verification" with bracketed text indicating unresolved issues, so the question properly targets the remaining uncertainty. 5. Consensus rule correctly described: The consensus requirement under Rule 28 does apply to the substantive final report, not just procedural session reports. The question correctly identifies that any single State Party present can effectively block adoption. 6. Diplomatic terminology matches: The terms "subsidiary body," "Open-Ended Working Group," and "verification/compliance mandate" are consistent with the actual diplomatic language appearing in the BWC working papers and draft texts. 7. Forecasters should note: The question effectively functions as a compound forecast—(i) will the entire final report be adopted by consensus AND (ii) will it contain the specific OEWG recommendation. Based on available evidence, condition (ii) seems likely if condition (i) is met, since there's reportedly "clear consensus" on the OEWG concept [c70740]. The primary uncertainty is condition (i), driven by broader substantive disagreements. This is a feature of the question (it captures meaningful uncertainty), not a flaw, but forecasters should understand where the real risk lies. OVERALL_RISK: MEDIUM ## Edge Case Analysis for BWC Working Group Verification/Compliance Question Based on research into the current state of BWC Working Group negotiations, including the 8th session's discussions on OEWG proposals and rolling text language [4d8f35], and the 6th session's proposals on compliance and verification [0f8b49], the following edge cases are identified: --- ### Edge Case 1: OEWG Recommended with a Broad Mandate that Includes but Is Not "Dedicated to" Verification/Compliance SCENARIO: The Working Group adopts a consensus final report recommending establishment of an OEWG with a mandate covering "all aspects of strengthening the Convention," including but not limited to verification and compliance (alongside scientific cooperation, confidence-building measures, and Article X implementation). The body is not "dedicated" exclusively to verification/compliance but includes it as one of several co-equal agenda items. This is plausible given that the current rolling text covers multiple thematic areas and bundling could be a consensus-building strategy. SEVERITY: HIGH — This is a very likely compromise outcome. The question requires a body "dedicated to verification or compliance measures," but a multipurpose body that addresses verification among other things would create genuine disagreement about resolution. FIX: Add language specifying: "The subsidiary body qualifies if verification or compliance is identified as a principal, named component of its mandate (e.g., as a specific agenda item or workstream), even if the body also addresses other aspects of Convention strengthening. However, a body with only a general mandate to 'strengthen the Convention in all its aspects' without specifically naming verification or compliance as a distinct element of its work does not qualify." --- ### Edge Case 2: Recommendation Uses Aspirational or Conditional Language Rather Than a Direct Establishment Recommendation SCENARIO: The final report's conclusions and recommendations section states that "the Working Group recommends that the Tenth Review Conference consider establishing" or "explore the feasibility of establishing" an OEWG on verification, rather than directly recommending establishment. This is plausible because, as observed at the 8th session, delegations disagreed on the scope and nature of verification provisions [4d8f35], and conditional language is a classic consensus-building technique in multilateral diplomacy. SEVERITY: HIGH — This is a very common diplomatic compromise technique and directly tests the boundary between "recommending establishment" and "recommending consideration of establishment." The resolution criteria define "recommendation" but the boundary between a recommendation to establish vs. a recommendation to consider establishing is where real disagreement would occur. FIX: Add language: "Language such as 'recommends that the Review Conference consider establishing,' 'recommends exploring the establishment of,' or 'recommends that States Parties consider the creation of' does NOT meet the threshold. The recommendation must use language that, if acted upon, would directly result in the establishment of the body — e.g., 'recommends that the Tenth Review Conference establish' or 'decides to recommend the establishment of.'" --- ### Edge Case 3: Consensus Adoption Contested Due to Reservations or Interpretive Statements SCENARIO: The final report is adopted by the Chair declaring consensus, but one or more States Parties (e.g., Russia) issue formal reservations, interpretive statements, or "understandings" recorded in the session record indicating they do not agree with the verification/compliance recommendation but chose not to block adoption. Two reasonable people could disagree on whether a report adopted with such formal reservations truly reflects "consensus" as defined. SEVERITY: MEDIUM — This is a well-known practice in BWC and other multilateral settings. The question defines consensus as adoption "without any State Party present formally objecting to the adoption" under Rule 28, but the distinction between a "formal objection to adoption" and a "reservation recorded after adoption" is procedurally nuanced. FIX: Add language: "For purposes of this question, 'consensus' is determined solely by whether the Chair declares the report adopted without a State Party formally blocking adoption at the moment of adoption. Post-adoption reservations, interpretive statements, or 'understandings' recorded in the session proceedings do not negate the consensus adoption." --- ### Edge Case 4: A Subsidiary Body Is Recommended with a Mandate Limited to "Studying" or "Discussing" Verification Rather Than Developing/Negotiating/Implementing Measures SCENARIO: The final report recommends establishing an OEWG with a mandate to "identify and examine methods, procedures, and techniques that could contribute to verification" or to "discuss possible approaches to compliance assessment" — language that mirrors the current Working Group's own study-oriented mandate rather than a mandate to develop, negotiate, or implement actual verification measures. Research from the 8th session shows the rolling text already contains language about "methods, procedures and techniques that could contribute to verification" [4d8f35], which is deliberately vague. SEVERITY: HIGH — This is the most likely compromise path. Russia and others resistant to binding verification could agree to a new body that merely "studies" or "examines" verification options, and there would be genuine disagreement about whether this constitutes a body "dedicated to verification or compliance measures" under the resolution criteria. FIX: Add language: "A subsidiary body mandated solely to 'study,' 'examine,' 'identify,' or 'discuss' verification-related concepts without being specifically tasked to 'develop,' 'negotiate,' 'draft,' or 'implement' concrete verification or compliance measures does NOT qualify. The mandate must include at least one action verb indicating the body will produce or advance specific verification or compliance measures, instruments, or protocols, not merely study the topic." --- ### Edge Case 5: Final Report vs. Interim or Procedural Report Ambiguity SCENARIO: At the 10th session (December 2026), the Working Group adopts a substantive report containing verification/compliance recommendations but labels it as an "interim report" or "progress report" to be finalized at the 2027 Review Conference, rather than the "final report" as defined in the mandate. This is plausible because the Working Group already missed its 2025 deadline and may choose to submit an interim product with substantive recommendations to the December 2026 Meeting of States Parties. SEVERITY: MEDIUM — The question specifically requires a "final report" as defined. But if a substantive report with consensus recommendations on verification bodies is adopted and forwarded to the Review Conference, reasonable people could disagree on whether it constitutes the "final report" even if not labeled as such. FIX: Add language: "The report must be explicitly titled or identified as the 'final report' of the Working Group, or must be the report submitted to the Tenth Review Conference or Meeting of States Parties as the Working Group's concluding substantive product containing 'conclusions and recommendations' as described in the mandate (BWC/CONF.IX/9, Part II, paragraph 16). An interim, progress, or session report that contains substantive recommendations but is not presented as the final product of the Working Group does not qualify." --- ### Edge Case 6: Recommendation Adopted at Meeting of States Parties Rather Than by Working Group SCENARIO: The Working Group fails to adopt a consensus final report at its 9th or 10th sessions, but the December 2026 Meeting of States Parties (MSP) itself adopts a decision to establish an OEWG on verification. The recommendation comes from the MSP rather than from the Working Group's own final report. SEVERITY: MEDIUM — The question specifically requires the "BWC Working Group on the Strengthening of the Convention" to adopt the final report. If the MSP independently decides to establish a verification body without the Working Group having formally recommended it in a consensus final report, this would not meet the criteria — but some could argue the spirit of the question is satisfied. FIX: Add language: "Only a recommendation contained in the Working Group's own adopted consensus final report qualifies. Decisions or recommendations adopted independently by the Meeting of States Parties, Review Conference, or any other BWC body — even if substantively identical — do not satisfy this question unless they are contained within or directly adopt the Working Group's consensus final report." --- ### Summary The highest-risk edge cases involve the likely diplomatic compromises around (1) whether a multi-mandate body counts as "dedicated to" verification, (2) whether conditional/aspirational recommendation language meets the threshold, and (4) whether a mandate to "study" verification qualifies as developing verification measures. These reflect the real negotiation dynamics where Russia and other skeptical states may agree to watered-down compromises that test the boundaries of the resolution criteria [4d8f35] [0f8b49].

Forecast rationale

This question asks whether the BWC Working Group will adopt a consensus final report with a specific recommendation to establish a new subsidiary body dedicated to verification/compliance by December 31, 2026. The resolution criteria are demanding: it requires not just any consensus report, but one with explicit language recommending a new body with a specific verification/compliance mandate. Factors favoring YES (~30% weight): - There is reported 'clear consensus' among many delegations that an OEWG on compliance and verification should be established [77190a, 2e556d] - Draft language already exists in the rolling text (BWC/WG/8/CRP.1/Rev.3) discussing establishment of such an OEWG [f2fbbb] - Historical precedent: VEREX (1991) and the Ad Hoc Group (1994) were both established by consensus, showing states can agree to create bodies even when disagreeing on substance - Strong institutional pressure to produce something tangible after 4 years (10 sessions) of work, especially before the Tenth Review Conference in 2027 - The 'process as progress' strategy - recommending a body is a lower bar than agreeing on verification substance itself - Russia and China have strategic reasons to support an OEWG (platform for their own concerns) Factors favoring NO (~70% weight): - After 8 sessions, no substantive final report has been adopted; the rolling text remains 'heavily bracketed' [654099, e61f82] - The consensus requirement gives any single state an effective veto - Russia, China, or even the US under the Trump administration could block - Irreconcilable scope disagreements persist: Articles I/II focus (Western) vs. Article X inclusion (NAM/China/Russia) [e61f82] - The 'legally-binding measures' language remains a poison pill [e61f82] - The 'thin gruel' problem: even if a report is adopted, consensus pressures may water down language to general/aspirational terms that wouldn't meet the specific resolution criteria - Expert opinion (Guthrie, Lentzos, Zanders) leans toward low probability for a substantive consensus report - Broader geopolitical tensions (Ukraine, US-China) reduce trust needed for agreement on verification - Only 2 substantive sessions remain (August, December 2026) - US policy under Trump administration is uncertain and may shift against multilateral verification bodies Key Uncertainties: 1. Russia's strategic calculus: If Russia sees more value in blocking than participating, it exercises its veto. If it sees OEWG as a platform for its own narratives, it may support. This single factor could swing probability ±15%. 2. Specificity vs. consensus tradeoff: The resolution criteria requires a 'specific mandate' for verification/compliance. Consensus may only be achievable with vaguer language. If the final text recommends 'further discussions' rather than a specific body, it resolves NO even if adopted. 3. US engagement level: Active US support for an OEWG would significantly boost chances; US withdrawal or opposition would likely doom it. 4. Last-session dynamics: Historical BWC practice shows some breakthroughs occur at final sessions under deadline pressure, but also shows that 'last-minute compromises' often gut substantive content. Base rate calibration: The 77% success rate for BWC Review Conference Final Declarations is relevant but overstates probability because those often include procedural elements, while this question demands specific verification language. The 0% success rate for legally binding verification protocol is somewhat relevant. Recent UN First Committee consensus rate of ~22% for disarmament resolutions provides a relevant environmental signal. I weight the VEREX/AHG precedent (100%) partially but discount it given the much more adversarial geopolitical environment. Expert/market signals: No direct prediction market exists. Expert opinion consistently leans toward low probability for substantive consensus. This is an important signal. Synthesizing all factors, I estimate approximately 15% probability. The broad conceptual support and existing draft language provide a non-trivial path to YES, but the consensus requirement, deep substantive disagreements, geopolitical barriers, and the demanding resolution criteria make NO the much more likely outcome.

Importance rationale

The absence of a verification mechanism has been the defining weakness of the Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) for half a century. A consensus recommendation to establish a dedicated verification or compliance body would be the most significant institutional development in the history of the treaty, directly impacting global arms control architecture. Knowing the answer is highly decision-relevant for national biosecurity strategies, diplomatic resource allocation, and the long-term stability of the biological disarmament regime. Such a step would represent a rare geopolitical breakthrough among major powers (USA, Russia, China) on a high-stakes security issue, serving as a leading indicator for the viability of multilateral disarmament in a period of high international tension.

Proto-question Stage 1

Will the OSTP Framework's October 13, 2026 deadline for reducing DNA synthesis screening windows to 50 nucleotides be maintained without postponement or rescission by the Trump administration by December 31, 2026?

Why this question? The paper discusses DNA synthesis screening evasion as a key risk factor. The OSTP Framework set an October 13, 2026 deadline for providers to screen orders down to 50 nucleotides, a significant technical tightening. However, the Trump administration has shown a deregulatory stance on AI, and the Framework was issued under the Biden administration. Whether this deadline survives is a genuinely uncertain upstream indicator of biosecurity governance.

Paper reference: The paper discusses AI-designed sequences capable of 'evading commercial DNA synthesis screening' (Wittmann et al. 2025) and notes that 'improved real-time information sharing and screening of dual-use materials may increase the economic and political costs of bioweapon development' (Section 3).

Refined question Stage 2

Question Title: Will U.S. federal policy require nucleic acid synthesis providers to screen orders at a 50-nucleotide window effective on or before October 13, 2026? --- Background: In September 2024, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) released the revised Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening (the "2024 Framework"). This document established a phased timeline for providers of synthetic nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) and manufacturers of benchtop nucleic acid synthesis equipment. The Framework requires that entities receiving U.S. federal funding only procure synthetic nucleic acids from providers who adhere to specified screening standards. Central to these standards is the concept of a "screening window"—the minimum length of a nucleotide sequence that must be checked against databases of sequences of concern (SOCs), which include potential bioweapon agents. Under the 2024 Framework's phased timeline: - October 26, 2024: Initial implementation; providers must screen orders of 200 nucleotides or longer. - October 13, 2025: Screening window decreases; providers must screen each window of nucleotides within an order. - October 13, 2026: Screening window decreases to 50 nucleotides, requiring providers to screen each 50-nucleotide window for SOCs. This is the most technically demanding requirement and is the focus of this question. DNA synthesis screening is a key biosecurity measure designed to prevent malicious actors from ordering synthetic DNA sequences that encode dangerous pathogens or toxins. The 50-nucleotide threshold is significant because shorter sequences are harder to screen but can still be assembled into dangerous constructs, particularly with AI-assisted sequence design. Trump Administration Actions: On May 5, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14292, "Improving the Safety and Security of Biological Research". Section 4(b) of this EO directed the OSTP Director to revise or replace the 2024 Framework within 90 days (approximately by August 3, 2025) to "ensure it takes a commonsense approach" and to develop a strategy for "comprehensive, scalable, and verifiable nucleic acid synthesis screening in non-federally funded settings." Current Status (as of March 2026): The 90-day revision deadline of approximately August 3, 2025 passed without OSTP publicly releasing a revised or replacement framework. According to the Arms Control Association (November 2025), "despite the passing of the deadline, no new framework has been announced, thereby leading to uncertainty surrounding the implementation and enforcement." NIH has indicated continued adherence to the 2024 Framework version, but other agencies' postures are less clear. Penn State University noted the EO effectively "paused implementation" of the Framework. The Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, in an October 2025 RFI response, called on the administration to "release the updated Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening." In July 2025, the Alliance for Responsible Innovation (ARI) recommended that any revised framework should actually accelerate the 50-nucleotide deadline to October 2025. Separately, on February 4, 2026, Senators Cotton and Klobuchar introduced the bipartisan Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026, which would codify nucleic acid synthesis screening into federal law, potentially providing a statutory basis independent of executive action. Reuters reported that this bill would create new rules around the sale of synthetic gene sequences. The question thus captures genuine uncertainty: will the 50-nucleotide screening requirement survive the transition from the Biden-era executive framework to whatever replaces it under the Trump administration—or via legislation—by the original October 13, 2026 deadline? --- Resolution Criteria: This question resolves YES if, as of December 31, 2026, 23:59 UTC, there exists an active, publicly available U.S. federal policy document that meets both of the following conditions: 1. It requires providers of synthetic nucleic acids who serve recipients of U.S. federal funding to screen nucleic acid orders at a window of 50 nucleotides or fewer for sequences of concern; AND 2. This requirement has an effective date on or before October 13, 2026, 23:59 UTC. Qualifying policy documents include any of the following: - A revised or replacement OSTP Framework or Memorandum issued under EO 14292; - The original 2024 OSTP Framework (September 2024 version), if it has not been formally superseded, rescinded, or revoked by a subsequent OSTP memorandum, executive order, or equivalent federal action; - A Federal Register Notice establishing such a requirement; - An Executive Order establishing or codifying such a requirement; - A federal statute (Act of Congress) signed into law that establishes such a requirement.
