Background

In September 2024, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) released the revised Framework for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening (the "2024 Framework"). This document established a phased timeline for providers of synthetic nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) and manufacturers of benchtop nucleic acid synthesis equipment. The Framework requires that entities receiving U.S. federal funding only procure synthetic nucleic acids from providers who adhere to specified screening standards. Central to these standards is the concept of a "screening window"—the minimum length of a nucleotide sequence that must be checked against databases of sequences of concern (SOCs), which include potential bioweapon agents. Under the 2024 Framework's phased timeline: - October 26, 2024: Initial implementation; providers must screen orders of 200 nucleotides or longer. - October 13, 2025: Screening window decreases; providers must screen each window of nucleotides within an order. - October 13, 2026: Screening window decreases to 50 nucleotides, requiring providers to screen each 50-nucleotide window for SOCs. This is the most technically demanding requirement and is the focus of this question. DNA synthesis screening is a key biosecurity measure designed to prevent malicious actors from ordering synthetic DNA sequences that encode dangerous pathogens or toxins. The 50-nucleotide threshold is significant because shorter sequences are harder to screen but can still be assembled into dangerous constructs, particularly with AI-assisted sequence design.

Resolution criteria

This question resolves YES if, as of December 31, 2026, 23:59 UTC, there exists an active, publicly available U.S. federal policy document that meets both of the following conditions: 1. It requires providers of synthetic nucleic acids (or any specific class thereof) who serve recipients of U.S. federal funding to screen nucleic acid orders at a window of 50 nucleotides or fewer for sequences of concern. The 50-nucleotide threshold (or equivalent length if different units are used, e.g., "base pairs") must be explicitly stated as a numeric value. If a policy does not specify a numeric screening window length, it does not satisfy this criterion. The requirement qualifies even if it only applies to a specific class of synthetic nucleic acid providers (e.g., double-stranded DNA providers), and need not apply to all provider types; AND 2. This requirement has an effective date on or before October 13, 2026, 23:59 UTC. Any effective date after October 13, 2026, 23:59 UTC results in a NO resolution, regardless of how close the date is to the deadline. Qualifying policy documents include any of the following: - A revised or replacement OSTP Framework or Memorandum issued under EO 14292; - The original 2024 OSTP Framework (September 2024 version), if it has not been formally superseded, rescinded, or revoked by a subsequent OSTP memorandum, executive order, or equivalent federal action, and it is affirmatively presented as active policy on at least one official federal implementation page (e.g., the ASPR/HHS page or equivalent). A framework that is merely archived or described solely as "under revision" without any affirmative statement that its requirements remain in effect does not qualify as active policy; - A Federal Register Notice establishing such a requirement; - An Executive Order establishing or codifying such a requirement; - A federal statute (Act of Congress) signed into law that establishes such a requirement. This question resolves NO if any of the following are true as of December 31, 2026, 23:59 UTC: - Rescinded: The 2024 Framework has been formally rescinded, revoked, or replaced by a document that does not include a 50-nucleotide screening requirement effective on or before October 13, 2026; OR - Postponed: The 2024 Framework or its replacement sets the effective date for the 50-nucleotide screening requirement to a date after October 13, 2026, 23:59 UTC; OR - Not affirmatively active: The 2024 Framework has not been formally rescinded but no official federal implementation page affirmatively presents the 50-nucleotide requirement as current, active policy (e.g., the requirement is described only as "under revision" or the implementation page states it will be updated once a new framework is available); OR - No active policy: No qualifying U.S. federal policy document containing a 50-nucleotide screening requirement with an effective date on or before October 13, 2026 can be identified.

ASSESSMENT: PASS REVIEW: This is a well-constructed forecasting question that captures genuine policy uncertainty. Key findings from research: 1. EO 14292 is accurately described. The executive order was signed May 5, 2025, and Section 4(b) directed OSTP to revise or replace the 2024 Framework within 90 days. This is confirmed in the Federal Register and multiple credible sources. 2. The 50-nucleotide threshold and phased timeline are correct. The September 2024 Framework specifies: 200nt screening starting October 26, 2024; intermediate screening changes on October 13, 2025; and the 50-nucleotide window effective October 13, 2026. Multiple authoritative sources (RAND, Johns Hopkins compliance table, the original framework PDF) confirm this timeline. 3. The Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026 (S. 3741) exists and is real, but with two minor caveats: (a) The introduction date may be January 29, 2026 per lawbc.com, not February 4, 2026 as stated (the question may be using the Reuters reporting date); (b) The bill primarily directs the Commerce Department to establish screening rules and compile lists of dangerous sequences [8b9b28], rather than directly "codifying" the 50-nucleotide threshold into law. The FAS analysis characterizes it more as an assessment-focused oversight measure [72736d]. However, the question's phrasing ("would codify nucleic acid synthesis screening into federal law, potentially providing a statutory basis") is broadly accurate and uses careful qualifying language. 4. The current policy status is genuinely uncertain. The ASPR/HHS page confirms the framework is "in a state of transition" following EO 14292 [2f83cb], but has not been formally rescinded or replaced. The 90-day revision deadline passed without a new framework. NIH continues referencing the original framework. Penn State notes implementation has been "paused." This is accurately reflected in the background. 5. The question is not effectively already resolved. The 50-nucleotide requirement is NOT already standard practice industry-wide — it represents a significant technical step-up from current 200nt screening. Some providers (like SecureDNA) already screen below 50bp, but this is not universal. The outcome depends on uncertain Trump administration actions and potential legislation over the next ~7 months. 6. Resolution criteria are well-designed. The Ambiguity Clause appropriately handles the "quiet non-enforcement" scenario. The evaluation date of December 31, 2026 allows retroactive assessment. The criteria correctly enumerate multiple qualifying policy vehicles (OSTP framework, Federal Register, EO, statute). 7. No evidence of formal postponement or acceleration of the October 13, 2026 deadline by any federal action as of March 2026. The deadline remains as stated in the 2024 Framework. Minor issues identified (none rising to NEEDS_REVISION): - The bill introduction date appears to be January 29, 2026, not February 4, 2026 - The characterization of the Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act could be slightly more precise - The ASPR/HHS "in a state of transition" language [2f83cb] could create minor resolution ambiguity, but the Ambiguity Clause is designed to handle exactly this scenario EVIDENCE: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/05/08/2025-08266/improving-the-safety-and-security-of-biological-research https://aspr.hhs.gov/S3/Pages/OSTP-Framework-for-Nucleic-Acid-Synthesis-Screening.aspx https://fas.org/publication/biosecurity-modernization-and-innovation-act-of-2026/ https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/us-lawmakers-introduce-bill-screen-sales-potentially-dangerous-synthetic-dna-2026-02-04/ https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/3741/text/is?format=txt https://www.lawbc.com/senate-bill-would-establish-federal-biotechnology-security-framework/ https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/OSTP-Nucleic-Acid_Synthesis_Screening_Framework-Sep2024-Final.pdf https://www.armscontrol.org/blog/2025-11-24/regulatory-gaps-benchtop-nucleic-acid-synthesis-create-biosecurity-vulnerabilities SUGGESTION:

Forecast rationale

This question asks whether, by December 31, 2026, an active U.S. federal policy will require 50-nucleotide screening with an effective date on or before October 13, 2026. The resolution criteria are quite specific and demanding. Current Status (Strong NO signal): The most critical factor is that the ASPR/HHS implementation page—the primary official federal implementation portal—currently describes the framework as in a 'state of transition' and states it will be updated once a new framework is available [fcc85b, af1946, a383f6]. Under the explicit resolution criteria, a framework described as 'under revision' without affirmative active status does NOT qualify as active policy. This alone currently satisfies the 'not affirmatively active' NO resolution condition. EO 14292 Impact: The Trump administration's Executive Order 14292 directed OSTP to 'revise or replace' the framework within 90 days (by ~August 3, 2025). That deadline passed over 7 months ago with no public replacement [b35193]. The administration's 'commonsense approach' language and aggressive deregulatory posture (129-to-1 ratio of eliminated to new regulations) suggest any replacement is unlikely to maintain the technically demanding 50-nt threshold with the original timeline. Legislative Path (S. 3741): The Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026 was introduced January 29, 2026. However: (1) historical base rates for any bill becoming law are 1-4% per Congress; (2) the bill does NOT specify a 50-nucleotide threshold, instead delegating technical standards to Commerce with a 1-year rulemaking window [521ddc, e7da3f]; (3) even if passed, Commerce rulemaking would not produce a 50-nt requirement effective by October 13, 2026. The ClawdINT 60-65% passage estimate [cb3dab] seems optimistic, but even at face value, passage alone would not resolve YES. Agency Signals: NIH guidance may have superseded earlier framework references [d822b3]. DOE's FAL 2025-03 may still reference the framework [c77063], but a single agency is insufficient under the resolution criteria (need OSTP affirmation or majority of NIH/NSF/DOE/DOD). Key Uncertainties: 1. Will OSTP release a revised framework maintaining the 50-nt/Oct 2026 deadline? If yes, resolves YES. However, the missed deadline, deregulatory posture, and 'commonsense' language make this unlikely. If the revised framework softens or delays the requirement, it resolves NO. 2. Will the 'state of transition' persist through December 2026? If so, the 'not affirmatively active' criterion resolves NO. Given historical patterns of paused guidance remaining in limbo (60-80% probability), this is the most likely scenario. 3. Could rapid legislative action codify 50-nt screening? Even with bipartisan support, the bill's delegation of technical standards to future rulemaking and the 1-year implementation timeline make this path nearly impossible for meeting the October 2026 effective date. 4. Could a biosecurity emergency accelerate action? An actual bioterrorism event or credible AI-enabled threat could catalyze rapid policy action, but this is a low-probability tail event. Synthesis: The current state already effectively meets NO resolution criteria ('not affirmatively active'). For YES, something must actively change: either OSTP must issue a revised framework with the 50-nt requirement and original deadline, or agencies must affirmatively reinstate it. Given the deregulatory environment, missed deadlines, and the practical impossibility of the legislative path meeting the specific October 2026 effective date requirement, the probability is low.

Importance rationale

This question is highly decision-relevant as it tracks the implementation of a critical biosecurity regulation. The 50-nucleotide screening window is a significant technical threshold intended to prevent the assembly of dangerous pathogens from small synthetic fragments, especially in an era of AI-assisted design. The transition from Biden-era frameworks to Trump administration policies—or potential legislative codification—creates substantial uncertainty for DNA synthesis providers and federally funded researchers. Knowing the outcome directly informs resource allocation for biosecurity compliance and national strategies for mitigating biological risks.

Tractability: Forecasting this question requires synthesizing multiple lines of evidence: bipartisan dynamics (Cotton-Klobuchar sponsorship), committee composition and priorities, legislative calendar constraints, executive branch posture (noting the May 2025 EO pausing the existing synthesis screening framework), industry lobbying positions, and competing legislative priorities. Historical base rates for Senate bills provide a starting point (most introduced bills never pass), and inside-view analysis of political dynamics can meaningfully adjust from that prior. However, the question ultimately reduces to tracking a relatively standard legislative process, and a lawbc.com forecast document suggested 'little if any legislation will be considered or passed in 2026' in the Senate, which provides a fairly strong anchor.

Soon: The bill was introduced on January 29, 2026, and the question asks about Senate passage before December 31, 2026 — well before the overall resolution deadline of December 31, 2027. The 119th Congress (2025-2026) session creates a natural legislative window that is closing. The outcome will be substantially determined within 2026, making the information time-sensitive. However, biosecurity legislation is likely to remain a policy priority beyond this specific session, so similar questions could recur.

Sudden: Legislative passage is a discrete event (the bill either passes or doesn't), but the process leading to it is generally visible through committee referrals, hearings, markups, and floor scheduling. The direction of travel becomes increasingly apparent as the legislative session progresses. Informed observers tracking committee activity would have advance notice of likely passage or failure. The bill could potentially be folded into a larger package (e.g., NDAA) somewhat suddenly, which adds a degree of unpredictability to the exact mechanism of passage.

Sharp: Legislative processes provide many 'warning shots' — committee hearings, markups, floor debates, and procedural votes all precede final passage. The broader biosecurity policy space has seen a gradual buildup of action: the 2023 HHS Guidance, the 2024 OSTP Framework, the May 2025 Executive Order, California's AB1864, and prior congressional discussions (National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology recommendations). These precursors mean this specific legislative outcome is not 'sharp' — the policy trajectory is visible and escalating gradually.

Proto-question Stage 1

Will any frontier AI model achieve a score above 70% on SecureBio's Virology Capabilities Test (VCT) by December 31, 2026?

Why this question? The paper highlights AI-enabled virology uplift as a key risk pathway (Table 9 mentions 'LLMs provide substantial high-risk virology uplift, e.g. >80% accuracy on VCT'). The VCT is a real benchmark published by SecureBio that measures AI capability to troubleshoot complex virology lab protocols. As of early 2026, the highest VCT score is 0.610 (61%) by Grok-4.1 Thinking. Given rapid AI capability improvements, whether models will cross the 70% threshold is genuinely uncertain and would represent a significant capability milestone in the paper's risk framework.

Paper reference: Table 9 identifies 'LLMs provide substantial high-risk virology uplift (e.g. >80% accuracy on VCT, wet-lab studies)' as a potential red line scenario that could affect P(BW) and P(PPP). Section 3 discusses AI as a 'Lab Coach' (Table 4, scenario 2C) providing cross-domain assistance with wet lab protocols.

Refined question Stage 2

Question Title: Will any frontier AI model achieve an accuracy score above 70% on SecureBio's Virology Capabilities Test (VCT) between March 19, 2026, and December 31, 2026 (11:59 PM UTC)? --- Background: The Virology Capabilities Test (VCT) is an expert-level, multimodal multiple-choice benchmark developed by SecureBio and the Center for AI Safety (CAIS) that measures an AI model's capability to troubleshoot complex virology laboratory protocols. The benchmark was published in 2025 and is available at https://www.virologytest.ai/. VCT is designed to assess dual-use virology knowledge — the kind of practical, contextualized assistance that could lower barriers to dangerous biological research. Expert virologists with internet access score an average of 22.1% on questions specifically within their sub-areas of expertise, making this a challenging benchmark even for human domain experts. VCT is referenced in the biosecurity literature as a key indicator of AI-enabled biological uplift risk. For instance, one prominent risk framework identifies "LLMs provide substantial high-risk virology uplift, e.g. >80% accuracy on VCT" as a potential red-line scenario that could materially affect the probability of catastrophic biological events. Current Status (as of March 19, 2026): - The highest publicly reported VCT score is 0.610 (61.0%), achieved by Grok-4.1 Thinking from xAI, as tracked on the llm-stats.com VCT leaderboard (https://llm-stats.com/benchmarks/vct). - Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 System Card reports a VCT score of 65.4% "with max effort" configuration, though this appears to reflect an optimized evaluation setup and may use the text-only subset (VCT-Text) rather than the full multimodal benchmark. - Other recent top scores include Claude Opus 4.6 at approximately 48–61% on the full multimodal VCT (varying by evaluation configuration), and earlier models like OpenAI's o3 at 43.8%. - No model has surpassed the 70% threshold as of March 19, 2026, on any publicly reported canonical VCT evaluation. - For reference, the VCT paper notes that some models are "only evaluated in a single run" (italicized in the paper's tables), while others use averaged results across multiple runs. Both reporting conventions appear on the leaderboard and in system cards. The 70% threshold is set between the current best score (~61–65%) and the paper's red-line threshold (80%), creating genuine uncertainty about whether it will be surpassed by end of 2026. Given the rapid pace of AI capability improvements — VCT top scores roughly quadrupled from early 2025 (o3 at 43.8%) to late 2025 (Grok-4.1 Thinking at 61.0%) — crossing 70% is plausible but by no means certain within the remaining ~9 months. Definition of "Frontier AI Model": For this question, a "frontier AI model" is defined as a general-purpose AI model that meets any of the following criteria: 1. It meets the definition of a "dual-use foundation model" as specified in U.S. Executive Order 14110, Section 3(k) (Federal Register, Oct. 30, 2023): "an AI model that is trained on broad data; generally uses self-supervision; contains at least tens of billions of parameters; is applicable across a wide range of contexts; and that exhibits, or could be easily modified to exhibit, high levels of performance at tasks that pose a serious risk to security, national economic security, national public health or safety, or any combination of those matters," including models trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations; OR 2. It is classified as a "general-purpose AI model with systemic risk" under the EU AI Act (Article 51); OR 3. It is developed and released (or made available via API) by a major AI laboratory (including but not limited to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, Meta AI, or Mistral AI) and is among the most capable models offered by that laboratory at the time of evaluation. --- Resolution Criteria: This question resolves Yes if, between March 19, 2026 and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM UTC, any frontier AI model (as defined above) achieves an accuracy score strictly greater than 70% (i.e., >0.700) on SecureBio's Virology Capabilities Test (VCT), as reported in any of the following credible sources: 1. The official VCT website (https://www.virologytest.ai/) or any official SecureBio publication; 2. The llm-stats.com VCT benchmark leaderboard (https://llm-stats.com/benchmarks/vct); 3. An AI developer's official system card or model card (e.g., published by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, etc.); 4. A peer-reviewed or preprint academic publication (e.g., on arXiv) that reports VCT evaluation results. The score must be on the standard VCT benchmark as defined in the original VCT paper (Götting et al., 2025; arXiv:2504.16137), which consists of 322 expert-validated virology questions. Both the full multimodal VCT and the text-only subset (VCT-Text, 101 questions) are eligible — the question resolves Yes if the 70% threshold is exceeded on either version, provided the version is clearly identified in the source. Scoring methodology clarification: The reported score may be from either a single evaluation run or an average of multiple runs, consistent with the VCT benchmark's established reporting conventions (the original paper uses both methods). The score must represent the model's accuracy (proportion of correct answers) on the VCT question set, as calculated per the standard VCT methodology. The question resolves No if no credible source reports a VCT score above 70% for any frontier AI model by December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM UTC. If the VCT benchmark is substantially revised, replaced, or discontinued before December 31, 2026, the question resolves based on the last available version of the benchmark that is consistent with the original VCT methodology. If no VCT evaluations are published during the resolution period, the question resolves No.

Background

The Virology Capabilities Test (VCT) is an expert-level, multimodal multiple-choice benchmark developed by SecureBio and the Center for AI Safety (CAIS) that measures an AI model's capability to troubleshoot complex virology laboratory protocols. The benchmark was published in 2025 and is available at https://www.virologytest.ai/. VCT is designed to assess dual-use virology knowledge — the kind of practical, contextualized assistance that could lower barriers to dangerous biological research. Expert virologists with internet access score an average of 22.1% on questions specifically within their sub-areas of expertise, making this a challenging benchmark even for human domain experts. The full multimodal VCT consists of 322 expert-validated virology questions, including both text-based and image-based questions. A separate text-only subset (VCT-Text, 101 questions) exists, on which AI models typically score substantially higher than on the full multimodal benchmark. This question resolves exclusively on the full multimodal VCT (322 questions), not VCT-Text, in order to maintain a well-calibrated threshold. VCT is referenced in the biosecurity literature as a key indicator of AI-enabled biological uplift risk. For instance, one prominent risk framework identifies "LLMs provide substantial high-risk virology uplift, e.g. >80% accuracy on VCT" as a potential red-line scenario that could materially affect the probability of catastrophic biological events.

Resolution criteria

This question resolves Yes if, between March 19, 2026 and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM UTC, any frontier AI model (as defined above) achieves an accuracy score strictly greater than 70% (i.e., >0.700) on the full multimodal SecureBio Virology Capabilities Test (VCT, 322 questions), as reported in any of the following credible sources: 1. The official VCT website (https://www.virologytest.ai/) or any official SecureBio publication; 2. The llm-stats.com VCT benchmark leaderboard (https://llm-stats.com/benchmarks/vct); 3. An AI developer's official system card or model card (e.g., published by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, etc.); 4. A peer-reviewed or preprint academic publication (e.g., on arXiv) that reports VCT evaluation results.

Verification scores Stage 3

Quality: 95.0   Ambiguity: 90.0

Quality notes: This question addresses a critical 'red-line' in AI safety. The threshold of 70% is well-chosen, sitting between current state-of-the-art (61-65%) and the expert/risk threshold (80%). The rapid improvement in VCT scores (4x in a year) ensures the question is timely and uncertain.

Ambiguity notes: The question defines 'Frontier AI Model' using multiple regulatory and functional criteria. It specifies the exact benchmark version (VCT vs VCT-Text) and allows for different reporting conventions (single run vs. average). The list of acceptable sources is comprehensive, minimizing ambiguity.

Adversarial review NEEDS_REVISION Edge risk: MEDIUM

Assessment: NEEDS_REVISION   Edge case risk: MEDIUM

ASSESSMENT: NEEDS_REVISION REVIEW: The question addresses a genuinely important and uncertain topic, and the VCT benchmark, arXiv paper (2504.16137), and llm-stats.com leaderboard all exist as described. However, there are several substantive issues: 1. VCT-Text eligibility undermines the threshold calibration. The question allows resolution on either the full multimodal VCT (322 questions) or VCT-Text (101 text-only questions). The 70% threshold appears calibrated to the full VCT, where the best score is ~61%. However, VCT-Text scores are typically significantly higher than full VCT scores (the EA Forum notes "4-fold" improvement on VCT-Text over the study period). The Claude Opus 4.6 System Card reports a 48.3% score on the full multimodal VCT [a252f8], yet the question claims 65.4% "with max effort" — this higher number likely comes from VCT-Text or a different evaluation variant, not the full multimodal benchmark. Allowing VCT-Text means the effective gap to 70% may be much smaller than the background section implies, potentially making this near-trivially YES. 2. The 65.4% claim from the Opus 4.6 System Card may be inaccurate or misleading. When I queried the actual Claude Opus 4.6 System Card PDF, the VCT score reported was 0.483 (48.3%) on the "multiple select" variant [a252f8]. A second query specifically looking for the 65.4% figure found no such VCT score in the document [8cbd75]. The 65.4% may refer to a different benchmark or a different evaluation setup than what the question implies. This factual error in the background section would mislead forecasters about the current state of play. 3. Conflation of VCT and VCT-Text in the "Current Status" section. The background presents "~61–65%" as the range of current top scores, but this conflates full VCT scores (Grok-4.1 Thinking at 61.0%) with what may be VCT-Text or differently-configured evaluation scores (the 65.4% claim). This creates a misleading impression of the gap to the 70% threshold. 4. The llm-stats.com leaderboard is extremely sparse. Google snippets indicate it currently "ranks 1 AI models" on VCT, making it a very limited resolution source. The question relies heavily on this leaderboard but it may not track new models promptly. 5. The "quadrupled from early 2025" framing is misleading. The background states "VCT top scores roughly quadrupled from early 2025 (o3 at 43.8%) to late 2025 (Grok-4.1 Thinking at 61.0%)." Going from 43.8% to 61.0% is roughly a 39% increase, not quadrupling. The "quadrupled" claim likely refers to VCT-Text scores specifically, further conflating the two benchmarks. EVIDENCE: https://llm-stats.com/benchmarks/vct https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16137 https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/14e4fb01875d2a69f646fa5e574dea2b1c0ff7b5.pdf https://www.virologytest.ai/ https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/5EhJhMAdjncpSzzEL/llms-outperform-experts-on-challenging-biology-benchmarks https://data.x.ai/2025-11-17-grok-4-1-model-card.pdf SUGGESTION: 1. Either restrict resolution to only the full multimodal VCT (322 questions), or set separate thresholds for VCT and VCT-Text. The two benchmarks have substantially different difficulty levels and conflating them makes the threshold poorly calibrated. If VCT-Text is included, the threshold should be higher (e.g., 80%) to maintain genuine uncertainty. 2. Correct or remove the 65.4% claim. The Claude Opus 4.6 System Card appears to report 48.3% on the full multimodal VCT, not 65.4%. Either verify the source of this number and correctly attribute it to the specific benchmark version, or remove it. 3. Fix the "quadrupled" claim. Full VCT scores went from ~43.8% to ~61.0%, which is not quadrupling. If referencing VCT-Text progress, label it clearly. 4. Revise the current status section to clearly separate full VCT scores from VCT-Text scores, so forecasters can accurately assess the gap to the threshold on each version.

Edge cases 8 scenarios

OVERALL_RISK: MEDIUM ## Edge Case Analysis for VCT 70% Threshold Question ### Edge Case 1: VCT-Text (101 questions) vs Full Multimodal VCT (322 questions) — Score Divergence SCENARIO: A frontier AI model scores 72% on VCT-Text (101 text-only questions) but only 63% on the full multimodal VCT (322 questions). The question explicitly allows either version, but VCT-Text is a substantially smaller and easier subset — with only 101 questions, random variance is higher and the text-only subset omits the hardest visual/multimodal questions. Some resolvers may argue this doesn't reflect "true" VCT capability, while others note the criteria clearly permit either version. SEVERITY: HIGH — This is already partially happening. The question text notes that Claude Opus 4.6's 65.4% "max effort" score "may use the text-only subset (VCT-Text) rather than the full multimodal benchmark," indicating that labs are already selectively reporting on the easier subset. As models approach 70%, the divergence between VCT-Text and full VCT scores will likely widen, making this a near-certain source of disagreement. FIX: Add: "For the avoidance of doubt, a score above 70% on VCT-Text alone is sufficient for YES resolution, but the reporting source must explicitly identify the score as being on VCT-Text (101 questions) or the full multimodal VCT (322 questions). If a source reports a VCT score without specifying which version, it shall be presumed to be the full multimodal VCT unless context clearly indicates otherwise." --- ### Edge Case 2: Discrepancy Between Credible Sources on the Same Model SCENARIO: xAI's next-generation model is reported at 71.2% on VCT in xAI's official system card using their internal evaluation pipeline, but the llm-stats.com leaderboard independently evaluates the same model and reports 68.5%, and SecureBio's official website reports 69.1%. The system card used a particular prompting strategy, number of runs, or evaluation configuration that differs from the independent evaluations. Two reasonable resolvers disagree: one says the system card is a listed credible source reporting >70%, the other says the independent evaluations disprove the claim. SEVERITY: MEDIUM — This is plausible given that the Claude Opus 4.6 system card already reports substantially different scores depending on evaluation configuration (48.3% on full multimodal VCT using "multiple select" scoring vs. 65.4% "with max effort" [4592fc]). Different sources using different evaluation setups for the same model is already observed behavior. FIX: Add: "If multiple credible sources report conflicting VCT scores for the same model that straddle the 70% threshold, the question resolves YES if ANY single credible source from the enumerated list reports a score strictly above 70%, regardless of whether other credible sources report scores below 70% for the same model. However, if a credible source's reported score is later formally retracted or corrected by the publishing entity, the retracted score shall not count." --- ### Edge Case 3: Scoring Methodology Variant — "Multiple Select" vs Standard Multiple-Choice SCENARIO: A model achieves 73% accuracy on VCT when scored using standard multiple-choice methodology (pick the single best answer), but only 67% when scored using the "multiple select" variant described in Anthropic's system card, where models must select ALL correct answers and none of the incorrect ones to receive credit [4592fc]. A resolver argues that the "multiple select" format is the canonical VCT methodology, while another argues that the standard multiple-choice scoring is what's reported on most leaderboards and in the original paper. SEVERITY: MEDIUM — The existence of multiple scoring variants is confirmed by the Claude Opus 4.6 system card, which specifically references the "multiple select" variant [4592fc]. If the VCT benchmark can be scored in meaningfully different ways, a model could cross 70% under one methodology but not another. FIX: Add: "The score must be calculated using the standard VCT scoring methodology as defined in the original VCT paper (Götting et al., 2025; arXiv:2504.16137). If a source reports a score using an alternative scoring variant (e.g., 'multiple select' scoring), this is eligible only if the original VCT paper defines or endorses that variant as a standard evaluation methodology. The reporting source must clearly identify the scoring method used." --- ### Edge Case 4: Single-Run Luck vs Averaged Performance Near the Threshold SCENARIO: A lab reports a single evaluation run where their model scores 70.5% (227/322 correct) on VCT, but does not report averaged results. Given VCT's established convention that "some models are only evaluated in a single run," this is consistent with benchmark norms. However, if the model were evaluated across 10 runs, its average might be 68.2%, with the 70.5% run being an outlier. A resolver argues the single-run score is valid per the benchmark's own reporting conventions; another argues it's cherry-picked. SEVERITY: MEDIUM — The question text itself acknowledges that VCT uses both single-run and averaged reporting. With 322 questions, the standard error of a proportion around 70% is approximately ±2.6 percentage points (for a single run), meaning a model with true accuracy of 67-68% could plausibly score above 70% on a single lucky run. FIX: Add: "A single-run score is acceptable for resolution, consistent with the VCT benchmark's established reporting conventions. However, if the same source that reports a single-run score above 70% also reports an averaged score across multiple runs that falls below 70%, the averaged score shall take precedence for resolution purposes." --- ### Edge Case 5: Frontier Model Definition — Lab Not Explicitly Named SCENARIO: A Chinese AI lab (e.g., DeepSeek or Zhipu AI) or a well-funded startup (e.g., Cohere, AI21 Labs, or Inflection AI) releases a model that scores 74% on VCT. The lab is not among those explicitly named in criterion 3 ("including but not limited to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, Meta AI, or Mistral AI"). The model has ~70 billion parameters (meeting the "tens of billions" threshold) but its exact training compute is not publicly disclosed, making criterion 1 hard to verify. It hasn't been classified under the EU AI Act (criterion 2). A resolver argues the "including but not limited to" language and the model's obvious capability make it frontier; another argues there's no verifiable evidence it meets any of the three specific criteria. SEVERITY: MEDIUM — Chinese labs like DeepSeek are rapidly advancing and could plausibly produce top VCT scores. The frontier model definition's three prongs each have verification challenges: compute thresholds are rarely disclosed precisely, EU AI Act classifications lag behind model releases, and the named lab list is explicitly non-exhaustive but provides no clear standard for inclusion. FIX: Add: "For criterion 3, a lab qualifies as a 'major AI laboratory' if it has publicly released at least one general-purpose model that is competitive with models from the explicitly named labs on widely-used benchmarks (e.g., top-20 on LMSYS Chatbot Arena or equivalent) at the time of VCT evaluation. The model must be 'among the most capable' offered by that lab, meaning it is the lab's flagship or most advanced generally-available model at the time of evaluation." --- ### Edge Case 6: "Max Effort" or Agentic Scaffolding Inflating Scores SCENARIO: A lab reports that its model achieves 71.8% on VCT "with max effort," using extended thinking time (e.g., 100K+ output tokens per question), tool use, or multi-turn agentic scaffolding where the model iteratively refines its answers. The model scores only 58% with standard evaluation settings. A resolver argues the "max effort" score reflects the model's capability and is reported by a credible source; another argues this is not a standard evaluation of the model's accuracy as the VCT benchmark is a multiple-choice test meant to be answered directly. SEVERITY: HIGH — This pattern is already visible: Claude Opus 4.6 shows a 10+ percentage point gap between "low effort" (55.1%) and "max effort" (65.4%) configurations, as noted in the question text. As models approach 70%, labs have strong incentives to push "max effort" configurations that inflate scores. FIX: Add: "The score must be achieved by the AI model answering VCT questions directly as a multiple-choice benchmark, consistent with the standard VCT evaluation protocol. Scores achieved through multi-agent scaffolding, iterative refinement loops, or tool-augmented pipelines are not eligible unless the original VCT paper explicitly endorses such evaluation methods. Extended thinking or chain-of-thought within a single model inference pass is permitted." --- ### Edge Case 7: VCT Benchmark Revision Creates Ambiguity SCENARIO: SecureBio releases VCT v2 in August 2026 with 50 new questions and 30 removed questions (now 342 total), recalibrating difficulty. A model scores 72% on VCT v2 but its score on the original 322-question VCT v1 (using the same questions) would have been 69%. The question says it resolves based on the "last available version consistent with the original VCT methodology" if the benchmark is "substantially revised," but minor updates may not clearly qualify as "substantially revised." SEVERITY: LOW — SecureBio hasn't announced plans to revise VCT, but benchmark updates are common practice. The boundary between a "minor update" and "substantially revised" is genuinely ambiguous. FIX: Add: "A VCT version is considered 'consistent with the original VCT methodology' if it retains at least 80% of the original 322 questions and uses the same scoring methodology. If a new version adds or removes questions but retains this core, scores on the new version are eligible. If a new version removes more than 20% of original questions or fundamentally changes the scoring method, only scores on the original 322-question set (or VCT-Text 101-question subset) are eligible." --- ### Summary of Risk Assessment The overall risk is MEDIUM. The question is well-constructed with multiple safeguards, but several plausible scenarios create genuine ambiguity: 1. The VCT-Text vs. full multimodal distinction is the most likely source of dispute (HIGH severity), as labs are already selectively reporting on easier subsets. 2. The "max effort" evaluation configuration issue is already manifesting in current results (HIGH severity). 3. Source disagreements, scoring methodology variants, and single-run variance are all plausible MEDIUM-severity concerns. 4. The frontier model definition, while thorough, has verification gaps for labs not explicitly named. The question would benefit most from tightening the language around (a) which VCT version/variant counts, (b) what evaluation configuration is permissible, and (c) how to handle conflicting scores from different credible sources.

If it is ambiguous whether the reported score refers to the full multimodal VCT or VCT-Text, the score shall not count for resolution purposes. Evaluation methodology requirements: - The score must be achieved by the AI model answering VCT questions directly as a multiple-choice benchmark, consistent with the standard VCT evaluation protocol as defined in the original VCT paper. Extended thinking or chain-of-thought reasoning within a single model inference pass is permitted. - Scores achieved through multi-agent scaffolding, iterative multi-turn refinement loops, external tool-augmented pipelines, or other agentic setups that go beyond the standard VCT evaluation protocol are not eligible for resolution, unless the original VCT paper explicitly endorses such evaluation methods as part of the standard benchmark protocol. For the avoidance of doubt, a score labeled as achieved "with max effort" or similar language in a system card is eligible only if the evaluation setup is consistent with the standard VCT evaluation protocol (i.e., the model directly answering multiple-choice questions, potentially with extended thinking, but without multi-agent loops or external tool use). Scoring methodology clarification: The reported score may be from either a single evaluation run or an average of multiple runs, consistent with the VCT benchmark's established reporting conventions (the original paper uses both methods). However, if the same source that reports a single-run score above 70% also reports an averaged score across multiple runs that falls below 70%, the averaged score shall take precedence for resolution purposes. The score must represent the model's accuracy (proportion of correct answers) on the full 322-question VCT set, as calculated per the standard VCT methodology. Handling conflicting scores from different credible sources: If multiple credible sources from the enumerated list report conflicting VCT scores for the same model that straddle the 70% threshold, the question resolves Yes if ANY single credible source from the enumerated list reports a score strictly above 70% on the full multimodal VCT, regardless of whether other credible sources report scores below 70% for the same model. However, if a credible source's reported score is later formally retracted or corrected by the publishing entity before the resolution date, the retracted score shall not count. The question resolves No if no credible source reports a full multimodal VCT score above 70% for any frontier AI model by December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM UTC. If the VCT benchmark is substantially revised, replaced, or discontinued before December 31, 2026, the question resolves based on the last available version of the benchmark that is consistent with the original VCT methodology. A VCT version is considered "consistent with the original VCT methodology" if it retains at least 80% of the original 322 questions and uses the same scoring methodology. If no VCT evaluations are published during the resolution period, the question resolves No.

Forecast rationale

Synthesis and Rationale: This question asks whether any frontier AI model will score above 70% on the full multimodal VCT (322 questions) before the end of 2026. As of March 19, 2026, the best publicly reported score is 61.0% by Grok-4.1 Thinking, requiring a 9 percentage point improvement within ~9.3 months. Historical trajectory is the strongest YES signal. Performance jumped from 43.8% (o3, early 2025) to 61.0% (Grok-4.1 Thinking, late 2025) — a 17.2pp gain in ~7 months. Even at half this rate (~1.2pp/month), the 70% mark would be reached within the window. The introduction of "thinking" / test-time-compute architectures was the primary driver, and this paradigm continues to scale. Max effort configurations are already approaching mid-60s. The research mentions Claude Opus 4.6 achieving ~65.4% with max effort configurations, which is only 4.6pp below the threshold. If newer models (GPT-5.4, Grok-5, Gemini 3.x/4) show similar or larger gains in their max-effort variants, crossing 70% becomes quite plausible. Multiple shots on goal. With 9+ months remaining and expected releases from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, and others, there will be at least 3-5 major frontier model releases, each representing an independent opportunity to cross the threshold. GPT-5.4 has already launched but lacks official VCT evaluation scores. However, the multimodal gap is real. The full VCT includes ~221 image-based questions requiring interpretation of lab imagery (gel electrophoresis, microscopy, schematics). Text-only VCT-Text scores are substantially higher, suggesting the visual reasoning component is a genuine bottleneck. Newer models (Claude Opus 4.6 at 48.3%, Gemini 3 Pro at 56.2%) have not beaten Grok-4.1's 61% on the full multimodal set, suggesting potential plateauing. Safety guardrails could depress scores. As VCT explicitly measures dual-use virology knowledge, labs may implement refusal behaviors for the most dangerous (and complex) questions, artificially lowering scores. Market signal: Metaculus community prediction is at ~35-40% [8db03a], reflecting cautious outlook. I diverge upward because: (1) the historical improvement rate strongly supports crossing 70%, (2) max-effort scores already near 65%, and (3) multiple unreleased/unevaluated next-gen models provide many opportunities. Key Uncertainties: 1. Is the ~61% score a genuine plateau or evaluation lag? If newer models (GPT-5.4, upcoming releases) simply haven't been evaluated yet, the effective SOTA may already be higher. If the plateau is real, crossing 70% becomes harder. 2. Will multimodal visual reasoning improve substantially? This is the core bottleneck. If native multimodal training improves significantly in 2026, the gap closes quickly. If not, the visual questions remain a ceiling. 3. Will safety considerations prevent high scores from being reported? Labs facing pressure around biological uplift risk may choose not to report scores, or may train models to refuse dual-use questions. 4. Will evaluation methodology remain strict? The resolution criteria exclude agentic/multi-tool approaches. If the only scores above 70% come from non-qualifying evaluation setups, the question resolves NO. Balancing the strong historical trajectory and multiple upcoming model releases against the multimodal ceiling, market skepticism, and safety considerations, I estimate this at moderately above the market consensus.

Importance rationale

This question tracks a critical leading indicator of AI-enabled biosecurity risk. The Virology Capabilities Test (VCT) specifically measures an AI model's 'dual-use' capability to provide expert-level assistance in troubleshooting dangerous biological research. Achieving a 70% accuracy score would signal that AI models are approaching a 'red-line' threshold (typically cited at 80%) where they could materially lower the barriers to producing or weaponizing pathogens. This result would likely catalyze immediate policy shifts regarding model access controls, safety guardrails, and 'Know Your Customer' requirements for AI labs.
